"As these models get to a quite significant level of capability, I think the importance of really doing this, closely engaging with the safety institutes in the U.S., the U.K. and elsewhere in the world, will become more important." Altman called Astra "a significant step forward." Context: Altman flew to the G20 Innovation Ministerial on Wednesday to speak with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick before an audience of commerce and technology ministers, who over two days heard the U.S. pitch on lead the world in AI. During a fireside chat with Lutnick at the summit lunch, Altman said he sees OpenAI as "the pragmatic centrists … We think people need to be at the center of the economy and society and global decision-making, and that people should run the future, not AI." Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, talking with Lutnick at the summit breakfast, warned against fear-driven AI messaging. "The worst outcome," he told the foreign leader, "is that you don't take advantage of it [AI], that you are left behind." Huang's message prompted nods from many of the ministers in the room. Altman, speaking with Axios, called for a "realistic" and "accurate" approach. "I think doomerism — for the sake of trying to have more power, control or enforce a worldview — is really bad," he said. "I think blind optimism without an acknowledgment of the risks is also bad." Between the lines: OpenAI and Anthropic have faced criticism that their support for some AI regulation could advantage the leading labs and make it harder for smaller competitors to keep up. The big picture: Altman said he expected Congress to establish a "basic framework" for advanced AI after he first testified before lawmakers in 2023, but that hasn't happened. "I thought at that time that Congress was going to do something," Altman told Axios. He said the inaction is likely due to the pace of the technology: "People have a hard time knowing how to regulate the right things and not slow down innovation," adding that "it appears to be very hard to get Congress to do big things." What's next: Expect OpenAI to continue releasing its models as nations grapple with safety questions. "Take our word for it that we have much, much, much more capable models coming soon, and try to think about what all the impacts of that on society could be and then need to get that right," Altman said.

item.title: EU tech chief: AI guardrails inevitable for U.S.
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.55
CHAPEL HILL, N.C. — The Trump administration used this week's G20 innovation summit to draw a bright line between U.S. and European approaches to AI regulation. The bloc's top tech official says the U.S. is ending up with many of the same guardrails anyway. Why it matters: The U.S. is urging countries to avoid Europe's sweeping approach to AI regulation, but the fight is shifting to which guardrails advanced AI needs and how governments put them in place. What they're saying: European Commission tech chief Henna Virkkunen told Axios that the two sides often end up addressing the same safety concerns, even if U.S. safeguards are starting to emerge through state laws and court cases rather than something broad like the EU AI Act. "We see when it comes to technologies that in the USA the culture is different. So often it's coming via court cases, but often very similar things anyway, very similar concerns." "I don't see that this is so like black and white," Virkkunen said. ChatGPT is officially facing strict rules under the Digital Services Act, for instance, and Virkkunen said it's important for the EU to simplify the bloc's rules and make the region "easier, simpler, faster" for businesses. The big picture: The U.S. hasn't adopted sweeping federal AI rules, but Washington is still shaping how companies develop and deploy advanced models through executive actions, voluntary frameworks, national security restrictions and other policy. Meanwhile, states are moving ahead with varying degrees of AI regulation, and product changes are being forced on companies through lawsuits. Zoom in: The EU is working on a framework for pre-deployment testing and trusted partner access, Virkkunen noted, another area where the EU is working through similar AI policy questions facing the U.S. "So in [the] European Union, we are also working for that blueprint, and we are continuing to discuss also under G7, especially with our partners, how we should work on this topic." The Trump administration has developed a voluntary framework for reviewing some advanced AI models before release, including potentially giving government officials access for up to 30 days. The White House does not plan to publicly release this framework. OpenAI's Sam Altman confirmed this week to Axios that the administration reviewed its Astra model and noted the process is voluntary: "But we of course did it." Industry leaders at the G20 innovation summit knocked the EU approach to regulation in remarks before Virkkunen as well as representatives from Germany, France and Italy. In response to White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios' question about what foreign governments should and should not do, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said an approach that's "relatively free of regulation" is the way to go. It's "pretty straightforward," Musk said. "You have to have an environment that's relatively free of regulation, meaning that new things must be default legal as opposed to default illegal." "In the EU, for example, we find that the regulation level is extraordinarily high, and things are generally default illegal, and this inhibits progress with new technologies. It slows it down." The bottom line: As AI has grown more powerful, Washington has increasingly gotten involved with model releases.

item.title: U.S. military reviewing deadly strike on Iranian wedding
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.30
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) is conducting an internal review of a civilian casualty incident at a wedding during the strikes in Iran last Tuesday, U.S. officials say. Why it matters: While it still hasn't been confirmed that the incident was caused by the U.S. strike , it is one of the more significant civilian casualty incidents since the war began six months ago. The most significant civilian casualty incident happened on the first day of the war when a U.S. strike hit a school, killing 150 people, most of them children. The U.S. military investigation into that incident is expected to be finalized soon, according to a U.S. official. Driving the news: According to the Iranian Red Crescent, a humanitarian network, five people were killed and 67 wounded in the blast that hit the home where the wedding was happening. Iranian officials accused the U.S. of striking the building and killing civilians. On Wednesday, CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper ordered an internal review of the strike, U.S. officials said. "We're aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media, and we are looking into them. The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC," CENTCOM spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said. What they're saying: "We're investigating it because obviously we care," Vice President JD Vance said Thursday during a White House press briefing. "We want to know, and if we do make mistakes, again, this is a big difference between us and Iran. When our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them. So we're investigating it very fully." Behind the scenes: U.S. officials said the strike in the area targeted a communication tower used for both civilian and military communications. As part of the preliminary investigation, CENTCOM is reviewing footage from drones that monitored the area during the strike and the procedures used to identify the target, U.S. officials said. A U.S. official said that in addition to checking whether munitions fired by the U.S. hit the wedding, the investigation will also look at the possibility that an errant Iranian munition fell near the home.

item.title: Alaska seeks oil revival while grappling with a warming future
item.description:
Source: Axios Score: 3.03
EXIT GLACIER, Alaska — America's 49th state is a study in contrasts: Rapidly melting glaciers like this one attract tourists, while the oil industry underpinning its economy is getting a fresh boost from Washington after decades of decline. Why it matters: Few places put the causes and consequences of global warming in such proximity, making Alaska a vivid window into the world's reliance on fossil fuels as climate impacts mount. Driving the news: "Alaska is a powerhouse," Energy Secretary Chris Wright said last week in Anchorage at the state oil and gas trade group's annual conference, according to Alaska News Source. "I think you could have an incredible several years, several decades coming with just some common sense policies to set Alaskans free." State of play: Alaska has emerged as perhaps the Trump administration's biggest geographic focus for expanding U.S. oil and gas development, with the government pushing new leasing , easier permitting , Arctic drilling and a massive natural gas pipeline. A major new North Slope oil field started producing in May, and another is expected to begin producing in 2029 . Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) told Axios this moment is a "second wind" for the state's oil industry. The big picture: No offense to Texas, but everything is actually bigger in Alaska. It's more than double the size of Texas and has more coastline than all other states combined. It ranks near the top for both proven oil and gas reserves in the nation, and it has the largest icefield wholly contained in the U.S., the Harding Icefield, which feeds Exit Glacier. Reality check: Alaska's heyday as a top oil powerhouse is likely behind it. Its oil production has been declining since the late 1980s, and projects underway aren't expected to restore anything close to that. Friction point: Some of Washington's efforts are facing hurdles. The Interior Department's June lease sale in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, a vast wilderness home to polar bears, caribou and hundreds of bird species, generated little industry interest . A separate sale for new drilling in Cook Inlet near Anchorage received zero bids. An Interior Department spokesperson described the wildlife refuge auction as "a success for this frontier area," and pointed to a record-breaking March lease sale elsewhere in Alaska's North Slope. Zoom in: The roughly $50 billion effort to pipe natural gas 800 miles from the North Slope to the Kenai Peninsula for export to Asian markets is struggling to move forward. Wright called it his "number one" energy infrastructure priority earlier this year. But last week, he said: "I'm disappointed that I'm sitting here right now and we're not talking about shovels in the ground," Alaska News reported. Jason Bordoff, founding director of Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy, who recently visited Alaska's northernmost regions, called the economics of the project "terrible." Inside the room: Or more aptly: next to the glacier. Signs along the hiking trail at Exit Glacier tell visitors how much this glacier has retreated dating back to the late 1880s; the most recent sign is from 2010. Its retreat has accelerated in recent decades due to human-caused warming, according to Albin Wells, who researches the topic at the University of Zurich. The seven glaciers near the ski town of Girdwood are all likely to vanish or be vastly reduced within 75 years, Wells said. One of our guides near Girdwood, describing how dramatically the glaciers had changed during his lifetime, said he avoids the term "climate change" because of its polarizing politics. Axios' Amy Harder, on Aug. 16, standing at the most recent sign showing where the Exit Glacier, pictured in the foreground, reached in 2010. Photo courtesy of Amy Harder/Axios Between the lines: The changes go far beyond glaciers: Thawing permafrost and disappearing sea ice are destabilizing land and accelerating erosion along parts of Alaska's coast. Follow the money: One of the nation's fastest-warming states remains deeply reliant on oil and gas. Decades of oil wealth helped build the Alaska Permanent Fund, which now provides more unrestricted state revenue than current oil and gas revenues do — as well as an annual dividend for residents. What we're watching: With energy security demanding attention amid the ongoing Iran war, climate change may be on the back burner, Bordoff said, "but it is going to come back in a nonlinear way because of the impacts we're seeing." Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: Plastic Is Poisoning the Earth—So This Designer Made a Backpacking Kit Without It
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.98
Transcript My name’s Tom Bonamici, I’m an assistant professor of product design at the University of Oregon , and I teach in general product design for undergraduates and also our master’s program in sports product design. So, my research is about lightweight backcountry travel, and I am particularly interested in backpacking, been doing it since I was a kid, and I’m also really interested as an Oregonian in sustainability issues. As we all know, backpacking is just rife with synthetic materials, and they’re really awesome. They’re super lightweight and waterproof and strong and badass, and they’re also made out of petrochemicals, which, you know, on the in end is a problem, on the out end it’s a problem. I was just curious to explore academically what it would mean to use a full backpacking kit without any petrochemicals at all, not to say that everyone should, but just to explore what compromises we’d make if we did that. And going in, I kind of anticipated it was going to be heavier, it was going to not perform as well, it might be weaker, but how cool to make a collection that could actually completely compost. I thought that would just be an interesting experiment and exploration. I think to start with, we can start with the backpack because we’re backpacking, and that’s one of the more more fun things to talk about. Generally throughout this collection, certainly with this backpack, I was using pretty normal ultralight backpacking designs and just adapting materials to be completely petrochemical free. So, this is a really kind of standard issue frameless lightweight backpacking pack. There’s no suspension at all. The sleeping pad forms the back panel and adds some rigidity when it’s all packed together. You know, we’ve got the normal big side pockets, the big back pocket, thick shoulder straps. I keep my pack light enough that I don’t typically use a waist strap, but I could certainly have added one. But the materials are what makes this compostable. So, I used a Ventile material. It’s basically a super strong, densely woven cotton material, and this one especially is ripstop. Same thing for the side pockets, it’s a Ventile, but a much lighter weight version. We’ve got cotton cord forming the drawstring in those side pockets and aluminum toggles with a metal spring, so that’s all plastic free. The back pocket is a stretch 100 percent Merino jersey, and we’ve got some more metal hardware holding that in place, another metal hook for the top closure. And the shoulder straps are lined with that same Merino jersey, Ventile on the outside, cotton webbing, and then I used a thick Merino felt as the padding for that back strap. And it’s a little on the stiff side. The more it gets used, the more it’s going to kind of conform. Felt is really good at that. But the challenge throughout this whole collection, and especially in something like a pack that needs to be really strong, is the thread. So, I used 100 percent cotton thread. This is kind of a super heavy-duty thread that is meant for sewing on buttons, for like a fancy suit coat. I ended up with a lot of formal wear overlaps with the materials I was using here. So, the thread I think is pretty strong, but it’s, you know, I can break it if I really yank on it, this very heavy-duty thread. And that’s not a great sign because with a synthetic, you know, typically backpacking packs are sewn with polyester thread, and I can’t break that, you know, like a Tex 80, Tex 100 thread. So, that’s a pretty heavy gauge. And this stuff I can totally break. So, I did adapt by, you know, sewing several times over some seams. If you sew too many times, you’re just going to over-perforate a fabric, and then it can tear like a check out of a checkbook. But we’ll just see how it goes. As as throughout the whole collection, it’s an experiment. But I’m quite excited about the pack. And again, I wasn’t getting weird with the design of it, just with the materials. For the sleeping bag, I did a sleeping quilt. This is the same quilt design that I’ve done in the past with synthetic materials, which is super light and super comfortable. I use my homemade quilt all the time. It’s the kind of usual idea where you have a somewhat tapered rectangle, and then it forms a footbox, and you can kind of tie up that footbox and cinch it at the bottom, and it works great. Instead of a zipper, although I could use a cotton taped, metal-toothed zipper, I just went ahead and used some little ties because I’ve done quilts with zippers in the footbox and I’ve also done quilts with just snaps across, and they both work just fine. This is for summer backpacking, so I don’t need like full Arctic enclosure. The shell material is a silk-cotton blend. This is meant for the lining material of a formal suit. So, again, one of those like formal wear overlaps with this collection. Cotton tape and cotton cord for the ties and the draw cord, and cotton thread. And then the material on the inside is a wool material. It’s called Lavalan, and it’s this puffy wool batting. Got a scrap here. That’s kind of very, very cleaned from how wool comes off the sheep, and then kind of spun and matted into this lighter weight and fluffy material. It’s really nice, it’s really warm. I used kind of a layer and a half. This is their almost heaviest weight and then I used a little bit more very lightweight quilt batting in there that was Merino quilt batting. This material is nice because it’s a little bit more resilient than some of the synthetic options. It is heavier. This quilt weighs a little under 2 pounds, and my homemade quilt weighs a little over 1 pound. So, it’s definitely heavier, but I think it’s going to be plenty warm. The feeling of that fabric is so nice, and totally compostable as with everything else. So, I’m excited about this one. It’s quite bulky. That’s one of the downsides of using the wool instead of a synthetic and certainly a down. But it actually compresses pretty well once you jam it into the backpack, then it holds its form, and it’s actually kind of nice when you’re backpacking with a frameless pack to let the pack be full because then you don’t have any flopping or shifting. You might wonder why didn’t I use down? Because down is natural. When you make something with down, it needs to use downproof fabric. And typically what that is is a really, really lightweight synthetic material that’s calendared. So, calendering means that you’re taking that material and putting it through these heated rollers, and it’s almost melting it, but it’s just like smushing the the yarns of that woven textile together and closing up all of the gaps in between the warp and the weft fibers, bringing those gaps together. And that means that those little stems on the down puffs can’t work their way through and pop out like they do on your pillows at home. So, there are there are certainly natural materials that could fit the bill. In fact, the Ventile materials that I used are probably dense enough to be downproof or like functionally downproof. And there are some upholstery materials that are all cotton that are meant to be downproof. But they’re super heavy. So, it would end up tripling maybe the weight of the of the quilt and adding to the bulk, too. One of the hardest challenges in this whole collection was doing a sleeping pad . And this is the one, the sleeping pad and the shoes, man, are just, that’s that’s the tough one. So, this, I know this is just kind of a punishing sleeping pad. It’s super narrow. It is full length, and I’m 6’2″, so it’s nice to have, you know, enough length. And it’s so flat. It’s not providing any cushion at all. This is just a thermal break. But I wanted a sleeping pad that could function as a back panel in the backpack, and I needed that thermal break. If you’ve ever had a inflatable pad that deflated during the night, we all know that the ground is just so cold. Imade this with, again, some of that Ventile material, the super lightweight, and then a really thin layer of cork, which is not going to hold up long term, I know it, because it kind of crumbles. And that’s sandwiched in with some Melton wool. And Melton wool is a a very dense, almost felted thick woven wool material. Sometimes it’s made with a Merino, usually it’s more of a strong wool because it’s just felted in so much, you don’t need that softness and kind of luxurious hand of Merino. And then the whole thing is bound with cotton twill tape and, again, cotton thread. And then I sewed across in some channels just to try to hold that cork into place long term. This is something where, as I said, the collection is about exploring compromises, and it’s a big compromise in comfort. I was backpacking last weekend and just loving my big plush, Big Agnes pad, you know, just like sprawled out on that and sleeping like a baby. And this isn’t going to be like that. It’s also heavy. This is just under 2 pounds, which is pretty painful because that’s well over double a Z Lite. So, if I’m going to be less comfortable, I’d rather have a Z Lite. But, you know, that’s just straight petrochemicals, so it didn’t work for this project. So, again, the the collection was about exploring compromises, and I’ve definitely found some compromise area with the sleeping pad. And that’s okay. I did look into whether or not it’d be possible to do inflatable natural pads and also just like thicker, squishier materials, you know, wool felt. I looked into kapok, which is this kind of tree seed pod husk material that was used for insulation and also for life jacket flotation before petrochemicals. It’s not as good as foam for a life jacket, so don’t get any ideas. And all this is possible. Like with natural latex rubber, it would theoretically be possible to make an inflatable pad, but roughly running the numbers, it would be much, much heavier than this, like 5 to 8 pounds for just the pad. They were available, you know, you look in old Abercrombie & Fitch catalogs from the early 1900s, and they had inflatable pads, and they weighed 10 to 15 pounds. So, you know, if you’re horse packing, maybe that’s a good option, but for the purpose of this project, again, I was trying to keep everything as light as possible. For trekking poles, I knew I wanted to use trekking poles, and I need them for my 40-year-old knees, and also to set up the tarp. And I looked into making them out of aluminum because metal was allowed in the confines of this project, but to make them extendable, adjustable, I think it could be done. You know, if I were a really amazing machinist, I’m sure I could make all those parts out of aluminum and have it be fine. I’m not an amazing machinist, and I didn’t want to use those plastic adjusters, which are so great and so good at what they do, but again, for the confines of this project, I wanted to keep it original. So, I ended up using Calcutta bamboo. And this is a species of bamboo that’s insanely strong. It’s still used for ski poles and for fishing gaffs, that’s the like big hook that you use to yank that 200-pound tuna in the boat. It’s way stronger in flexion than aluminum, which is pretty sweet, and not too heavy at all. It has a really thick wall. So, this is a little chunk of it, and it’s got this thicker, denser wall, and it’s just a lot tougher than normal bamboo. And then in Slovenia, of all places, I found a ski pole DIY supply house. With the tariffs, I paid a phenomenal amount of money to get these ferrules, which are meant to be used with bamboo poles. So, these are all aluminum with a carbide tip, just like a normal trekking pole. So, we’ve got a really durable way to hit the ground. I used a suede grip. I made a wrist strap, adjustable with an aluminum buckle, Merino wool lining, Ventile outer shell. And then I even found some I put in a brass threaded insert in the top of the pole and a really nice bolt to hold the whole thing in place. So, it’s super comfortable, it’s super strong, I think stronger than my carbon fiber poles, which I’ve broken, just crossing a river and I don’t think these are going to have that issue at all. And then in order to avoid, you know, I didn’t want this project to look too hippy-dippy or Ren Faire or like, you know, Civil War reenactor or anything, so while the bamboo is beautiful naturally, I just coated the whole thing in some ink, some Sumi calligraphy ink. I had that for woodworking marking, and it applied beautifully. I had to just sand the outside of the bamboo to remove that natural waxy finish, and then the ink went on, and it’s staying on, and it doesn’t rub off or anything. So, these poles I think are going to be maybe the the strongest part of this collection, like physically strongest. I think a lot of the textiles have to be a little bit weaker, mostly because of using a natural thread, but these poles are going to be stronger than the aluminum or carbon fiber equivalents that are at REI. I’d say the only bummer or compromise about these is that they’re not height adjustable. No problem to just make them appropriate for my height for use, but I wouldn’t then be able to adjust it even taller to use with a a tent, for instance. And it’s possible to lash two poles together, but it’s a lot easier with like a Voile strap, or something, you know, synthetic. So, it’s it’s just interesting how the the confines of this project, the rules of the project, just put a lot of constraints on the decision making all throughout. For the tent or shelter, I did a tarp, and I usually sleep under a tarp when I’m backpacking, and they work great. I live in the West, and am blessed to have pretty predictable stretches of good weather and fewer bugs. For the situation we get to backpack in out West, it’s nice to not need to worry about the bugs so much. So, I did this very lightweight tarp design. Again, it’s very similar to tarps that I’ve made in the past. So, it’s basically a 9-foot long tarp, and it’s, you know, catenary-cut curves so that the tension is really even on the seams and on the sides, and tensioning lines, and I use trekking poles to set it up. The difference about this tarp, being petrochemical free, is that it’s made out of oiled silk. And this is a really unusual material nowadays. I found a lot of references to it in literature from over 100 years ago, but almost nothing since then. And that’s probably because synthetics are a lot stronger and a lot more predictably waterproof, and that’s okay. But given the confines of the project, I needed to find something lightweight and waterproof enough. So, this is waterproof enough. I haven’t done a hydrostatic head test on it, but I can fill up a embroidery frame with this material on it with water, and it doesn’t drip through even over 24 hours. And, you know, with a rough garden hose test, it’s managed to just kind of bead that water off really, really nicely. What is oiled silk? It is a silk taffeta, so it’s a really, really lightweight almost a ballgown type material, and then I soak it in a blend of linseed oil and natural turpentine. Turpentine is basically distilled pine tar or pine sap. You distill it like you would distill whiskey and you end up with turpentine. That’s the same stuff that artists use to cut their paints. And I use the turpentine to cut down the linseed oil so that it can flow through the fabric more easily and that I can wring it out more easily. If there’s too much in there, it’ll end up getting really sticky and like, yeah, too too sticky and gross. Ugh. But with with the right blend and the right amount of kind of wringing out and careful drying, I can get it to where it’s this really nice, predictable hand and waterproof enough without being too sticky. You can see that it’s yellowed, and some of my older samples have yellowed a lot more. This is a kind of interesting anecdote because what we read about as oilskins, that’s what fishermen wore, like in Captains Courageous or something, you know, those books from 150 years ago about people fishing in the North Sea, they’re all wearing oilskins. Oilskins are basically a canvas smock soaked in linseed oil. And as it ages and oxidizes, it turns yellow, and that’s why Paddington Bear and, you know, all those traditional raincoats are yellow, because it’s kind of an inheritance from the oilskin. Kind of an interesting detail. When I first made this tarp, it was this like just ivory off-white, and that was 2 months, 3 months ago, and it’s already turned started to turn yellow, and the older it gets, the more yellow it’s going to get. So, I did use some reinforcements at important areas, like the the main seam attachment point of the tarp. I used a kind of a Ventile patch in some areas and just a self-fabric patch in other areas. I used cotton tape to reinforce those attachment points. I did a lot of kind of repetitive straight stitching, but again, not too close together, so it doesn’t get perforated and just rip out. We’ll see how this holds up. This is not nearly as strong as synthetics, but this is one where I’m pleased to say it’s actually lighter weight. I used, due to the width of the fabric, this tarp is even a little bit smaller than the one I usually use, that’s sil- sil-coated polyester. And this is this is 440 grams, so that’s just under a pound. It’s like about, I don’t know, 14 ounces or something, the the weights that we expect out of ultralight shelters.

item.title: Dale ‘Grey Beard’ Sanders Fell 71 Times and Quit Once Before Setting His Latest Appalachian Trail Record
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.64
Dale "Grey Beard" Sanders on his 2026 thru-hike of the Appalachian Trail. (Photo: Courtesy of Dale Sanders) Dale ‘Grey Beard’ Sanders, 91, was about two tenths of a mile from the top of Mount Katahdin when he took a hard fall. Just steps away from becoming the oldest person to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail in a calendar year, he hit the ground for the 71st time on his 12-month journey. Two days later, he told Backpacker, “I’m a little sore on both legs from that, but it’s simply just small contusions and no bones or anything is broken or damaged.” Out of the 71 falls that Sanders took, the vast majority were “soft falls,” which meant that he quickly got up, brushed himself off and kept walking without pain. But seven of those falls left him in a daze. “I laid down on the ground, and I didn’t care who saw me,” he said. “I was all moaning and groaning for a while.” Sanders says his balance was noticeably worse than in 2017, when he had set a previous Appalachian Trail age record by hiking the trail at 82. “When you get older, it seems that our body starts to deteriorate, and we simply do not physically have the abilities that we had when we were under 40 and below,” Sanders said. “The older you get past say 50 or 60, it starts going down.” In order to claim the age record for a thru-hike of the Appalachian Trail, hikers have to tackle the whole 2,200-mile trail within a 12-month period. They must also hike past every white blaze (“in some cases, crawl by,” said Sanders, alluding to his experience on Mount Katahdin). Neither the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC) nor Guinness currently differentiate between supported, self-supported, and unsupported age records on the trail. Prior to Sanders’ record, M.J. ‘Nimblewill’ Eberhart last claimed the title at age 83 in 2021, taking the record from Sanders. To Sanders’s knowledge, no other 90-year-old has attempted to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail. Compared to his 2017 thru-hike, Sanders had to significantly dial down his mileage. As an 82 year old, he hiked many 20-mile days, but averaged closer to 11 miles per day this year. It was also tough on his mind, which occasionally wavered at the sight of a steep climb. While he trained for six months before setting out on his latest thru-hike, he still underestimated the difficulty of the Appalachian Trail. “I realized quickly that my ceiling of physical ability was much lower than it was at 82 years old,” he said. Most AT thru-hikers blaze through the route, tackling it in four to six months. Sanders nearly took the entire 365 days to complete his trek, hiking for 200 of those days. On one occasion, he even quit the trail. He was in Maine when it happened: A hard fall 142 miles short of the northern terminus landed him in the hospital, where doctors checked for internal bleeding and ran tests to see why he was experiencing numbness in his left arm. One doctor suggested that it was time to hang up his hiking poles to head home and talk to his primary care physician and neurologist. “I didn’t want to go home because it was so close to the end,” he reflected. But after receiving a call about his mother-in-law’s death, his fate was decided: He was going home to Tennessee. After attending the funeral, resting, and scheduling new doctor’s appointments, his neurologist determined that Sanders had experienced bleeding in his brain, but it wasn’t active and it appeared to be old. His numb arm was due to a pinched nerve. Both that doctor and his primary care provider cleared him to hike. Given the short window of time that Sanders had to finish the final stretch of trail, he knew it was unlikely that he’d finish before time ran out. But he decided he wanted to see Katahdin, even if it meant he’d only land the age record for a section hike instead of a thru-hike. With a bit of luck and sheer determination, Sanders ultimately made it to the northern terminus of the Appalachian Trail with 5 days to spare. When asked why he was so determined to get back on trail, Sanders explained that the record felt bigger than he was. “I hold several age records in several different venues, most of them hiking and paddling, and in each and every one of those, it seems that I’ve given people hope. [It’s when] people have hope that they have inspiration,” he said. “Hope is really important.”

item.title: Why Nepal floods should worry India
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 6.40
- Published Nepal's devastating floods have exposed a risk that does not stop at its borders. India and Nepal share the rivers that rise in the Himalayas, but the relationship between a flood in Nepal and a disaster in India is more complicated than a simple story of water flowing downstream, say experts. Some floods can race out of the mountains carrying enormous quantities of mud, rock and debris. Others may lose much of their force as they reach the plains, leaving behind a more conventional flood. And whether that water becomes a disaster in India depends not only on how much rain has fallen in Nepal, but also on rainfall, river levels, embankments, drainage and development on the Indian side. Nepal's floods are a warning for India - not simply because water flows south across the border, but because the two countries share a vast and increasingly volatile Himalayan river system. How many Nepal rivers flow into India? Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges. Three major systems dominate: the Kosi in the east, the Gandaki (Gandak in India) in the centre and the Karnali (Ghaghara in India) in the west, with the Mahakali (Sharda) along the western border. A dozen smaller rivers rising in the Siwaliks and Chure - including the Bagmati, Kamala, Rapti and Babai - are less famous but can produce faster, more unpredictable floods because their catchments are small and steep. Seven to nine major rivers flow from Nepal into the Indian plains, and they are responsible for flooding in India, according to Manish Shrestha, a hydrologist at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD). India's Central Water Commission identifies the Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati and Ghaghara as some of the main transboundary rivers. Which Indian states are most exposed? Bihar is by far the most exposed Indian state, with roughly three-quarters of north Bihar officially classified as flood-prone. Almost all the major rivers that flood the state originate in Nepal, with the Kosi - the "sorrow of Bihar" - the most notorious, followed by the Gandak, Bagmati and Kamala. But the risk extends beyond Bihar. Eastern Uttar Pradesh is vulnerable to the Ghaghara, Rapti and Gandak rivers. Districts like Gorakhpur, Bahraich, Lakhimpur Kheri and Shravasti are regularly affected. Uttarakhand state shares the Mahakali-Sharda rivers. North Bengal receives the Mechi and Mahananda. "Bihar dominates in scale. Uttar Pradesh is second and often under-reported," says Pradeep Man Dangol, hydrologist at ICIMOD. Bihar bears the greatest burden, but Uttar Pradesh is a significant and often overlooked part of the risk. When Nepal floods, what determines India's fate? Think of it as a three-part chain, say hydrologists. First, the rain: where it falls and how heavily. Flood peaks reaching India are often generated not in the high Himalayas but lower down, in the Siwaliks, Chure and Terai, where intense monsoon rain can fall on steep, small catchments. Second, the river. Nepal's rivers cross a sharp break in slope at the mountain front, drop their sediment, and spread across the plains as braided, shifting channels. Third, when the water meets India. How bad the flooding becomes depends on what the water encounters - the volume of rain on the Indian side, how full the Ganges is, embankments and barrages, and blocked drainage from roads, railways and settlements on the floodplain. So the peak flow at the border is largely determined by rainfall in Nepal. The severity of flooding depends at least as much on conditions in India. The 2008 Kosi disaster shows why: the river was carrying far less water than the embankment was designed to handle. The catastrophe was caused by the embankment failing, not by an exceptional flood. So how much depends on Nepal v India? "For the peak flow arriving at the border, largely Nepal's rainfall; for the severity of flooding once it arrives, at least as much on Indian conditions," says Saswata Sanyal, ICIMOD's intervention manager for disaster risk reduction. How Nepal's rain becomes India's flood risk The 2008 Kosi disaster is a powerful illustration. Nearly 400 people died in Bihar after the Kosi breached an embankment in Nepal. But, remarkably, it was not an extraordinary high-flow event on the river. According to Rajiv Sinha, a professor of earth sciences at Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Kanpur, the flow was only about a tenth of the river's carrying capacity. The catastrophe was caused by a breach in an embankment built decades earlier and inadequately maintained. "The embankments constructed in the 1950s and 1960s had not been properly maintained. They had become eroded and eventually developed a weak point. The river breached its embankment through these vulnerable points and entered parts of India that had not seen flooding for perhaps 100 years," says Sinha. The failure, in other words, was "structural, not hydrological", adds Sanyal. How much warning can India get from Nepal? For ordinary monsoon floods, India may have "roughly 12 hours to two days of warning", according to Sanyal, depending on how quickly the water travels downstream. Water can take about a day to reach the Bihar plains from the Nepal mountain front along the Kosi and Gandak, and somewhat longer along the Ghaghara. Flash floods from the Chure rivers can arrive within hours. A landslide-dam burst or debris flow can be even faster - in the current floods, the peak surge from Rasuwa reached Triveni, near the Indian border, in about seven-and-a-half hours. India and Nepal do share real-time rainfall and river-level data from a network of stations. Nepal's Department of Hydrology and Meteorology feeds rainfall and river levels to India's Central Water Commission, which uses them for flood forecasts. But important gaps remain, says Sanyal. They include too few real-time monitoring stations in the fastest-flowing Chure catchments. There's also no single shared forecasting model between the two countries; and limited routine sharing on embankment conditions, river-channel changes and sediment. And then there's, crucially, the last mile. A warning reaching a district office is not the same as reaching a family in danger. For these transboundary rivers, Sinha says, "cooperation on information sharing and early-warning systems is extremely important. We need rapid continuous monitoring of glacial lakes, their outflows and how they are changing over time". What is the biggest misconception around Nepal and floods in India? A common misconception is that Nepal "releases" water into India, say scientists. Nepal has almost no large reservoirs capable of doing this: its main storage dam, Kulekhani, holds less than a tenth of a cubic kilometre, "so there's nothing to release", says Sanyal. The Kosi and Gandak barrages are operated by India. When floodwater reaches the border, it is overwhelmingly because rain has fallen upstream - not because Nepal has opened a gate. But there is an important truth behind the claim: much of the water that floods north Bihar and eastern UP has fallen as rain in Nepal, so Nepal's rainfall largely determines the timing and size of flood peaks reaching India. Nepal supplies around 40% of the average annual flow of the Ganges - and a much larger share in the dry season - making its hydrology critical to India. "What is too simplistic is treating that as a story of cause and blame. Rain is not a decision," says Sanyal. Whether a given flow becomes a disaster depends on conditions in India as much as in Nepal the Ganges' level, Indian rainfall, embankment integrity, drainage and sediment. "And the effects run both ways: embankments and barrages built for India's protection have raised water levels and caused backwater flooding in Nepal's Terai, which is Nepal's long-standing concern,' says Sanyal. Nepal and India share one river system, with one country upstream and the other downstream. The answer is therefore not blame, but better shared data, forecasting and river management. So what should worry India the most? "India should be worried. but not necessarily because of the Kosi river in Nepal," says Rajiv Sinha. In other words, experts say, the real warning is about what is happening in the Himalayas - and what happens when water, rock, ice and enormous quantities of sediment suddenly combine. Sinha says the latest Nepal disaster resembles a series of catastrophic events that India has experienced in recent years, including the 2021 Chamoli disaster and the 2025 Dharali disaster in Uttarakhand. The Nepal event, he says, was "perhaps five to 10 times larger". "The fundamental point is that these are not normal hydrological floods," Sinha says. A conventional flood is largely water. But when water from intense rain, melting ice or a sudden discharge mixes with huge quantities of sediment, the result can become a thick, high-energy slurry capable of destroying almost everything in its path. That was the lesson of the Chamoli disaster in 2021, when a large chunk of a Himalayan glacier collapsed in the valley of Chamoli in northern India, sending a cascade of debris and water downstream that killed 200 people and damaged hydropower infrastructure. It was also evident at Dharali in Uttarakhand in 2025, after heavy rains triggered a flash flood and the flow of debris buried parts of a village under metres of material. And then there's climate change. Extreme rainfall is intensifying: the region is warming faster than the global average, a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, and the monsoon is delivering more rain in fewer, heavier bursts, say experts. High-mountain hazards are also growing. As permafrost degrades, glacial lake outbursts and rock-ice avalanches are expected to increase, producing faster, debris-laden floods that are harder to forecast. And more extreme events mean more landslides and sediment in rivers, raising riverbeds and reducing channel capacity on both sides of the border. They are manifestations of the same broad Himalayan hazard system. And India's exposure is considerable.

item.title: How could US-Iran conflict end? Three experts give their views
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 5.34
- Published The prospect of an imminent agreement to end the conflict between the US and Iran again seems unlikely, with the warring sides exchanging strikes and uncompromising rhetoric. The attacks come days after the US said it was moving into a new phase - a sweeping economic blockade against Iran and countries which trade with it. The US aim was to force Iran to negotiate and to stop its attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The key commercial shipping route has been effectively closed since the US and Israel started the conflict in February. A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) the two sides signed in June and meant to result in a permanent ceasefire and a deal within 60 days has expired. As the conflict enters its seventh month, we asked three experts for their thoughts on how it may play out. US hopes military and economic pressure will weaken Iran's negotiating power Jason Campbell, Senior Fellow at the Middle East Institute, Washington DC The problem is we still do not know definitively what the US strategic objectives are in Iran. The White House is persistently re-evaluating what it is willing to live with from a political standpoint. It was assumed the military component would be enough for a quick victory and that has not had the desired effect. What we are seeing is different levers - both military and economic - that the US is trying to pull at. Right now, the administration appears satisfied with some form of stasis. I think they are satisfied with maintaining the blockade and with allowing some periodic targeting against Iran's capability to upset the shipping lane in the strait. US officials are hopeful that the new sanctions will be enough to compel the Iranian regime to come to the negotiating table in a weaker position. US forces have seemingly been able to facilitate a sufficient trickle through the Strait of Hormuz in recent days to avert an oil-price shock or a global economic collapse. But those were not the US objectives when starting the war. My sense is that Iran is likely to demand a high price to get to a resolution, which is likely to remain politically untenable for the Trump administration. Iran will wait for US concessions Dr Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi, Associate Fellow with Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme, London I do not think the latest strikes really alter Iranian calculations on the war. I think Tehran is preparing for an increased squeeze on its economy, and a continuation of the on and off attacks which we have seen over the past couple of months. Their intent will be to respond to these attacks in a proportionate manner in order not to spiral a larger conflict. On the economic side, obviously this is likely to hurt the Iranian economy which has already been affected by the war and has had underlying structural issues anyway, as we know from the December and January demonstrations in Iran. But I do not feel like there is the sense from the Iranian side that the economic squeeze is going to alter the Iranian calculation any time soon, including on any negotiations. That does not mean Iran is not looking for an off ramp, but I think what we are seeing is that it is waiting for the US to go back to the MoU, or to at least offer some sort of concession. Tehran does not want to cave in to US pressure or alter its own approach in response to sanctions or additional attacks. US knows what to do - go back to the ceasefire deal Nicholas Hopton, Distinguished Fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute think tank in London and former UK ambassador to Iran The latest spike in military action is not going to produce Iran's capitulation - it is just the latest twist. Economic pressure is also unlikely to work because China, Russia and many other countries which trade with Iran are not going to support unilateral US sanctions. Iran can continue to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz - they have a thumb on the jugular of the global economy. What is the White House's exit strategy? Well, the US has already found it. If Trump was able to put a sustained effort into negotiating the deal outlined in June's MoU, that is the off-ramp. Not only would a deal give the US a kind of victory because it would weaken the hardliners in the Islamic Republic, but also reassure everyone that Iran is not going to get a nuclear weapon. There is a silver bullet in the MoU which is the lifting of all US sanctions on Iran. What lifting those sanctions would do over time is weaken Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC). Economic engagement between the outside world and Iran in a new way would gradually force radical political and social change - so you end up with an Islamic regime, but of a very different nature. Of course, that would not be straightforward to achieve, because of extensive IRGC penetration of the Iranian economy. But it should work, if given enough time and if the US and its partners exercised strategic patience which, sadly, is in short supply at this point. For the time being, I think we're going to carry on with a messy, inconclusive situation that is bad for everyone.

item.title: 'Layer upon layer of miracles' to find tunnel survivors, Nepal rescue adviser tells BBC
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 5.13
- Published A tunnelling expert involved in the rescue operation at a blocked Nepalese hydropower tunnel has described to the BBC how they managed to reach survivors. Arnold Dix has been advising Nepal's hydropower authorities on how to dig through the blocked tunnel to Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, which was one of several stations hit by last week's massive flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border. "It's like layer upon layer of miracles" that they found two men on Friday, he said, given the multiple challenges that they faced. The first hurdle was to locate the entrance to the tunnel, in a landscape rendered nearly unrecognisable by the flood that has so far killed 1,300 people. "I've never known a rescue operation where you had to look for an entrance of a tunnel that was previously up the hill, that was now underground. You can imagine the enormity of the avalanche, it completely buried the entrance," said Dix, who is the president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association. Using engineering techniques, old topographic maps, satellite imagery of the area after the disaster, video footage from helicopters and "anything else we could find on the surface of the mountain such as power poles", Dix and his team triangulated the likely position of the entrance and started digging. They found it - but the next challenge was to locate the survivors. "We knew they would be up ahead, but we didn't know where exactly. So you just have to start digging in the right direction. And you listen out if you can hear anybody," he said. Rescuers had to get through a tunnel blocked entirely by mud and rocks - some bigger than cars - and had to use explosives to clear the way, something they would "normally never do because of the risk of blowing up people [trapped in the tunnel] and blowing ourselves up," Dix said. He credited the Nepalese army for doing "a wonderful job" in managing the explosions with precision to ensure they would not destabilise the tunnel. At the same time, they discovered it was still full of water. Using excavators and pumping machines, Nepalese rescuers dug a series of trenches from the tunnel all the way to the river outside, so they could drain the water. Finally, they had to dig a passageway, "a tiny tunnel the size of a person", through the debris at the top of the tunnel. The advantage of this location "is that you can use the original tunnel's roof as your little tunnel's roof. Also, it mitigates risk of flooding," Dix explained. In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices. According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay". Shortly after that, they pulled out Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan, alive. But with dozens of people still thought to be trapped inside the tunnel, the work is far from over. Rescuers heading to 'Goldilocks zone' Dix estimated that they had dug about 60m from the entrance by now, and they would need to dig another 150m more to reach the hydropower station located deep inside the mountain. Rescuers are hoping that the debris from the flood did not reach the station, because if it did, "there would be all kinds of complications - anybody in the station could have been hit by rocks and mud or it could be flooded". The team on the ground are still facing significant dangers. "Up ahead, even now, we might run into water which would drown the people tunnelling," Dix said. "And we also have the risk of another flood outside happening, so water could come from behind. So there's the risk of facing water on both ends." But, buoyed by Friday's successful rescue, the team is now hopeful it will reach more survivors in time. "It's a big relief, that we are on the right track. And it gives us renewed energy that our thinking [on how to conduct the rescue] works... we have never done something like this before." Dix said they are now heading towards what he called the "Goldilocks zone" which would be "more friendly to life". This zone is at the uppermost level of the hydropower station where there is some space where survivors may be located. "We got two people out. If we were playing at a casino, some might say it's time to walk away, but we say game on, time to take on the house."

item.title: Volkswagen board approves plan to cut another 50,000 jobs
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 4.93
- Published The board of German car giant Volkswagen has approved a plan to cut another 50,000 jobs as part of the biggest restructuring in the group's almost nine-decade history. It brings the total number of roles the carmaker plans to shed by 2030 to 100,000, after announcing in March that it would cut 50,000 roles. The group - which includes Audi, Porsche, Skoda as well as the VW brand - is also considering the future of four of its German plants. The move is a "strong signal" for the future of the firm, which is "taking responsibility for our entire workforce", VW's chief executive Oliver Blume said in a statement on Thursday. Blume said in July that the firm was looking to make the additional cuts. Shares in the company were up by around 7% in Frankfurt on Friday morning. The Golf-maker has been hit by a drop in profits due to falling sales and fierce competition, especially from Chinese brands. The firm also said that by 2035 it would cut the number of models it produces by 50% and reduce the complexity of its offering by 75%. VW will also prioritise the "most compelling vehicles" and make more of each model, which will help lower costs, it said. A "fundamental adjustment of the global workforce capability is necessary" to safeguard the competitiveness of the company, which faces shifting demand and technological change. It added "a group-wide workforce adjustment of approximately 50,000 positions - including management roles - will be necessary." The company is also weighing options for operations in Emden, Zwickau, Hanover and Neckarsulm, where it has said production capacity exceeds demand. "Alternative uses for these plants are being assessed," it said. As of 2025, VW employed more than 660,000 people worldwide. Its brands also include Seat, Bentley and Lamborghini. Christianne Benner - the president of Europe's largest industrial union IG Metall and deputy chair of VW's Supervisory Board - said the carmaker had "fought hard for good solutions" to address a "crisis situation". VW's profits have fallen sharply in recent years, hit by falling sales in China, which was once one of its biggest markets. Sales have also fallen in the US, partly due to the impact of tariffs on car imports that were introduced by President Donald Trump's administration. Chinese carmakers have been expanding aggressively as they roll out new technologies while benefiting from lower production costs than their rivals. In recent years, firms such as BYD have seen their sales rise sharply in markets including the UK, European Union and South East Asia.

item.title: UN warns of 'supersized' El Niño as countries prepare for impact
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.97
- Published The world has entered a "danger zone of extreme weather" as the impacts of El Niño start to be felt globally, UN head António Guterres has warned. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has released the latest data on the natural weather phenomenon showing it could be the strongest for more than 70 years and last until at least February 2027. El Niño changes weather patterns around the world, pushing some regions into drought whilst others experience stronger typhoons and flooding. Forecasters also say El Niño will boost temperatures in some places, coming on top of rising heat globally from human-induced climate change. "El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," Guterres said. The BBC spoke with governments and scientists about the measures being taken globally to reduce the risk of deaths, displacement and environmental damage. Early warning systems have been strengthened and deployment of pre-emptive medical assistance, but the strength of this particular event has raised serious concerns particularly for vulnerable groups. The WMO - a UN agency - said it has undertaken a "major mobilisation" to try to circulate its forecasts of potential extreme weather events, linked to El Niño, to as many communities as possible. WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo warned: "El Niño has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world." El Niño is a natural weather phenomenon that develops in the Pacific Ocean and is linked to a change in wind patterns. It allows warm water to spread eastwards and releases heat into the atmosphere. Sea temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific have risen sharply in recent months - a clear sign of a strengthening El Niño. In the Pacific's key monitoring region, surface temperatures have been well over 2C above average in recent weeks, putting it on track to be declared a "very strong" event. But it is expected to surpass even that marker. Monthly sea surface temperatures could get close to 4C above average, forecasts suggest. This would make it the strongest El Niño since at least 1950, by potentially a large margin. Temperatures are even more exceptional below the surface of the Pacific - in places more than 8C above average. Above-normal sea temperatures are also expected in other parts of the world including the Indian Ocean, tropical Atlantic and around parts of the Australian coast. With its rich marine life, changes in ocean heat are of particular concern to Australia. It has been plagued by marine heatwaves in recent years - driven by climate change - leading to widespread coral bleaching and algae blooms, causing "unprecedented damage". El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it tends to bring the kind of extreme heat which also drives those disasters, Dr Alistair Hobday, chief researcher at Australia's science agency, told the BBC. This year, marine heatwave forecasts indicate the Great Barrier Reef will be spared the worst of the conditions, giving coral there more time to recover. "[But] Southern Australia is getting slammed. It had an algal bloom last year, it's got bird flu now, and it looks like marine heatwaves will be stronger there this summer," said Hobday. Last time a marine heatwave hit South Australia and Tasmania, there were starving penguins, fish kills, suffocating algae outbreaks, and jellyfish invasions. Australia has recently introduced early warning systems for marine crises - this gives time for financial relief for fisheries to be established, relocation of crucial species and increased coral monitoring. But this event is shaping up to be unprecedented - and Hobday admits he is quite worried. Reduced rainfall brings drought and trade disruption While the impacts on global weather are likely to be felt well into 2027, the WMO expects significant changes in rainfall patterns over the next few months. Drier-than-usual conditions are forecast across large areas of South East Asia, Central America and northern parts of South America, increasing the risk of droughts and wildfires. On Thursday, the number of vessels passing through the Panama Canal will be reduced by more than 10% in anticipation of lower rainfall. About 14,000 ships per year use the artificial waterway - as well as being a crucial route for global trade, it is also a key source of income for Panama, bringing in about $3bn (£2.2bn) a year. Indonesia is racing to contain wildfires that have burned more than 107,000 hectares of land nationwide this dry season. Like some other parts of South East Asia, it is facing a longer season this year. A resident in Central Kalimantan told BBC News Indonesia he had been experiencing wildfires "for more than a month". "The smoke has become quite thick. When we step outside, our eyes start to sting. The smell of the smoke is also quite strong," said Darwin Romy. Authorities have said they are deploying cloud-seeding aircraft to trigger rains to extinguish these fires, and its government has promised resources to contain the fire and arrested dozens over allegations of using it to clear land. Stronger typhoons and landslide risk Thousands of miles away, China is expecting seven typhoons to make landfall in this year alone – something the country's experts have said is linked to the effects of a super El Niño. In July alone, China experienced three typhoons - Bavi, Noul and Maysak - which left dozens dead. And in August, more than a million people were forced to evacuate their homes as Typhoon Dolphin hit – bringing heavy rains and strong winds. Similarly, wetter-than-average weather is expected in parts of eastern Africa, southern Brazil and the southern US, raising the chances of flooding. "We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies," said Prof Celeste Saulo, secretary general of the WMO. This is all happening on top of long-term human-caused warming, making the impacts potentially more intense. Some scientists believe climate change could even be making El Niño events stronger, but this is not yet certain. Peru is particularly vulnerable to El Niño, as its coastline borders the eastern Pacific. Parts of the country, along with Ecuador and parts of Brazil, have previously experienced increased rainfall, resulting in flash flooding and landslides, particularly in urban centres where the water is less able to drain away. Miguel Aréstegui, climate resilience lead at Practical Action, which helps countries prepare for extreme weather, said "we are significantly concerned, but that concern needs to translate into preparedness rather than alarm." He said Practical Action had been working with partners over recent years to make sure the public had better access to early warning systems, including sharing information on river levels, flood risks and weather forecasts. At the end of last month, the US announced it was deploying the vessel USNS Comfort to the Peruvian coast to provide additional medical assistance and technical equipment for when El Niño reaches its peak. However, Aréstegui said El Niño "does not arrive in a vacuum". There are bigger, structural issues that make these events worse and which take much longer to resolve such as "housing in exposed areas, fragile water and sanitation systems, and a weak healthcare system", he said.

item.title: Around 2,000 fall ill in Indonesia after eating free school meals
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.89
- Published Around 2,000 students and teachers across Indonesia have fallen ill with food poisoning over the past three days linked to the government's free school meals programme. In the latest case, 777 people became unwell after consuming the food at a high school in Rembang, Central Java, the institution's headteacher said. The meals were provided through a multibillion-dollar scheme that is one of President Prabowo Subianto's signature policies, aiming to improve nutrition for Indonesia's schoolchildren. But, as well as being the suspected source of a string of mass food poisonings, the programme has been dogged by allegations of corruption and criticism of its cost. A total of 752 students and 25 teachers experienced symptoms of food poisoning after eating meals provided through the Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG) programme at the high school in Lasem on Wednesday lunchtime. "They had diarrhoea and took turns using the toilet," headteacher Juhartutik told BBC News Indonesia. "There are 40 toilets in total, so they can't accommodate everyone." The school has since sent nearly 1,200 pupils and 95 members of staff home, while several were taken to hospital. Juhartutik said the government would cover any medical costs and that the local food distributor had come to the school to "take responsibility". The suspected outbreak came after 730 people fell ill after consuming MBG meals at an Islamic boarding school in Sidoarjo, East Java, on Tuesday, a local health official said. Reni said their child felt dizzy and nauseous before developing stomach problems after eating the meal. Some of those affected required hospital treatment, with some students being transported in wheelchairs because they were too weak to stand. Hundreds of others have been affected by suspected cases of food poisoning linked to the free school meals this week, including hundreds across several schools in Tana Toraja, South Sulawesi. Improper storage or poorly prepared food are often to blame for cases of food poisoning, in which the body rejects the contaminated food. Parents and teachers have told reporters of slimy chicken, as well as food that appeared undercooked and had a fishy odour. Local authorities are investigating the cause of the suspected outbreaks, with food samples being tested for possible contamination. The head of the food distribution unit in Lasem, Achmad Sholeh Syarifudin, apologised and took "full responsibility for the recovery of students and teachers". He said the unit would conduct a comprehensive evaluation of its operation following the incident. The head of Indonesia's National Nutrition Agency has said: "If it is identified that there was negligence and there are criminal elements, I apologise, we cannot help."

item.title: Tensions flare as judge declines to remove juror in Lindsay Clancy trial
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.84
- Published A judge has again told the deadlocked jury in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial to keep trying to reach a verdict after a dramatic sixth day of deliberations in a case that has gripped America. Tensions flared in court after the jury forewoman sent the judge a note saying one juror would not follow the judge's instructions on reasonable doubt. There was audible shock in the room when the defence team asked for the juror to be removed, a request that was denied by the judge. Clancy, 36, is charged with three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children - Cora, five, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan - at her Massachusetts family home on 24 January 2023. Warning: This article contains distressing details The former labour and delivery nurse does not deny strangling her two sons and daughter in the basement of their house. But her lawyer argues she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time, and could not distinguish right from wrong. The jury of nine women and three men in Plymouth has deliberated for some 35 hours without a verdict, following nearly six weeks of trial proceedings. The panel has twice previously sent the judge notes saying it could not come to a unanimous decision, but Thursday was the first hint of rancour in the deliberation room. Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, said in court that the jury forewoman had sent another note, this one complaining to Judge William Sullivan that a juror was refusing to listen to the law on reasonable doubt. Reddington and prosecutor Jennifer Sprague had an animated discussion with the judge in court. Reporters in the room could not hear the exchange, but the BBC saw exasperated facial expressions and gestures from Clancy's lawyer. Reddington then went over to Clancy to explain what had just happened, in what seemed to be a tense conversation. Clancy, who was paralysed from the waist down when she jumped out of a second-floor window after killing her children, was pushed in her wheelchair by her lawyer to join a discussion with the judge. Afterwards, Judge Sullivan brought in each juror individually and questioned them. He reminded the panel they must unanimously believe beyond reasonable doubt that the defendant is guilty in order to convict her of a crime. As each juror came up, some looked at Clancy, while others did not. When the defence lawyer told the court about his request to have a juror removed, there were gasps and reporters quickly began typing. Judge Sullivan said the holdout juror could stay and deliberations could continue. "I don't feel it is proper for me to side with one side or the other of the deliberations," the judge said. Sprague, the prosecutor, said the judge's instructions to the jurors were appropriate. "There's no way to determine what the deliberations are, who's correct, who's incorrect, nor should we attempt to," she said. Clancy bowed her head as the media begin to exit the room. Reddington, looking upset, could be seen consoling his client, holding her in a side hug and rubbing her back as journalists left court. The defence lawyer told reporters afterwards that the forewoman's note to the judge stated that there was one holdout in the jury who, as he described it, "refuses to listen to the law... on reasonable doubt". Reddington said he had suggested to the judge "a motion to remove the juror who refuses to accept your instructions on the law on a reasonable doubt". The defence lawyer said he had no indication of what this lone juror was thinking and he did not confirm the 11-1 split the jury forewoman reported earlier. The issue with the juror is expected to be addressed again when court convenes at 09:00 EST (14:00 BST) on Friday. If the jury does not reach a verdict and Judge Sullivan declares a mistrial, prosecutors would need to decide whether to retry the case. Clancy faces life in prison without parole if convicted of first-degree murder. If found not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility, or reason of insanity, she could be committed to a state psychiatric hospital. Under US law, a jury must unanimously believe "beyond a reasonable doubt" that someone is guilty in order to convict them of a crime. The designation is the strictest standard in the US legal system. It places the burden on the government to prove that the accused is guilty, and not the accused to prove their innocence. If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org. In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.

item.title: Argentine leader threatens to sanction oil firms and reiterates Falklands claim
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.83
- Published Argentina's president has heightened tensions with the UK over the Falkland Islands, warning he will impose economic sanctions on firms which exploit oil close to the British overseas territory. In a national address, Javier Milei said the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the islands, emboldened by signs the US might reconsider its stance of neutrality on the issue. Milei said the Sea Lion oilfield, where a British and an Israeli firm are due to begin exploration work, was a "clear and present danger". Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK's position on the islands was "unwavering", and they would remain British as "that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders." Earlier Downing Street said reaffirmed its position that the islands would remain a British Overseas Territory "for as long as the Islanders wish". "This is not the first time Argentine governments have made economic threats against the islanders. We are clear that the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination extends to the right to exploit their own natural resources." More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Britain and Argentina. Milei announced his sanctions plan surrounded by his cabinet at the presidential palace, reiterating that the Falklands were "historically and legally" Argentinean. It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable". "Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he said on X. In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against. Teslyn Barkman, a former member of the Falkland Islands Legislative Assembly, told the BBC that Milei's speech had "probably irked every single Falkland islander". Speaking from the capital Stanley, she added that "we have a burgeoning economy for a small place... we will remain forever British". The crux was a proposal to introduce a bill to parliament to impose sanctions on energy firms planning to begin oil exploration off the Falklands. The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil . Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow. Rockhopper has described the field as containing "highly marketable crude". In a video posted earlier this year, Navitas highlighted the work it is already carrying out in the Falklands including building a dock, a heliport and accommodation for oil workers. In a statement, Rockhopper and Navitas said the two firms believed that "the recent developments are not expected to have a material effect on the development activities of the Sea Lion Project, including the timetable for completion of the Project's development". Milei said "If we do not act swiftly in a few months, they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea – something that has never happened before," Milei said. There is both a domestic and a regional political dimension to this latest escalation on the Falklands. At home, Milei needs to shore up votes amid his plummeting popularity, currently languishing at around 34%. There is only a year to go before he faces a presidential election and a serious challenge from his erstwhile vice-president, Victoria Villarruel. A pro-military politician, she has criticised his diplomatic efforts to secure change on the question of Falklands sovereignty. The sanctions may be part of a wider attempt to stave off accusations that he's weak on an issue which is so fundamental to Argentine identity. It helps Milei that this is about something concrete – the impending oil exploration of an oilfield rather than broad questions of sovereignty and self-determination. He argues that the UK is acting in violation of a UN resolution urging the two sides not to take unilateral action while the dispute remains unresolved. Milei also announced plans for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego in the south of Argentina, saying Trump and the US were "assessing their historical position in regard to the Falklands", which Argentina refers to as Las Malvinas. "That is not empty words as they understand that Argentina is a reliable partner and a valuable ally for decades to come," he said, describing the UK as a nation "in decline". "There are winds of change in the world that are favourable to our claim," Milei added. When asked in an interview with GB News earlier on Thursday if the US would "come to the UK's aid" during a potential territorial dispute, Trump replied that Britain had "not been there to help me" with his country's war with Iran. Trump's latest remarks come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review. Hours before Milei's speech, Sarah Rogers, a senior official in the US state department, posted a photo of herself with Milei alongside the caption: "Exciting things are happening in the Western Hemisphere." Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them. The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel. In a sign of the ongoing tensions between the two countries over the issue, Argentina players celebrated their victory over England in the World Cup by waving a banner in support of their country's territorial claim.

item.title: Could robots be the future of theme parks?
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.80
Could robots be the future of theme parks? This is Galaxy Robot Park, a 16,500-square-meter venue that’s opened near Seoul in South Korea . The company behind the park says their aim is to bring artificial intelligence and robotics into the world of entertainment. The question is, can robots keep people coming back?

item.title: Kenya's chai tea lovers are not happy as the nation's cows run dry
item.description:
Source: BBC News Score: 3.80
- Published Kenyans love their milky tea, or chai, but some are facing the worrying possibility of doing without as the country has been hit by a milk shortage. A breakfast here is often incomplete without a cup of chai, made by boiling tea in generous amounts of milk, sometimes flavoured with ginger and spices.
