item.title: The Best Fall Foliage in the USA: A Guide to Where to Go This Autumn
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.82
It’s a rare occasion that vast swaths of the United States experience a season in a similar way—but the sepia-toned mosaic of fall foliage soon to sprawl across the country in a few short weeks proves that fall is the one exception to that rule. Starting as early as late September and extending well into November, you can expect to find some combination of red, gold, yellow, and orange bathing the trees from coast to coast. But anyone well-versed in leaf-peeping—or the colloquial nickname given to any tourist with a proclivity for fall foliage gazing—knows that some states and regions have more colorful and sweeping offerings than others. So for any looking to leaf-peep-maxx this upcoming fall, we took the liberty of rounding up the states, parks, and areas from across the country where you can expect to find the most vibrant fall tableaus come this October. Blue Ridge Mountains, North Georgia Way down on the south of the eastern shore you’ll find a range of mountains absolutely awash for fall. The Blue Ridge Mountain region of North Georgia makes up a smaller enclave of the greater Appalachian Mountains—and though you can’t go wrong with any stop along the Appalachian Trail when it comes to fall foliage, this little corner right on the border between Georgia and Tennessee is especially ideal for the changing seasons. The Southern climate makes things a little milder, without having to sacrifice the fall grandeur. The area skews more towards nature aficionados, with plenty of nature paths and mountain trails to climb. One particular favorite includes Brasstown Bald, where you can catch the best view of the leaves in peak color. Where to stay in the Blue Ridge Mountains: - A charming Victorian B&B: Blue Ridge Inn Bed & Breakfast - A peaceful mountain escape: The Copperhead Lodge The Berkshires, Massachusetts When it comes to the idyllic pastoral regions of New England, Massachusetts’s Berkshires are right up there with the likes of New York's Adirondacks. One look around and you can see exactly how the lush area inspired writers like Edith Wharton and artists like Norman Rockwell (and if you don’t, just take a quick trip to the Norman Rockwell Museum). Other highlights for our Berkshires guide includes shopping at stores like Fluff Alpaca, hiking up Monument Mountain’s three different trails, grabbing some coffee beans from West Stockbridge’s famous No. Six Depot, and ordering a bite off the farm-to-table menu at Prairie Whale. Pair all of that with the area’s bustling boutique hotel scene in Lenox, Massachusetts, and you’ve got one must-see stop on your Great American leaf-peeping tour. Where to stay in the Berkshires: - For an artistic flair: 33 Main - A motor-lodge-turned luxury hotel: Life House Stowe, Vermont Nestled in the embrace of Vermont’s Green Mountains, Stowe might be known for its slopes and skiing—but it’s also one of the best places to catch a verifiable sea of fall foliage come October and November. This is your quintessential idyllic northern New England escape. While it’s had its fair share of development, there are plenty of locals who reside in the town year-round. Pre-game leaf-peeping by exploring the microbrewing scene or shopping for some top-of-the-line maple products at Shaw’s General Store. It’s also something of a hikers paradise, with absolutely no small shortage of trails for the ambitious explorers and gentler strollers alike. No matter what you choose, there’s sure to be one fantastic view. Where to stay in Stowe, Vermont: - For a hygge vibe: Field Guide - A spa-retreat: AWOL Stowe - A traditionally intimate ski lodge: Edson Hill Great Smoky Mountains, Tennessee and North Carolina The Great Smoky Mountains that trail up the border between Tennessee and North Carolina earned their name from the natural, gauzy fog that often drapes across the region. It gives the area an ethereal, almost otherworldly quality during any time of year. Add in a mosaic of fall foliage and it's no wonder why this spot is home to some of the best fall foliage in the USA. See the sights from the famous Cades Cove loop or hike the Laurel Falls Trail or any of the many paths along the mountains. You’ll also find a range of different lodging options in the area—including glamping experiences, cabins, farms, and more. Where to stay in the Great Smoky Mountains: - An irreverent farm getaway: Blackberry Farm - A sprawling ranch: Cataloochee Ranch - A one-of-a-kind glamping stay: Under Canvas Great Smoky Mountains Aspen, Colorado Aspen is one of those cold weather destinations that’s spoken of with an undeniable air of prestige—the same way you would speak of Lake Como in the spring, or the French Riviera in summer. Like Stowe, it’s most famous for its skiing, but it’s got its fair share of foliage to show off around fall. Especially ideal for those who have a taste for the finer things in life, Aspen’s also a prime luxury shopping destination. Shop high end designer brands like Prada or Gucci, and grab a chic cowboy hat from Kemo Sabe. And you can’t forget the decadent fare available at eateries like Bosq, White House Tavern, Matsushia, and more. Where to stay in Aspen, Colorado: - An Aspen mainstay: Hotel Jerome Sun Valley, Idaho Another skiing staple, Sun Valley has long charmed celebrities and nature-lovers alike. It’s renowned for its skiing but offers golden escape during the shoulder season of fall. Sun Valley’s especially great for any leaf peepers who happen to also be fans of Ernest Hemingway. The famous Lost Generation author loved the region and even finished his book For Whom The Bell Tolls in the Sun Valley Resort’s suite 206. Hemingway’s admiration of and attachment to the area is immortalized with with a memorial and free audio walking tour. Where to stay in Sun Valley, Idaho: - A historic ski resort: Sun Valley Resort - For a laidback lodging: Limelight Ketchum North Cascades, Washington New England often takes the cake when it comes to fall foliage, but don’t write off the Pacific Northwest. One drive along the Cascade Loop will show that this craggy region has its own verdancy amid the snow dusted mountains. Often referred to as the American Alps, there are plenty of peaks and summits to see the leaves—such as the Washington Pass overlooking the Liberty Bell Mountain—while hiking trails like the Maple Pass Loop and Blue Lake offer some of the best opportunities for leaf-peeping. Where to stay in North Cascades, Washington: - A floating cabin: Ross Lake Resort Laurel Hill, Pennsylvania There are plenty of trails and state parks you can take advantage of to gaze at the Pennsylvania foliage. There’s Mount Davis, Ohiopyle State Park, Laurel Hill state park, and so much more. You really can’t go wrong with any of them. But we’d recommend conducting your leaf peeping from inside, specifically inside one of famous architect Frank Lloyd Wright’s most well-known works. Dubbed Fallingwater, this quintessentially mid-century modern structure sits atop a waterfall and is entirely ensconced in a forest of trees—making its airy interiors the ideal framing for the lush colors of fall. Where to stay in Laurel Highlands Pennsylvania: - A sprawling estate: Nemacolin Franconia Notch State Park, New Hampshire Rounding off the New England stops, this nature reserve is nestled in the middle of New Hampshire’s White Mountain National Forest. Here, you’ll find parts of the larger Appalachian Trail, as well as hikes up well-known peaks like Artist Bluff—which afford panoramic views of the area’s famous Echo Lake. The body of water sits at the base of Cannon Mountain and perfectly reflects the prism of color around it, even more so when those colors are the rich reds, golds, yellows, and oranges of fall. Where to stay in Franconia Notch State Park, New Hampshire: - A mansion inn: The Franconia Inn Adirondacks, New York You just need to watch one episode of Gilmore Girls to know that New England is one of the top best places to see fall foliage, and the Adirondacks is one of the region’s best fall exports. Located just about four hours outside of New York City, this mountain area encompasses much of New York’s storied “upstate” region—where people escape from the city to ensconce themselves in the privacy of cozy cabins, lake houses, and more. Here, you’ll find over 3,000 lakes and ponds—such as the famous Lake Placid—and the Adirondack High Peaks. Grab a quick drink at Raquette River Brewing or fill up on French-Canadian comfort dishes at Woodshed on Park, before heading out to take in the vivid leaves. Where to stay in the Adirondacks: - For a luxurious lake island resort: The Sagamore Resort - A rustic log cabin experience: The Point - A Lake Placid classic: Great Adirondack Hotel Columbia River Gorge, Northern Oregon Just above California and below other fall foliage fave Washington, the Northern Oregon region similarly offers plenty of mystically foggy places to peep some leaves. What’s even better is you get the best of both worlds with forests and beaches colliding to make up this scenic coast. Travel through the Columbia River Gorge to see all the leaves, then take a road trip out to Cannon Beach to top the adventure off. Where to stay in Northern Oregon: - A water-front property: Cannery Pier Hotel & Spa Shenandoah National Park, Virginia Just off the Blue Ridge Parkway, and not too far from the border of West Virginia, Shenandoah National Park extends about 197,439 acres across Virginia’s Blue Ridge region. It’s got breathtaking views and nature, making it ideal to catch some of the best fall foliage in the USA. After all, there's a reason we named it one of the best national parks to enjoy during the fall. Shenandoah is mostly visited for hiking, with over 500 miles of trails—many of which you can find along the area’s Skyline Drive—that offer ample opportunity to take in nature, no matter the time of year.

item.title: The Most Beautiful Italian Coastal Towns
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.12
Most first-time visitors to Italy tend to concentrate on cities like Rome, Florence, and Venice, but if you ask us, off-the-beaten-path Italian coastal towns are some of the most beautiful places in the country. After all, Italy has nearly 5,000 miles of coastline, and some of the country’s coastal settlements predate the Roman Empire. From Liguria all the way down to Calabria, not to mention the Adriatic Coast and the islands, there are charming seaside villages that offer a wide variety of experiences. You might want the glamour of world-famous resort towns like Portofino, Capri, and Taormina, where your dolce vita fantasies can come to life. Or perhaps you’d prefer more under-the-radar towns like Maratea and Carloforte, where you can get an authentic taste of local life. In Italy, most coastal towns come alive in the summer, when visitors from around the world hit the beaches. If you want to avoid the crowds, plan to visit coastal towns in the off-season, but keep in mind that some of them all but shut down in the winter. Spring and fall are usually a good compromise. Read on to learn about 25 of the best Italian coastal towns, with Condé Nast Traveler-approved recommendations of where to stay. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: Asanas at Sea? The Best Places for Yoga Around the World Are Also the Most Unconventional
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.12
The best places for yoga are at once picturesque and contemplative, whether it be pranayama in Ladakh’s austere landscape, dhanurasana in the thick of Thailand’s jungles, or shavasana beside an Alpine lake in New Zealand. These experiences offer as much external peace as they do internal, and even long after the session and trip have ended, it's those stirring, outdoor moments that endure. They feel like they’ve stopped time and are worth going out of the way for—planned or spontaneous. And what's better than practicing your asanas in a phenomenal natural setting? With these 10 best places for yoga, grab your go-to mat and embrace your inner yogini. Lux* South Ari Atoll, Maldives The middle of the Indian Ocean is possibly the most unique spot one can find to do yoga. Practice asanas while sailing on a traditional wooden dhow at this Maldivian resort. Lux* South Ari Atoll organizes this cruise at golden hour with an instructor guiding you on Tibetan Sound Bowl therapy, breathwork, and yoga. Sip on a refreshing drink, inhale a mood-enhancing oil blend, and float on the waves as you meditate and feel your mind reset. The Kyagar, Nubra Valley, India This boutique hotel is located on the ancient Silk Route in Ladakh’s stunning but stark landscape. Sitting on the sandy banks of the Siachen River and surrounded by the icy Karakoram peaks, it has a very special location that owner Rinchen Kalon believes furthers your yoga practice. To that end, she hosts a retreat at the property every season, and when the weather permits, outdoor classes are held on a river trail surrounded by wildflowers and sea buckthorn bushes. The Kyagar's regular yoga classes are free of charge for guests and last 30 to 90 minutes. Haritha Villas and Spa, Sri Lanka This luxury villa property in Hikkaduwa has an open-air jungle yoga pavilion nestled amidst lush tropical greenery, overlooking the serene canopy of the surrounding forest. Haritha offers hour-long, private lessons in Hatha Yoga, which are apt for beginners. Guests love the serene jungle setting with sweet birdsong in the background and a gentle wind rustling through the trees. Many cite the yoga lesson as one of the most memorable parts of their stay here. Anantara Al Jabal Al Akhdar Resort, Oman This rocky mountain resort is one of the highest hotels in the world and has a spectacular deck which can be booked for a yoga session (based on weather and availability). Diana’s Point is a platform where Diana, Princess of Wales, once stood back in 1986 and has a breathtaking canyon view of the fabled Green Mountain. Anantara offers hatha, sarvanga, meditation, and monthly full-moon yoga classes, but this spot is not for the fainthearted, as it juts out into a valley with a steep drop-off. March to May is rose season in this region, and the entire valley below erupts into unbelievably fragrant Damask roses. The Kumaon, India The exquisitely-designed Kumaon is located in a remote part of the Himalayas, and its most magical setting for yoga is the rooftop terrace located at the highest point of the property. Views extend to the valley of the Kosi River on one side and the Binsar Forest on the other, all under the watchful gaze of the upper Himalayas, including the divine Nanda Devi peak. With reclaimed Himalayan slate as the cooling floor of the terrace, a wispy breeze scented with pine and carrying birdsong, Kumaon's yoga space feels magical. It offers traditional hatha yoga along with basic pranayama, and guests describe them as rejuvenating and peaceful. Qasr Al Sarab, Desert Resort by Anantara, Abu Dhabi Doing yoga surrounded by vast sand dunes is certainly an unusual proposition. The wellness and meditation center at Qasr Al Sarab by Anantara is nestled on the edge of the resort, a sanctuary that opens to an uninterrupted panorama of the golden Liwa Desert. Guests can practice in the midst of raw nature as the sun rises or sets; in the early morning, the desert sky turns pink and gold, while at twilight, it twinkles with stars. Yoga instruction is available year-round, and the resort also collaborates with yoga gurus specializing in yin yoga, immersive sound healing, and yoga nidra from October to April. Those looking for silence and stillness to escape a chaotic lifestyle will truly appreciate this setting. Keemala Resort and Spa, Thailand This luxury jungle resort in Phuket has a special focus on wellness with a tropical spa, healthy cuisine, and eco-friendly operations. Keemala has two outdoor yoga spaces, one intimate wedding venue nestled within the forest, and the other on a rooftop, offering scenic views. The forest yoga takes place amid lush foliage under a 300-year-old Takian tree; guests are encouraged to practice barefoot so that they can ground themselves directly to the earth for a soulful experience. The resort also has a meditation cave with a waterfall designed to help guests heighten their focus and fully immerse in the present moment. Group classes are complimentary, and private instruction is available at an additional charge. Aro Hā Wellness Retreat, New Zealand A world-famous retreat in the Southern Alps, Aro Hā is located on serene Lake Wakatipu, just 40 minutes from Queenstown. Its yoga classes take place in the Aro Hā Room, which is well known for its striking views of the alpine lake. It offers a range of hatha styles that cater to a wide range of skill level, and all classes are complimentary. Yoga is a key element of their larger program, which also includes subalpine hikes, daily massages and spa time, and a variety of wellness workshops. Jumeirah Olhahali Island, Maldives You may have done yoga on a beach, but have you ever done yoga on a private sandbank? Jumeirah Olhahali Island takes guests on a five-minute speedboat ride to reach a private sandbank at sunrise or sunset. Its Oceanic Balance Retreat is an all-encompassing yoga experience tailored to its surroundings, whether energizing at dawn or grounding at sunset. Pleasant ocean breezes, uninterrupted horizons, and the sense of pure seclusion create space for profound clarity and calm. Acro Suites, Greece Located on the cliffs of Crete, Acro Suites describes itself as a restorative retreat. Its asana wellness studios are sleekly designed with bamboo and local stone, overlooking the Aegean Sea and dramatic cliffs of Mononaftis Bay. The studios offer a variety of yoga styles, including hatha, vinyasa, yin, and yoga nidra, all guided by certified instructors. In addition to complimentary daily practices, guests can also partake in intimate couples sessions, healing circles, and sound healing journeys, each designed to deepen connection. A version of this article originally appeared on Condé Nast Traveller India.

item.title: What does the EU's new hand luggage rule mean for travellers? Here’s everything you need to know about the updated air passenger rights
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.21
On Tuesday 1 September, Members of the European Parliament confirmed changes to air passenger rights that were first reported earlier in 2026. These rules have been in place for more than 20 years, since 2004, and aim to protect passengers against disruption to their travels. While many of our rights, such as compensation if flights are delayed by a certain number of hours, will simply be upheld by the latest vote, there are some changes due to come into effect, too. Extra costs for hand luggage have been something that’s plagued travellers for decades, but new regulations are set to change that. After more than a decade of negotiations between the Council of the EU and the European Parliament, a landmark agreement has been reached. What is the new rule for hand luggage? New rules will include the right for passengers to carry one personal item such as a small bag or backpack with them onboard without incurring an extra cost. Airlines will also be required by law to display air fares that include carry-on luggage while booking to improve transparency and comparability between airlines and tickets. Airlines may still offer cheaper tickets who travel without hand luggage, MEPs say. A small catch to be aware of, however, is that this regulation applies to EU airlines only. This means that on non-EU airlines, like easyJet and Jet2, passengers may still be bound to the old regulations – except on flights returning to the UK from an EU country. Which other rights have been introduced? Several new rights are set to improve passenger safety and protection. These include rules to make it easier for passengers to claim compensation and access assistance in case of delay or cancellation, as well as new regulations reinforcing rights for persons with specific needs, such as persons with disabilities or reduced mobility and pregnant passengers. Air passenger rights changes to know - The right to carry on board, without extra cost, one personal item, such as a small bag or backpack - Passengers will no longer be charged for correcting spelling errors or for a printed version of a boarding pass if they have already checked in - Passengers will be able to take the return flight of a two-way ticket even if they did not use the first flight - Clearer and quicker reimbursement for flight disruption and travel delays - Passengers with disabilities and reduced mobility will have the right to compensation, rerouting and assistance if they miss a flight due to the airport’s failure to help them reach the gate on time - Any person accompanying a child below the age of 14 will be entitled to an adjacent seat without paying extra. The same right will apply to passengers with disabilities and reduced mobility, and to pregnant women. “I’m proud that, after 13 years of negotiations, we reached a landmark agreement to strengthen EU air passenger rights,” announced Alexis Vafeades, minister of transport, communications and works of the Republic of Cyprus. “This modernised framework will deliver certainty, fairness and stronger protection for millions of European air passengers. The agreement strikes a fair balance for our airlines, helping preserve connectivity that is vital to the EU’s internal market and its citizens.”

item.title: Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The sophomore season expands beyond English country piles to Mafia-held Italian palazzos
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.81
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The second season of Guy Ritchie’s hit Netflix series, The Gentleman, is here. The first series introduced us to Eddie Horniman (Theo James), a young British aristocrat who had inherited his father’s grand country estate, only to discover that behind the family money was a secret cannabis empire. In Season 2, Horniman, now the Duke of Halstead, is keen to expand the operation, alongside his business partner, Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario). This will take them out of the English countryside and subterranean criminal worlds of the East End and Liverpool, and thrust them instead into the world of the Mafia, as they attempt to go international and do business with the dangerous Capo dei Capi, Marco Moretti (Sergio Castellito). “The madness of Italy’s beauty, its culture, its history and its traditions were something I felt would fit perfectly into our show,” says Ritchie. “I had wanted to expand the canvas of The Gentlemen in this season. Italy was just an obvious choice. British gangsters colliding with the Italian Mafia just feels so right for our world. Some fruit hangs low and looks so tasty you just can’t resist for very long.” Here are some of the key locations used in the filming of The Gentleman Seasons 1 and 2, from Ritchie’s Ashcombe Estate to Lake Maggiore in Italy. Is The Gentlemen based on a real-life story? Both the film of the same name and the two seasons of The Gentlemen are not based on a true story, though of course, they borrow elements from the criminal underworld and its cast of characters. The situation that Eddie Horniman and his family find themselves in – of having to find new ways to monetise their vast aristocratic estates – is a reality, however. There are no real life examples of aristocrats running cannabis empires that we know of though. The main thrust of the action in Season 2 of The Gentlemen takes place in Lake Maggiore, connecting Horniman and his business partner Katie Glass to Italy’s criminal gangs – the mafia. Historically, the area has not been known as a mafia heartland – unlike regions like Sicily, for example – but it does have a relationship with organised crime. In particular, the ’Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, have reportedly used the area for cocaine and weapons trafficking, thanks to its close proximity to the Swiss border. Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The Badminton Estate, Gloucestershire While some scenes of The Gentleman were filmed on stage sets at Alperton Studios in Wembley, London, the exterior of Halstead Manor, the fictional home of the Horniman family, is The Badminton Estate. The real-life home of the Duke and Duchess of Beaufort is a popular filming location and wedding venue in the south Gloucestershire countryside. Viewers with a keen eye may recognise the property from Netflix favourite Bridgerton and movies including Pearl Harbour and 28 Days Later. The sprawling estate has been occupied for thousands of years, and the remains of several Roman villas surround the main home. The medieval property was owned by the Boteler family before Edward Somerset, fourth Earl of Worcester, purchased the manors of Great and Little Badminton in 1612. It’s his son, Sir Thomas Somerset, who made significant alterations to the original house, and the property has captured the imagination of high society and even the royal family over the centuries – Charles II stayed in the house, and the late Queen Elizabeth II was a regular visitor to the annual Horse Trials. “Badminton felt immediately right for Halstead,” says supervising location Manager Iggy Ellis, “because it’s a proper, lived-in home rather than a National Trust museum. So inside, there’d be some walking sticks by the door or a few shotgun rounds from where they’d been out shooting. There were cracks and tired bits, as you’d get in every family home. But there was also oil painting and history and majesty. It felt perfect for our story.” Ashcombe Estate, Wiltshire In episode one, Ritchie made his own country estate, Ashcombe Park, available for filming a shooting party scene. “That was a lot of fun but tricky at times too,” says production designer Martyn John. “You’re in the middle of nowhere with no phone signal or internet. We had to take everything in; so, flowers, food, dogs, guns and also… frozen partridges.” Ashcombe is a working farm set in 1,100 acres of rolling chalk land, and is named after the ash trees and the valleys (‘combes’) that monopolise much of it. It has been the family home of Ritchie since 2001 (when he bought it with ex-wife Madonna for £9 million), and was previously the home of photographer Cecil Beaton. Loseley Park, Surrey Much like in season one, some of the exterior and interior scenes at Halstead Manor were filmed at Loseley Park, a historic home just outside of Guildford that is now used as a wedding venue. “Where possible we tried to maximise every location because when you move around it costs money that could be on the screen,” explains supervising locations manager Iggy Ellis. “So we used a cottage in the grounds of Loseley for the exteriors of gamekeeper Geoff’s cottage and built the interior in the studio because we needed lots of camera space and somewhere for Geoff’s menagerie of animals.” Swakeleys House, Ickenham Another multi-purpose location was Swakeleys House, a 17th-century mansion in Ickenham. “It was a great find because we were able to use it for so many things,” explains Ellis. “From the rehab centre where Freddie is recovering from the cocaine habit he acquired in the first series to the interior of the prison where Bobby Glass is meant to be serving time.” Built in 1638, it is an excellent example of the ‘Artisan Mannerism’ architectural style, a form of Jacobean architecture that features decorative classical flourishes such as gable ends. It was the home of Sir Edmund Wright, Lord Mayor of London, and was visited twice by the famed diarist Samuel Pepys. The Adelphi Building, London The Adelphi Building off The Strand was transformed into an auction house for a scene in which Susie Glass bids millions for a Botticelli painting, which is later snatched by a gang on e-bikes outside. “I wanted to use that network of streets around the Savoy Hotel, including a secret little tunnel that cuts between John Adam Street and the riverside,” explains Ellis of the chase. “It takes at least three months’ notice to get London streets closed for filming, and there were some careful negotiations with everyone from Westminster Council to building owners and the Savoy Hotel itself. But that amazing chase really is one of the things I’m most proud of.” The Grade II-listed Adelphi has retained many of its original 1930s Art Deco features, including its impressive stone facade, classic columns and Gilbert Ledwood sculptures. Today it is predominantly used as an office space, and houses the publisher Condé Nast, whose titles include not only Condé Nast Traveller, but also Vogue, Tatler and GQ. Villa Rusconi Clerici, Lake Maggiore Villa Rusconi Clerici became the glamorous palazzo home of Mafia heiress (and Eddie’s love interest) Contessa Isabella Savanza de Parme, known as Bella. “We spent three full days looking at several amazing palazzos, including one on Lake Como,” shares John. “But as soon as I saw the one at Lake Maggiore, I knew this was the one. It was in a much less touristy area and it had such great light and glittering water. You could point the camera anywhere and it just looked beautiful.” The interiors too were perfect for Bella’s home. “I wanted a house or a villa which reflected the taste – if not the scale – of Eddie’s country estate, Halstead Manor” says Ellis. “I wanted these two aristocratic families to merge, stylistically. So, you have all the antiques and the paintings that reflect tradition and ancestry, but also modern pieces because, despite the centuries-old history of both families, there’s a new generation in charge now.” Villa Rusconi Clerici is a beautifully preserved 19th-century palazzo on the Piedmont shore of Lake Maggiore, and unsurprisingly is popular as a wedding venue. The villa that exists today was built for a Hungarian colonel and revolutionary, Stefano Türr, who was married to one of Emperor Napoleon’s cousins and became intrinsic to the unification of Italy. The interiors are Art Nouveau in style, including a grand staircase featuring a wrought iron balustrade. Grand Hotel Majestic, Lake Maggiore The Grand Hotel Majestic stood in for the fictional The Grand Hotel, where a wedding takes place later in the series. First built in 1870, it was one of the finest examples of luxury hospitality in the area, and was immediately popular with the international elite. Unsurprisingly, considering its location on the shores of Lake Maggiore, it is often chosen as a wedding venue for modern couples, much like in the show. One of its chief assets is the view across the lake to Borromeo Island, with actor Theo James pictured standing on one of the balconies looking out across the water in one scene. While the interiors are French in style, with parquet flooring and chandeliers, the grounds are also particularly lavish, with centuries-old trees and flowers, and there’s even a small private beach. Chiesa San Leonardo, Lake Maggiore The 16th-century church Chiesa San Leonardo also features in the new season. Located in the lakeside village of Pallanza, the church features striking columns of pink Baveno granite, as well as 17th-century wooden sculptures and altars. There’s also a 65-metre high bell tower, as well as access to the lake from a dramatic staircase. Where was The Gentleman Season 1 filmed? Stoke Court, Buckinghamshire The Badminton Estate gets much of the credit for appearing as the exterior of the fictional Halstead Manor, but some of the interior scenes used Stoke Court in Buckinghamshire. Stoke Court is home to the study, where Freddie shoots Liverpudlian drug dealer Tommy after a memorable scene featuring a chicken costume, Halstead Manor’s boot room, drawing room and orangery. The real-life property is best known for its association with mid-18th-century poet Thomas Gray, who holidayed there during his childhood. Wrotham Park, Hertfordshire Wrotham Park in Hertfordshire plays the part of the home of extravagantly wealthy drug lord Stanley Johnson, aka Bridgewater House. The neo-Palladian English country house was designed by Isaac Ware in 1754, and it’s where we see Susie Glass and Stanley engage in a polite-ish war of words over his desire to take over her father’s empire. London The Gentleman’s filming locations depict two sides of the coin: lavish country houses owned by the landed gentry and hideouts used by the criminal underworld. For the latter, the locations team looked to London. Locations used across the capital include The Reform Club in Pall Mall, which doubled up for Pinky’s Club, and Billingsgate Market, which is mentioned by name in the series as the headquarters of the Liverpudlian drug group. The exterior shots of the Croydon Tower Block were taken at Brandon Estate, while the boxing ring is the now-closed party venue Printworks in Rotherhithe.

item.title: Flying with children is about to get cheaper and easier thanks to new EU rules – here's everything you need to know
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.45
Ever found yourself fuming that in order to ensure you get a seat next to your child on the way to your family holiday, you have to pay extra for a seat for each of you – on top of what's probably an already hefty ticket price? You're not alone. But changes to EU air passenger rights will make this annoyance a thing of the past, as the right for children under the age of 14 to sit next to an accompanying adult free of charge will be protected. In September 2026, Members of the European Parliament approved changes to rules on air passenger rights that have been protected since 2004. There's a slate of changes due to come into force, but the parents among the Condé Nast Traveller team were particularly intrigued by the promise that a free adjacent seat will be guaranteed for a child under the age of 14 and the adult accompanying them. That means airlines cannot split up families at seat allocation, and cannot charge you extra to sit together. Why under the age of 14? For most airlines, children under 14 cannot travel without an accompanying adult on the same flight. The change means that adding extra fees to allow parents and children to sit together – which can quickly add up as they're charged per person – will be a thing of the past. The rules come into effect 12 months and 20 days after their publication in the Official Journal of the European Union – around August 2027, just in time for any end-of-summer holidays. Other rights that will come into practice next August thanks to these include: - Making it easier to claim compensation if your flight is delayed or cancelled - Transparent pricing that displays ticket prices including cabin baggage by default - Personal items stored under the seat should be free of charge

item.title: The UK’s oldest recorded town has more than 2,000 years of history – and where it is may surprise you
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.33
When I found out where the UK’s oldest town was, I wasn't expecting it to be a place I've passed through quite so frequently, or one still thriving today. I’ve been lucky enough to travel the breadth of Britain over my 31 years, from tiny hamlets in the Scottish Highlands to artsy towns in Cornwall. I’ve spent half my life calling London home and the other half in East Anglia; holidayed in Wales, visiting beaches accessible only by wooden swing; slept in cabins in the Cotswolds; road-tripped through Northern Ireland; and spent years studying in Newcastle. All of which is to say, if you’d asked me to guess where it was, I’d have imagined a barely-there archaeological site somewhere in rural Northumberland, rather than a thriving modern city in Essex, close to the Suffolk border and just 60 miles northeast of London. I’m talking, of course, about Colchester. Today, the city is popular for its fast commuter trains into the capital, relatively affordable housing, open green spaces and, of course, its rich history. But in around AD 43, it was known as Camulodunum: the first major Roman city and the initial capital of Roman Britain, before it was destroyed during Boudica’s rebellion in AD 61. The story of the Roman settlement didn’t end there, however, and Colchester was rebuilt in the years that followed. During the Anglo-Saxon era, the city was largely neglected before later falling under Viking control. In AD 917, Edward the Elder drove the Vikings out, and Colchester began to regain its former stature. Following the Norman Conquest, Colchester Castle was built in 1066 over the ruins of an earlier Roman temple. Dating to the 1070s, it became the first and largest of the Normans’ great keeps, cementing Colchester’s importance as one of England’s key centres. But the city’s history stretches back even further than the Roman conquest. Colchester began as an Iron Age settlement, ruled by Cunobelin, known as the ‘King of the Britons’. Evidence of this early history can still be found in the city today, including a collection of Iron Age and Roman artefacts at Colchester & Ipswich Museums. There’s something slightly confusing about calling Colchester the oldest town in the UK, given that it is also one of the country’s newest cities. It gained city status in November 2022 as part of the late Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Civic Honours, one of eight towns to receive the upgrade. It joined Doncaster, Milton Keynes, Dunfermline, Bangor, Wrexham, Douglas and Stanley. Of course, when compared with some of the world’s oldest cities, Colchester is relatively young in the grand scheme of human history. Jericho, on the West Bank near the Jordan River, is thought to have been inhabited as early as 9000 BCE, and is often described as the world’s oldest known walled city. Across Britain, several places lay claim to the title of oldest town, from Thetford in Norfolk and Ipswich in Suffolk to Amesbury, near Stonehenge, where evidence of settlement dates back as far as 8820 BC. Colchester’s claim rests on a specific point of difference: it is officially recognised as the UK's oldest town on record, based on a reference to the settlement by the Roman writer Pliny the Elder.

item.title: Best eSIMs for travellers 2026: How to beat airport Wi-Fi and extortionate roaming fees for good, tried-and-tested by our editors
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.21
On the list of additional costs that can trip up travellers, the dreaded roaming data charge is one of the most irritating. While there are usually phone plan kiosks or the odd SIM card vending machine at the airport, by the point you’ve reached the arrivals lounge, you’re a captive audience and beholden to whatever rate is offered. You also might need data before leaving the airport: I’m still scarred by the charge I incurred in the connecting terminal in Singapore when the WiFi wasn’t working and I needed to let my partner know I’d arrived. But there is a way to beat the charges before you’ve even left the country – and that’s by using an eSIM. Often, purchasing a dedicated travel SIM works out cheaper than buying the additional data bundles offered by your UK phone network, especially for frequent fliers and those headed further than Europe. Plus, by using a digital SIM rather than a physical one, there’s no need to wait for it to arrive or worry about losing your regular SIM card while it’s not in use. Below, we’ve outlined the best eSIM services to know in time for your next trip, along with the price for a week’s worth of data for a long-haul flight to Indonesia as a price comparison guide. The best eSims for travellers at a glance: - Best overall: Ubigi - Best for digital nomads: Saily - Best for customisable data top-ups: aloSIM - Best for heavy data users and longer stays: Holafly - Best pay-as-you-go eSIM: Roamless - Best value eSIM: Airhub - Best for app-free setup: easySim - Best for short trips: GoMo World - Best for security and extra perks: Yesim - Best for essential app-only coverage: Honest Mobile - Best for rewards and younger travellers: Global YO - Best for business travel: Maya Mobile Ubigi Best eSIM overall - Pros: Top-up possible without WiFi or data remaining, worldwide data plans, 5G available - Cons: Little pricier than some of the other services on our list for some countries - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £6 Ubigi is a comprehensive data service for over 200 countries, with data plans from 500mb to unlimited. There are one-off, monthly and annual services, so digital nomads, business travellers and holidaymakers alike will all be covered. If you run out of data, you can top up without being connected to WiFi even without any remaining data, which is an additional safety boon that other services on this list can't always match. 5G connectivity is also available at no extra cost where possible. You can also save 10 per cent on prices on your first order with the code CNTRAVELLER. Editor review: I used a Ubigi eSim when I travelled to Yellowstone from London recently. I think the tell that a service like this is working well is to realise you don’t think about it at all. My internet in the States was just as speedy as when I’m in the UK, and worked as soon as I landed at Denver airport to await my transfer. I appreciate this as a lot of airports charge for WiFi or make you hunt down one of those tedious booths for a code before you’re granted the privilege to log on – if you can’t find one or it’s out of order, as happened to me in Hong Kong one time, then you’re either stuck internetless or have to suck it up and pay your network’s extortionate roaming fee. By activating my eSim immediately upon landing, I didn’t have to worry about connecting to the airport WiFi at all. But the main boon was being able to top up via the app even without being connected to WiFi. Wyoming is very large, very empty, and free fast WiFi was often in short supply. I was grateful to be able to top up without WiFi on one day trip – I didn’t realise I was running low on data before leaving and would have had a whole day without connectivity otherwise. This would have been anxiety-producing as a solo traveller very far from home! Charley Ward Saily Best eSIM for digital nomads - Pros: Good variety of plans, regional and global plans available - Cons: A little more expensive than some of the others listed - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6.89 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £6.89 If you’re looking for data abroad, you’re sorted with Saily, whether you’re going on a quick three-day hop to longer three-month treks. You can buy per country or per region – handy if you’re island hopping across Asia, for example – and there are even worldwide plans for the most intrepid travellers. We like how seamless this service is, especially. You can purchase the data in the UK and when you arrive at your destination, it’ll switch on automatically, so you’re never without data and prevents being hit by accidental roaming charges in the airport. Saily has unlimited data plans in 37 destinations including the US, Japan, France, Spain, Italy and Thailand, plus an unlimited European data plan that works in 36 European countries. The app also has various tours and experiences bookable within the Saily app dependent on where you're headed. New users can use code CNT10 for 10 per cent off all mobile data plans worldwide. aloSIM Best for customisable data top-ups - Pros: Easy-to-use app, transparent pricing, flexible data top-ups without hidden fees - Cons: Data-only plans (no traditional phone calls or SMS) - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: Approx. £8.20 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: Approx. £6.70 If you prefer straightforward, data-only coverage without signing up for unnecessary bells and whistles, aloSIM is a reliable contender. It operates across more than 170 countries, is easy to set up via the minimal mobile app – which allows you to calculate and purchase the exact amount of data you’ll need before stepping onto the plane; not something that can be said of all of the brands featured here. Installation is instant via a quick QR code scan and topping up takes mere seconds in the app should you run out of data or your trip is extended. One note: this brand’s eSims don’t support traditional voice minutes or SMS. However, for seamless 4G/5G connectivity for internet-based messaging apps, navigation, and streaming, it’s a worthy choice. Holafly Best for heavy data users and longer stays - Pros: Unlimited data packages in most destinations, 24/7 customer support, customisable plan durations - Cons: Considerably higher price point if you’re taking short trips, limited hotspot capabilities on some plans - Price for 7 days of unlimited data for Indonesia: Approx. £20.40 - Price for 7 days of unlimited data for USA: Approx. £20.40 For travellers who refuse to count megabytes or hunt down hotel WiFi, Holafly is the go-to provider. Rather than capped data tiers, Holafly built its reputation on offering unlimited data plans across 180+ destinations – essentially, wherever you are in the world, this is the eSim for you. You can tailor your package to the exact length of your trip – whether that’s three days or a full month – ensuring you never pay for extra days you don’t need. It is undeniably pricier upfront than fixed-data alternatives, but for remote workers, heavy video streamers, or anyone who relies heavily on maps and ride-hailing apps on the move, should find the peace of mind worth the investment. Roamless Best pay-as-you-go eSim - Pros: Pay-as-you-go data options ensures no wasted data, voice calls available, well priced - Cons: Although potentially more convenient, pay-as-you-go plans can work out more expensive than fixed plans - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6.70 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £6.70 It’s a problem I’ve had when travelling a couple of times: you have to top up your eSim a day or so before the end of your trip, but then leave the country without using all the new data, thus wasting it (and, therefore, the money you paid for it). Not so with Roamless, which has pay-as-you-go options that won’t expire after 30 days. That means if you don’t burn through all your data on your trip, you can use it on your next getaway, even if you’re not returning to the same destination. The brand also has regular data packages for over 200 countries worldwide from free 500MB packs up to to 20GB, as well as packages including call-time, all for a very reasonable price point that’s lower than some of our other favourites on this list. You can save 20 per cent on your first purchase with the code CNT20. Airalo - Pros: 200+ destinations, regional and global deals, great connection - Cons: highest prices on our list, most packs are data-only - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6.50 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £8.50 Habits are hard to break, and I must admit I was sceptical about using my first eSIM. But after one-too-many surprise phone bills, I finally decided to take the leap during a sunny Croatia break, and where better to start than the world’s first and largest eSIM provider: Airalo. Steady Wi-Fi for around twenty minutes is necessary for installing the eSIM, so I’d recommend doing so before you travel, but you can activate the actual data plan within minutes once you land. Airalo’s easy-to-follow setup guide clearly directed me through the process, and I quickly found myself connected to my new data plan – with noticeably improved connection. I was staying in an off-grid beach village near Dubrovnik, and while my travel buddy struggled for internet access in our hotel room, my connection was fast and reliable at all times. Editor review: The sim is all based around Airalo’s no-frills mobile app, where you can flick through the loaded catalogue of national, regional, and global packs. My 3GB package (priced at £7.50) turned out to be plenty for a five-day trip, but the app also provides instant data top-ups in case you run out. It’s worth noting that almost all Airalo packages are data-only, so text and calls have to be supplied through your original provider, but for me, this feature was ideal. With the eSIM neatly slotting alongside my physical sim, there was no need for the confusing chore of switching phone numbers, and so this eSIM lived up to the hassle-free hype in all areas. Layla Quaedvlieg. Airhub Best value eSIM - Pros: Yearly and monthly subscriptions, unlimited data and voice options available - Cons: None that we can see - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £4.75 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £2.37 This is our best value eSIM option – Airhub is a great service for frequent travellers and digital nomads especially. The app is intuitive and easy to use, and there are plenty of different plans available for trips of all lengths. One perk this service offers over the others we like is the yearly and monthly subscriptions, which make financially savvy options for those on longer trips – for example if you’re stationed somewhere for work or taking advantage of that post-Covid ‘work from anywhere’ lifestyle. There are also plans that include voice minutes and SMS services, which is an additional boast that the other services here can’t match. Editor review: On a recent work trip, I realised how useful the combined voice and data plans can be when travelling. In the UK I rarely make traditional voice calls, but on this particular trip I needed to connect with a contact that didn’t use WhatsApp, so I couldn’t make a call over the internet. I’ve a spend cap on my regular sim which, as I learned, prevented me from making calls abroad. I was left in a frustrating situation where I wasn’t quite sure how to get hold of the guy. The problem was resolved by downloading this eSim, and also meant I didn’t have to spend time removing and then re-adding the spend cap on my regular plan when I got home. If you travel a business and make a lot of calls, I’d recommend this eSim. Charley Ward EasySim - Pros: Diverse range of data plans, many plans work across multiple countries, no need for an app - Cons: No family feature for managing multiple eSIMS per account - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £8.50 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £8.50 Editor review: EasySim is part of the EasyJet family of brands, so they know a thing or two about roaming. True to form, it’s one of the most comprehensive services on offer, with a good range of plans at some of the best prices we’ve seen. Some may not like the lack of an app, but the website is easy to use and does the job perfectly well. As a bonus, this service covers a wide range of phones. Not all the options on this list are compatible with my Motorola – an admittedly niche handset – so the compatibility here adds an additional sweetener to this service for me. GoMo World Best eSIM for short trips - Pros: Low starting prices - Cons: Fewer cross-country compatible plans than EasySim, calls, SMS and MMS services aren’t currently provided - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: No 3GB plan available; 1.5GB for £3.99 or 15GB for £20 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: No 3GB plan available; 1GB for £3.99 or 15GB for £20 As someone who travels regularly for work, and often only for a few days at a time, I’ve sometimes found myself paying over the odds for week-long data plans when I’m only away a few days. Case in point on a recent trip to the Maldives, where I was beholden to the airport’s singular 10gb data SIM offering despite only being in the country for three days. So, if you’re one for regular short hops, GoMo World’s smaller plans are ones to consider for maximum cost-saving benefits. Yesim - Pros: Coverage in 200+ destinations worldwide and a ‘refer a friend’ rewards system to save money on data plans. - Cons: Connection speeds limited to local carrier availability - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: 3GB £9 for 30 days, 5GB £11.70 for 15 days, 10GB £19.80 for 30 days - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: 3GB not available, 500MB for 0.45p for 3 days, 10GB £14.40 for 30 days, 15GB £16.20 for 30 days This Swiss-based eSIM provider boasts excellent reviews on Trustpilot and with good reason. The broad, global coverage offers fast, consistent internet activity in over 200 countries, is easy to use and set up, and is reasonably priced with no hidden extras. The built-in VPN technology offers enhanced security and reassurance when travelling, while the fast customer support service is there ready to answer any questions or fix problems, should they arise, with ease. We’re impressed by the virtual phone number rental capability, too – a rare addition among eSIM providers. Honest Mobile - Pros: Perfect if you’re only planning on using apps rather than making calls. - Cons: Doesn’t support internet calling or streaming - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: from £3.75 per month for unlimited data roaming - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: from £3.75 per month for unlimited data roaming This smart SIM automatically switches to EE, O2, or Three when your main SIM loses signal and provides free, unlimited global roaming for over 200 essential apps, including Google Maps, Skyscanner, and Uber, across 180+ countries. This eliminates the stress of data caps and roaming charges while on your travels. It’s a great idea for keeping costs low, just be careful to stick within the limits of what this eSIM can offer. Maya The best eSIM for business travel - Pros: Money-back guarantee for 180 days, high-speed internet connection, global packages - Cons: None as far as we can see - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: From £5.39 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: From £7.19 For a solid choice with no hidden fees, Maya is a good option. No contracts, 24/7 customer service, and a money back guarantee for up to 180 days. This means that if disaster strikes and your trip is cancelled, you can request an immediate refund with no extra charges. The SIMs are compatible with IOS and Android devices, and with at least two (if not more) networks available in each destination, the 4G/5G internet truly is high-speed. We love their new global eSIM package too, which includes across 119 destinations and starts from as low as £4.79, as well as the special business options, revolutionising the company work trip with shared data pooling. FAQs How we tested the best eSims To find the best travel eSIMs, our editors tested a variety of eSims across a range of long-haul and short-haul trips – from quick European city breaks to multi-stop journeys through Asia and North America. We evaluated how straightforward the provider’s app and setup process was, measuring how quickly we could download, install, and activate data profiles before departure. Once on the ground, we put network reliability, download speeds, and signal strength to the test in a variety of locations, including busy airport arrival lounges, remote countryside, and dense city centres. Finally, we compared overall value for money, flexibility, data-top-up ease, and customer support responsiveness. What is an eSIM? In plain English, it’s a virtual sim card that you install via an app rather than by inserting a physical card into your phone. They are activated remotely, so there’s no need to visit your local phone shop or wait for it to arrive. In your phone’s settings, you’ll be able to toggle between your existing physical sim card and the eSim, even being able to use both simultaneously, such as using one for mobile data and the other for calls and texts. This is handy if your eSim plan is data only but you’d still like the phone and SMS capability while away. It means that, if you download and install the eSim before you head off, you can activate it in the airport when you land and beat pricey roaming charges forevermore. The setup is simple. After registering online, all it takes is a quick scan of a QR code and you’re good to go. If you run out of data, you don’t need to download a new one – just top up your existing plan. Each eSIM has its own inclusions, from calls, texts, and internet streaming, to exclusive access to essential apps like Google Maps, so make sure to check in advance which plan best suits your needs. If that’s not enough to convince you, the entirely virtual setup means that they are also kinder to the planet than the plastic chips of traditional SIMs. Is my phone eSim compatible? Most Apple iPhone, Google Pixel, and Samsung Galaxy models released in the UK since 2018 are eSIM compatible. For other smartphones, the quickest way to check eSIM compatibility is by dialing *#06# on your phone's keypad – a screen pop-up including an EID number indicates your device is eSIM-friendly. You will also need to make sure that your device is not locked to a single network. If this is the case, provided you’ve reached the end of your original contract, you can ask your provider to unlock it for free by requesting a Network Unlock Code (NUC). Do I need a different eSIM for each country I visit? No. All eSIMs are suitable for use worldwide, so you’ll only need to install one eSIM. Do check, however, that the eSim provider you select has data plans available for the country you want to visit – all of the brands below have hundreds of countries available, so this shouldn’t be a problem in the vast majority of instances. Some plans are suitable for use in multiple countries, too, which is good if you’re taking a longer trip hopping from place to place – like if taking a cruise, for example. Airalo, for instance, has packages valid for use in up to 137 countries, from Jamaica to Japan.

item.title: Is Germany's economic slump finally over?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.68
The German economy is showing tentative signs of recovery after a prolonged period of gloom. Europe's largest economy is on track for its strongest GDP growth since 2022, while business sentiment is finally trending upwards again after a lengthy spell in the doldrums. The country's official statistics office reported last week that the economy grew by 0.3% in the second quarter of 2026, beating estimates and building on robust figures for the previous two quarters. Several others have revised their forecasts upwards. The Ifo Institute, Kiel Institute for the World Economy and the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research are all now predicting growth of 1.3% or more for 2026. Meanwhile, the Ifo business climate index — a key barometer of the country's corporate mood — returned its highest reading in a year for August. "It's more than a flash in the pan," Clemens Fuest, president of the Ifo Institute, told DW. "It could be a recovery." "The momentum is positive and the economy has shown a better-than-feared level of resilience," said Carsten Brzeski, ING's global head of macro research. However, he cautioned against too much cheer, saying some of the economy's fundamental problems remain. "In order to really transform this into a longer-term recovery story, we still need more," he said. Where has the good news come from? The positive figures come as negative headlines related to Germany's economy continue to stack up. Volkswagen, one of the country's most iconic companies, is in the midst of a bitter downsizing — reflecting a wider restructuring across the country in the face of competition from China and other global headwinds. This summer, record low water levels on key German waterways such as the Rhine and Danube significantly disrupted trade and economic activity while the war in Iran continues to drive energy prices upwards. Yet part of the reason for the upturn relates to how the German economy has handled some of those challenges, notably the closure of the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the Iran war. Germany's exports and industrial base have powered GDP growth, with new orders increasing for the third month in a row, leading to the strongest production growth since early 2022. The VDMA, which represents the German mechanical and plant engineering sector, reported a 2% increase in foreign orders for July year-on-year. Brzeski told DW that many German manufacturing firms, especially in energy-intensive sectors such as chemicals, have benefited from the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. They have increased orders and taken some market share from Asian suppliers who were more severely dependent on Middle Eastern oil. "There was a bit of a rechanneling of industrial orders away from Asia to Europe and Germany," he said. The German Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action itself identified this factor in its August statement, saying Asian rivals "were more affected by price increases and supply bottlenecks." It said that the multiple shocks of recent years have led German companies to diversify supply chains. "Many companies have altered their transport logistics in recent years, are maintaining larger stocks, and are using a variety of transport routes in order to make their supply chains more resilient," it added. Can the German government take some credit? Analysts also think Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government deserves some credit for the turnaround, despite it hitting historic levels of unpopularity in 2026. "It's driven by government demand and debt-financed spending, particularly in defense," said Fuest. The government's economic plans are built around a €500 billion ($580 billion) infrastructure investment drive, a massive increase in defense spending and a major reform proposal aimed at boosting competitiveness. It has also introduced some energy price relief measures and a €10 billion tax relief plan for lower-income households. "Companies are more optimistic and a big part has to be the stimulus," said Brzeski. "It is gradually reaching the economy." Germany's structural problems remain Despite the positive data, many of the issues which have dogged the German economy in recent years remain. The recent uptick is driven by export demand, with practically no increase in domestic demand. According to the Federal Statistical Office, public and private consumption spending was flat, while investment declined. "Even though everyone is happy that we have some positive news, we need to watch out and not fall into the trap of thinking that now 'everything is fine,'" said Brzeski, noting that the factors undermining German competitiveness persist. "Chinese competition is still there," he said. "The long loss in international competitiveness in the automotive industry and other industries is still here," he added, stressing that these structural challenges would be difficult to alter or reverse. Tentative optimism among Germany's businesses Yet the positive sentiment remains. Indicators for the third quarter of 2026 suggest significant optimism among business leaders about the future, while overall German growth is now on track for a 1.2% increase for 2026. That puts it ahead of other European countries such as France, the UK and the Netherlands. In the wake of the war in Ukraine, Germany's economy fell into a sustained slump from which it has struggled to emerge since 2022. While other economies showed signs of recovery, Germany remained in the doldrums. For some analysts, the recent positive data reflects a sense that things had reached a natural "bottoming out" and that a return to growth was inevitable. "It could hardly have gotten much worse," said Brzeski. "We're bouncing back from low levels. This is not wirtschaftswunder ["economic miracle"] 3.0, we have to keep that in mind." He also thinks part of the optimism is related to corporate Germany finally accepting some harsh truths about how it had fallen behind in key areas such as innovation and digitalization, and belatedly trying to improve. "They realize they simply have to embrace technological change, AI and so on, and have to start investing," he said. "They are no longer waiting for what's happening in Berlin in terms of reform packages; it's a question of survival." For Fuest, the data suggests Germany's "industrial core" remains intact. He said three-quarters of German manufacturing companies are still expanding, but warns that the recovery will be short-lived unless bigger change follows. "It is urgent to allow for structural change and to find new areas where German companies have competitive advantages," he said. Edited by: Rob Mudge

item.title: Can communities be proteced from melting glaciers?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.17
High mountain glaciers formed in the ice age are retreating and becoming unstable as the burning of fossil fuels heats the climate and leads to a decline in snowfall. The instability creates the conditions for large glacial sections to collapse, triggering ice and rock avalanches that can dam river valleys before tidal waves of water are released. Following the glacier collapse that triggered what is known as a mountain tsunami in Nepal and Tibet on August 26, thousands are still missing and feared dead. Unlike the 2025 glacier avalanche that destroyed the town of Blatten in Switzerland — where nearly all inhabitants were evacuated — a lack of early warning systems in the Himalayas left locals and tourists at the mercy of flash floods. How much is climate change to blame? The causes of glacier collapse are part of a complex web of interrelated changes to high mountain landscapes due in part to rising global temperatures, say scientists. Levan Tielidze, research fellow in glacial geomorphology at Australia's Monash University, said the Himalayas are not, as is often imagined, a "frozen and relatively stable environment," but "dynamic systems in which glaciers, snow, permafrost, rock slopes, rivers and monsoon processes interact." "As the climate warms, these components are changing simultaneously, meaning hazards can cascade from one process into another," he told DW. When rock, ice and water interact in more unpredictable ways on the world's highest peaks, the resulting debris flows "can transform into a catastrophic flood far downstream." Almost 25 years ago, in what was then the biggest glacial collapse in history, one glacier crashed onto another in the Caucasus Mountains of North Ossetia in Russia. The event caused avalanches of ice and debris that slid more than 24 kilometers (15 miles) and killed around 125 people. "The Kolka Glacier disaster was one of the early warnings of the increasing occurrence and potential severity of such glacier-related hazards," said Tielidze. Meanwhile, the UN says glaciers in Nepalese mountains have declined by one-third in 30 years, which has added to their instability. Some research suggests that even if emissions from burning fossil fuels were low enough to prevent the planet from heating by more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 Fahrenheit) compared to pre-industrial times, the wider Hindu Kush Himalayan region could lose up to half its glacier cover — compared to 2020 levels — by the end of the century. For Dipesh Chapagain, senior scientist at the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security, there is "ample scientific evidence linking greenhouse gas emissions to global climate change, which in turn is driving glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and ice avalanches." "These changes are increasing both the frequency and intensity of climate-related disasters in mountain regions," he added. Chapagain has studied hundreds of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region — caused when meltwater from glaciers and snow creates a lake that eventually bursts and sends extreme flash floods downstream. The number of these events per decade has increased fivefold since the 1950s. The glacier collapse in Nepal and Tibet shares similarities to a GLOF event. However, the former was very different as it skipped the "intermediate lake-formation stage entirely … and directly triggered the flash flood," said Chapagain. The avalanche also generated seismic activity equivalent to about magnitude 5.2 before the momentum of the water-rich debris flow that entered the river system saw it travel roughly 100 kilometers, noted Tielidze. "These hazards are becoming so difficult to classify," he said, in reference to the way mountain rock, ice and water are interacting in more unpredictable ways due to climate change. Is it possible to adapt to more extreme glacier collapse impacts? The 2025 glacial collapse in the Swiss Alps that destroyed the entire village of Blatten resulted in one fatality. Detailed surveillance of glacier deformation and the surrounding terrain allowed authorities to evacuate the population before the catastrophic collapse. But this is less possible in the Hindu Kush Himalaya, which contains more than 63,700 glaciers, said Tielidze. "In the Himalayas, we need to move beyond monitoring only individual dangerous lakes," he said. "We need integrated systems combining satellite observations, seismic detection, glacier and slope monitoring, river gauges, weather forecasts and automated warnings." For rapidly evolving events such as the Nepal disaster, detecting seismic movement could give downstream communities "precious minutes of warning," he added. Chapagain said the transboundary nature of glacial hazards in the Himalayas makes "cross-border and regional cooperation on disaster preparedness" just as urgent as early-warning systems. However, currently available adaptation technology and capacity may be insufficient to "respond to a disaster on the scale we've just witnessed on the Bhotekoshi River in Nepal." "What we have learned from this is we can adapt to climate change but not to climate apocalypse," said Shreya K.C., the Kathmandu-based advocacy working group cocoordinator of the Loss and Damage Youth Coalition, in a statement. A rapid reduction in planet-heating emissions that are at driving glacial melt and instability will need to accompany any adaptation measures. "We cannot engineer our way out of unlimited warming," said Tielidze. "Some mountain hazards will remain unpredictable and some changes will eventually exceed the capacity of communities and infrastructure to adapt." Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: Berlin: BER Airport Terminal 1 reopened after security scare
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.08
Terminal 1 at Berlin Brandenburg Airport (BER) was reopened on Thursday evening following an earlier evacuation due to a security scare. "The police operation has ended," said an airport spokeswoman. Federal police, responsible for transportation security in Germany, had evacuated BER Terminal 1 at around 5:45 p.m. after a woman reportedly told security staff at a service point that she had a dangerous substance in her luggage. "A potential threat from the unidentified substance could not be ruled out," the police spokesperson told the dpa news agency. Police then gave the all-clear at around 8:45 p.m. and confirmed that nobody had been in danger at any point. Police initially provided no information as to the nature of the substance in question, with analysis results expected in the coming days. Berlin: BER operations remain restricted Despite the all-clear, operations at BER remained restricted on Thursday evening. "Due to the police operation, we will still be experiencing delays and some cancelations until the end of the day," said the airport spokeswoman. She advised travelers to double-check the status of their flight before arriving at BER and to keep an eye on the boards while at the airport. "Flights were not stopped," she insisted, emphasizing that there were only delays. "Regular operations will resume on Friday." What did the airport say about departures and arrivals? The airport had confirmed the incident itself earlier on Thursday but said planes that were already prepared to depart could take off as normal and incoming arrivals could also continue to land. Passenger processing was "relocated to Terminal 2 to the extent that it's possible," a spokesperson said. Many but not all flights departing Terminal 1 from around 7 p.m. local time were marked as delayed on the airport's website. An airport press officer told DW that around 30 flights had been delayed but that they were trying to avoid cancellations by redirecting departures to Terminal 2. Trains were also impacted by the operation for a time. The city's S-Bahn train service confirmed disruptions on both lines to airport, while Deutsche Bahn also reported widespread disruptions to regional trains. BER or the "Willy Brandt Airport" in Schönefeld is Berlin's busiest and Germany's third-busiest airport since it opened in 2020. It also serves as the primary airport for many federal government flights. Some 26 million passengers travel through it each year. The last comparable security disruption at the airport was in March of this year, when flights were disrupted but because of a potentially suspicious aerial object rather than a suspicious item in the terminal. item.title: South Africa airline behind viral stadium flyby scraps repeat display
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.79
South African aviation authorities are reviewing a low-altitude flyover by two Airlink passenger planes at an international rugby match in Cape Town last weekend. The regional airline, meanwhile, said it had canceled another flypast scheduled for Saturday's rugby test between South Africa and New Zealand in Johannesburg this weekend, citing unfavorable weather. In a statement, the South African Civil Aviation Authority (SACAA) said it was carrying out a "compliance verification" of the August 29 flyover at Cape Town's DHL stadium to ensure "all safety protocols were adhered to by the crew." Footage of the flyby, showing two planes in formation passing over the crowd, was widely shared on social media and prompted discussion about potential safety risks. According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, the lead aircraft passed less than 15 meters (50 feet) above the top of the packed stadium. What did SACAA and Airlink say? The SACAA said it was analyzing flight data provided by Airlink and would go over additional information requested from the carrier before issuing a report. The regulator said the airline had made applications for the flyovers, which were approved in line with the requirements for special air events. Airlink, for its part, said the maneuver had been carefully planned and rehearsed, with safety being "the first consideration at every stage of the process." It said each aircraft had three senior captains on board with a combined 75,000 hours of flying experience. Nevertheless, it also recognized what it described as the "valid questions and concerns." Airlink Chief Executive de Villiers Engelbrecht said the decision had been made to withdraw plans for this weekend's stadium flypast in Johannesburg because "the forecast weather points to unfavorable conditions for a safe formation flyby." A history of flybys in rugby Stadium flybys have long been tradition at major rugby matches in South Africa, dating back to the 1995 Rugby World Cup final in Johannesburg, when a Boeing 747 swept overhead before the Springboks faced the All Blacks. The SACAA said in a statement that South Africa "is ranked seventh globally and first in Africa for our aviation safety standards by the International Civil Aviation Organization." There have been no fatal accidents in its commercial airline operations space for over four decades, it added. Edited by: Louis Oelofse If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Norway's new King Haakon VIII takes oath in parliament
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.33
New King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance to Norway's consititution in the parliament in Oslo on Tuesday, following him succeeding his father Harald V, who died last week. This follows a day after Harald's coffin was taken to the chapel of the royal palace, where it will remain for the public to pay their last respects until a funeral on September 9. What happened in the parliamentary ceremony? Haakon was driven the short distance from the royal palace to the Storting, or parliament in Oslo. House speaker Masud Gharahkhani read the official announcement of Harald's death and Haakon's succession before the new constitutional monarch took the oath. "I promise and swear that I will govern the Kingdom of Norway in according with its constitution and laws, so help me god, the almighty and omniscient," the 53-year-old said. Queen Mette-Marit skips event amid complications following lung transplant Ahead of he ceremony, the palace said that Haakon's wife Queen Mette-Marit would not be attending. She had made her first public appearance since assuming the title on Monday in the coffin procession but is recovering after a lung transplant in June. In a statement, the palace quoted Are Holm, a pulmonologist at Oslo's University Hospital, as saying that complications following a transplant are not uncommon and that Mette-Marit had experienced them on several occasions, including Tuesday. "As a result, the Queen must remain under observation throughout the day. Unfortunately, the Queen will therefore be unable to attend the swearing-in ceremony at the Storting today," he said. What's the role of Norway's largely symbolic monarchy? Norway's royal family can trace its roots bak to the ninth century. When the country regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters supported the idea of reinstating a largely symbolic constitutional monarchy in a plebiscite. Most political power lies with the elected government and parliament, but Norway's royals retain a predominantly soft power role in diplomacy and promoting the country around the world.
