And when I exported both the Books and Authors datasets as CSV files, the new records and their relationships were included. Finally, I reset the app, and everything returned to the original 40 authors and 180 books. Gemini made some surprisingly good decisions But there's one thing to be aware of I've run lots of experiments on making AI tools produce working code, so I wasn't surprised that Gemini could generate a working app from spreadsheet data. But what did surprise me was the quality of the decisions behind the app. The overview wasn't overloaded, the four charts were easy to understand, the summary cards gave me the headline figures, and deeper information was available when I needed it rather than being pushed onto the main screen. That restraint is probably the part I'd find hardest to reproduce if I started building the interface myself. Gemini effectively acted as the person saying, "That's enough." One thing I'd keep in mind, though, is the size of the dataset. In an earlier experiment with a much larger dataset of around 5,000 records, Gemini struggled to embed something of that size into a single standalone HTML app. That wasn't an issue with this 180-book library, but if I were working with a much larger dataset, I'd consider manipulating or reducing the data first rather than expecting Gemini to package everything into one file. Gemini gave me something that felt like a real app I set out to escape my usual Excel dashboard rabbit hole, where I would normally keep adding charts and tweaking the layout until I convinced myself everything was covered. This time, I handed those decisions to Gemini, and the result was an app that felt like it had been designed around my data rather than around Excel.

item.title: Google's new Pixel phone revives a classic feature that other phones already do better
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.73
The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL bring back notification lights with a feature called HiLight. It's a nice touch, but Google isn't the first to modernize this idea, and its version currently trails what's already on the market. What is HiLight? A glowing ring built around the Pixel 11 Pro's camera flash HiLight is Google's attempt to revive the notification LED, a feature that used to be common on phones before AMOLED displays and always-on screens made it feel unnecessary. On the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, Google repurposed the LED built into the camera flash housing so it can glow in different colors and patterns, giving you glanceable information without lighting up the entire screen or requiring you to pick up the phone. The most visible use case ties into Gemini. When you prompt the assistant, the light shifts through different patterns to indicate whether it's listening, thinking, or responding, turning what used to be a purely audio or on-screen interaction into something you can register out of the corner of your eye. Google is also using HiLight for calls, letting you assign custom colors to specific contacts so you can tell who's calling without turning the phone over. Google frames this as a way to stay connected without distraction, especially when the phone is resting face down on a desk or nightstand. Instead of a buzzing, screen-lit interruption, you get a quiet pulse of color that only escalates to something more if you choose to engage with it. The company has also said more capabilities are coming, including notifications for messages from favorite contacts, suggesting HiLight is meant to grow into a broader notification system over time rather than launching as a finished one. It's a clever piece of hardware reuse, since Google didn't need to add new components to bring the feature to life. But as it stands today, HiLight is a fairly narrow implementation of an idea that other companies have been building out for years. Where does HiLight fall short? Limited to three phones and a small handful of triggers The first limitation is availability. HiLight is exclusive to the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, as well as the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, so anyone buying the standard Pixel 11 doesn't get it. That's a reasonable way to differentiate the higher-end models, but it also means the feature Google is using to market the whole lineup is unavailable to most buyers. The second issue is scope. At launch, HiLight only reacts to two things: Gemini's listening and response states, and incoming calls from contacts you've assigned a color to. It still doesn't support the kinds of notifications people rely on most, like messages, calendar reminders, or third-party app alerts. Google has said this is coming, but for now, HiLight functions more like a proof of concept than a fully useful feature There's also the matter of hardware design. HiLight uses a single LED zone wrapped around the camera flash, which limits how expressive the lighting can be. You get color and pulse patterns, but not the kind of segmented, multi-zone lighting that can represent more complex information at a glance, like a countdown or a progress indicator. Finally, HiLight only works when the phone is face down, which mirrors the same constraint that made old notification LEDs less useful once phones started living in pockets and bags rather than sitting screen-up on a desk. If your phone isn't positioned just right, the feature does nothing, and no companion app or settings menu lets you customize behavior beyond the contact colors Google has already built in. What are competitors doing? Nothing's Glyph interface set a much higher bar already Google isn't the first phone maker to bring notification lighting into the modern era. Nothing Phone has built its entire brand identity around the idea with its Glyph Interface, which debuted on the original Nothing Phone in 2022 and has been refined across several generations since. Instead of one lighting zone, Glyph uses (depending on the phone) multiple independent LED segments on the back of the phone, allowing far more expressive patterns than a single ring around a camera lens. Nothing also went further on functionality. Its Glyph Toys let you turn the lighting system into small interactive tools, including a visual countdown timer, a battery meter, and a flip-to-silence indicator, all controlled through light segments rather than the screen. Perhaps more importantly, Nothing opened a Glyph Developer Kit, letting third-party apps hook into the lighting system and trigger their own custom patterns. That means the feature isn't limited to whatever notifications the manufacturer decided to prioritize at launch, which is exactly where HiLight currently falls short.Other companies have experimented with similar ideas in different forms. Asus has used RGB lighting on its ROG gaming phones for alerts and ambient effects, and we've seen some phones do full-blown back displays. None of these approaches are identical to HiLight, but they demonstrate that the general concept of ambient, screen-free notifications has already had several years to mature elsewhere. Google Pixel 11 Pro - Brand - SoC - Google Tensor G6 - Display - 6.3-inch Super Actua display - RAM - 12 or 16GB - Storage - 256GB, 512GB, or 1TB - Battery - 4850 mAh The Google Pixel 11 Pro brings improved cameras, a faster Tensor G6 chip, and the HiLight notification LED to Android's official flagship phone. Compared to Nothing's approach in particular, HiLight looks like a first attempt rather than a fully realized feature. It's restricted to two phones, a narrow set of triggers, and a single lighting zone, with no way for developers or users to expand it. Google may well build HiLight into something more capable, but for now, it's playing catch-up to an idea the rest of the industry already validated. HiLight is a promising start, not a finish HiLight is a genuinely nice idea, and it's easy to see it growing into something useful. But in its current form, it's a narrower, less flexible take on a concept Nothing and others have already spent years perfecting.

item.title: 6 Intel CPUs that have aged like milk
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.30
Intel has had a colorful history over the years. While many people have made the switch to AMD Ryzen, plenty still remain loyal to Intel—and for good reasons. If you spent a lot of money on an Intel CPU years ago, it's reasonable to expect it to last a very long time. Or perhaps you're building a budget PC and found an older Intel chip that looks like a compelling deal. Whatever the case, be careful with the CPUs on this list, because they've long since outstayed their welcome. The Core i7-2600K has been living on borrowed time for years Time to retire Sandy Bridge for good The i7-2600K is a pretty old chip that came out way back in 2011, so even though it was one of the best consumer-grade processors when it launched, its appearance on today's list should hopefully come as a surprise to no one. This 4-core, 8-thread Sandy Bridge processor was beloved by enthusiasts for its powerful single-core performance in games and apps, which allowed it to stay relevant for many years. It was incredibly overclockable, with many users pushing the stock 3.8GHz Turbo Boost clock up to 4.5GHz with appropriate cooling. However, no amount of raw performance can save it from old age—not that it has a lot of it compared to modern CPUs anyway. This CPU and everything around it is simply too old for a modern machine. DDR3 offers a fraction of the memory bandwidth available from modern DDR4 and DDR5 platforms, and the CPU only supports PCIe 2.0. The ancient interface can become particularly limiting with some modern budget GPUs that rely on fewer but faster PCIe lanes, so you can't just drop in a budget graphics card to upgrade such an old system. If you're still rocking this chip, you're years overdue for an upgrade. The Core i7-4790K was a legend, but its time is up It earned its retirement The i7-4790K was one of Intel's best CPUs of all time. Like the 2600K, it held up incredibly well for years thanks to its excellent single-core performance, while its 4 cores and 8 threads kept it surprisingly competitive against CPUs that came out years later. Although it wasn't quite as overclockable as the 2600K, it was built on a much more efficient 22nm process and came with a respectable 4.4GHz Turbo Boost clock from the factory, which made it more than enough for most gamers. Unfortunately, the 4790K still falls victim to old age, as this chip is now 12 years old. Even entry-level chips have vastly superior IPC (Instructions Per Clock). Thanks to several generational leaps in architectural efficiency, budget chips can now run circles around the once-legendary 4790K. And although its PCIe 3.0 support makes modern graphics card upgrades more feasible (but far from ideal), its reliance on slower DDR3 memory makes it a poor choice for many modern applications and games. The Core i5-7600K aged much worse than anyone could've expected Four cores don't go far anymore The Intel Core i5-7600K came out during a transitional period. Depending on the motherboard, this CPU can support either DDR3L or the much faster DDR4 RAM that's still relevant today. However, that alone isn't enough to hide the fact that this CPU came out in early 2017. It's an old processor that performs about as well as you'd expect. The worst part of the i5-7600K's design is its 4-core, 4-thread architecture. It came out in an era when single-core performance was king in both apps and games, but now that things have shifted in favor of more cores and threads, the i5-7600K is being left behind. In short, you'd be wasting your hard-earned dollars if you combined DDR4, which is a hot commodity right now, with this old CPU that's worth less than a stick of 8GB DDR4 RAM on the used market. The Core i3-8100 was never great, but it's especially bad today Definitely time to upgrade The Intel Core i3-8100 is a generation newer than the i5-7600K, but that doesn't mean much when both CPUs were built on the same 14nm node and use a 4-core, 4-thread design. In fact, the i3-8100 is a bit weaker, but it was also considerably cheaper at just $120, making it a compelling pick for budget gaming and office PCs throughout late 2017 and 2018. Given that popularity, it's not surprising that some people are still running this old chip today. You can still encounter it relatively frequently in the wild. However, just because the i3-8100 technically meets the minimum requirement for running Windows 11 doesn't necessarily make it a good processor. Its lack of Hyper-Threading and measly 3.6GHz base clock with no Turbo Boost make it an extremely underpowered CPU for running modern apps, especially when you consider that its IPC is several generations behind that of modern Intel and AMD chips. The Core i7-8700K is still fast enough to fool you into keeping it This is a hard one to let go Okay, so the i3-8100 was a budget-oriented CPU from 2017, so it stands to reason that a flagship model from the same generation would be considerably better—and it is. On paper, the i7-8700K sounds like it should still be a fairly capable CPU to this day. It has a 6-core, 12-thread design that you can argue is still the sweet spot for many modern games in 2026, and it has a boost clock speed of up to 4.7GHz with some overclocking potential. It can also run Windows 11 and a wide range of modern games and programs, thanks to its extensive instruction set support, although it notably lacks AVX-512. However, even the i7-8700K isn't immune to aging, and after almost 10 years, it's getting harder to justify keeping it in your main machine when newer CPUs are considerably better. You'd need to pair it with an appropriate LGA1151 motherboard to get the most out of this chip, including features like XMP memory support and NVMe SSD support. When you put all those things together, the platform simply isn't worth investing the money these parts tend to go for on the used market, as you'd ultimately still end up with an outdated machine. The Core i5-11400 still looks modern, which makes it a trap for new PC builders Intel fumbled the transition At the surface level, the i5-11400 looks like a fairly compelling CPU for a budget build today. The i5-11400 is a 6-core, 12-thread chip that came out in 2021, making it only five years old. It's not exactly the latest technology has to offer, but a chip that's this old should theoretically still be a fine pick for an office or 1080p gaming PC. However, its age is somewhat misleading, as the Rocket Lake processors that the i5-11400 belongs to are ultimately built on the much-refined but ultimately mature 14nm node that dates all the way back to Intel's 6th-generation Skylake chips. AMD had already been building chips on TSMC's 7nm node for a couple of years by that point and was working toward 5nm, which makes the i5-11400 look like ancient technology by comparison. It runs surprisingly hot and gets inefficient when power limit restrictions are removed, which makes newer budget chips make way more sense. Aside from that, while the i5-11400 does support PCIe Gen 4, which should make it a bit more relevant when pairing it with budget GPUs and NVMe SSDs, the LGA 1200 socket is ultimately a dead end with a severely limited upgrade path. Intel's 12th-generation Alder Lake chips are a substantially better choice, with a couple more generations to upgrade to if you're on a very tight budget, and it's what I strongly recommend picking over the 11400 if you're dead-set on going with Intel. Some of these old CPUs can still make sense today, but context matters While most of the CPUs I've mentioned today don't make much sense in a modern Windows office or gaming PC anymore, that doesn't mean they're ready for the recycling bin. If you're running Linux, you can stretch this older hardware surprisingly far, and these chips can also make a great foundation for a low-cost home server built from old PC parts. Just be wary of their power consumption, because some of these aging CPUs can draw far more power than their performance is worth, making a cheaper, more modern alternative the better choice in the long run.

item.title: Google's new AirTag alternative fails to deliver the one feature I want from an Android tracker
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.16
The Pixel Tag gives Android users their first true first-party rival to Apple's AirTag, backed by Google's massive Find Hub network. But after looking into how it actually works, one omission stood out immediately, and it's the single feature I've wanted from an Android tracker for years. What it's lacking No simultaneous support for Find Hub and Find My Google's Pixel Tag ties itself exclusively to Find Hub, the crowdsourced network formerly known as Find My Device, and there's no other way to pair it. Outside direct Bluetooth range, the tag relies on nearby Android phones to anonymously relay its last known location to Google's servers, all end-to-end encrypted so even Google can't see exactly where the device sits. With Ultra-Wideband precision finding reportedly on board alongside IP67 water and dust resistance, the hardware itself is a legitimate answer to the AirTag, priced close to Apple's tag as well. What the Pixel Tag doesn't do, though, and what no first-party tracker from either company does, is broadcast to two networks at once. Once you set up a Pixel Tag on Find Hub, it reports only to that network. If you own an iPhone, or share a household with someone who does, that device is functionally invisible to your tag, since Apple's Find My network won't recognize or relay location pings from anything that isn't broadcasting the correct signal. This isn't unique to Google — and I'm not singling out Google here by any means. Third-party trackers that advertise support for "both" networks only mean you can choose one platform during setup, not that the tag talks to both at the same time; switching later requires a full factory reset and re-pairing. The Pixel Tag works exactly like every other single-network tracker already on the market, just with a Google logo on it. Why this is important Bigger networks mean faster, more reliable recovery The reason simultaneous network support matters comes down to simple math: a crowdsourced finding network is only as useful as the number of nearby devices that can detect and report your tag's location. Apple's Find My network runs by default on essentially every iPhone, while Android's Find Hub requires users to manually enable a setting called "Network in all areas" to unlock its broadest coverage, meaning fewer Android phones actively contribute than the raw device count suggests. For most people, this asymmetry is invisible until they lose something in a place their tracker's network doesn't reach well. Airports, mixed-ownership households, and cities with a heavier iPhone presence are exactly the scenarios where relying on a single network becomes a liability. If a Pixel Tag is attached to a backpack and it goes missing somewhere dominated by iPhones, the tag has no way of getting picked up unless an Android phone happens to walk by first. On top of that, that Android phone might not even have the specific toggle it needs to broadcast the tag's location. A tag that could broadcast to Find Hub and Find My at the same time wouldn't ask users to pick a side. It would draw on Google's stated figure of more than a billion Android devices and Apple's comparably massive iPhone install base at once, meaningfully raising the odds that a lost item gets spotted quickly. That's a different outcome than choosing the "better" single network and hoping for the best. There's also a practical convenience angle for anyone who switches phones or lives in a mixed household. Right now, moving a tracker from one ecosystem to the other means a factory reset and a fresh pairing process, not a toggle in a settings menu. Are there any alternatives that have this? A few trackers support both, but not at once A handful of trackers already market themselves as compatible with both Apple Find My and Google Find Hub, and they're worth knowing about if this feature matters to you as much as it does to me. Chipolo's Pop, priced at $29, is probably the best-known example, alongside Pebblebee's fifth-generation Clip, Card, and Tag Universal trackers, KeySmart's SmartCard Gen 3, and Rolling Square's AirCard Pro line. The catch is the same across all of them: compatibility isn't simultaneous. Each of these trackers connects to a single network at a time, chosen during initial setup, and switching between them requires a factory reset before re-pairing with the other app. Chipolo has been fairly explicit that this is a deliberate design decision rather than a technical limitation waiting to be patched, since a tag simply can't function on both networks at once as things currently stand. As of now, no consumer Bluetooth tracker from Google, Apple, or any third party genuinely broadcasts to both major finding networks at the same time. The Pixel Tag had a real opportunity to be the exception, given Google's control over both the hardware and the Find Hub software stack, but it chose compatibility with its own ecosystem over interoperability with everyone else's. For what it's worth, though, this probably isn't up to Google to implement either. Even if it could tap into Apple's Find My network, it'll probably have a hard time actually relaying Find My info to Android phones, or Find Hub info to iPhones — which is the scenario where it would become useful. This is one of those things where Google should go all-in and annoy Apple until it eventually opens up Find My, just like it did with RCS. It can be way more useful this way. One network still isn't enough The Pixel Tag is a solid AirTag alternative, but its refusal to bridge Find Hub and Apple Find My keeps Android users boxed into one crowdsourced network. Until a tracker broadcasts to both simultaneously, mixed households and travelers will keep losing out on faster, more reliable item recovery.

item.title: Samsung turned its old smartwatches into e-waste, and the FOSS community is struggling to keep them alive
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.12
Samsung spent over a decade building a smartwatch platform on Tizen, then walked away from it in under two years. Now open-source developers are racing to keep thousands of orphaned watches functional before batteries outlast the software. Why Tizen smartwatches are becoming e-waste Samsung's shutdown timeline leaves working hardware stranded Samsung previously confirmed that support for its Tizen-powered smartwatches would officially end in September 2025, just a year ago, closing out an era that began with the original Galaxy Watch. The wind-down actually started earlier, with Samsung notifying users it planned to sunset Tizen OS by the end of 2025 and immediately blocking new Tizen watch content from the Galaxy Store. The rollback traces back to September 30, 2024, when the Galaxy Store stopped offering paid content for Tizen devices, and purchases users had already made would stop being available for download, though existing downloads already on a device would remain there. This cutoff affects every Samsung Gear smartwatch and Galaxy-branded Tizen watch, including the Galaxy Watch, Galaxy Watch 3, Galaxy Watch Active, and Galaxy Watch Active 2. Devices released after the Galaxy Watch 3, starting with the Galaxy Watch 4 line, are unaffected because Samsung had already moved them onto Wear OS, the Google-backed platform it now builds its watches around. Not only is Wear OS the superior platform when it comes to ecosystem and adoption, but with Samsung's old watches being the only watches to use Tizen, users would run into trouble even if Samsung hadn't cut off downloads. For watch owners, then, the practical result is a watch that still boots and still tells time, but can no longer install new faces, apps, or updates. It isn't bricked, but it's frozen in place, and a frozen smartwatch with no upgrade path is, functionally, headed for a drawer or a landfill. The hurdles toward a second life Tizen's closed hardware layer resists the usual open-source playbook That doesn't mean that developers aren't trying to make something out of these watches, but it's hard. The most active volunteer effort here is AsteroidOS, an open-source, Linux-based smartwatch platform built on components like OpenEmbedded, opkg, Wayland, Qt5, systemd, BlueZ, and PulseAudio, originally developed by French programmer Florent Revest. The project has had real success reviving watches, but almost all of that success has come on Wear OS hardware, not Tizen hardware, and the reason comes down to plumbing. AsteroidOS typically relies on libhybris to port itself onto Android-based watches, a compatibility layer that lets Linux software talk to Android's proprietary hardware drivers. Samsung's Tizen watches were never built with that Android driver layer in the first place. That gap shows up clearly in AsteroidOS's own documentation. For the Samsung Gear S2 Classic, the project notes that the device's vendor kernel is a very old 3.4 build with no existing abstraction for the Tizen hardware layer, so developers are attempting a mainline Linux kernel port instead of the usual libhybris route. But even sourcing the code to work from is a hurdle: downstream kernel sources for that watch are hosted on a contributor's personal GitHub page because Samsung no longer hosts them itself. Flashing anything onto the hardware brings its own friction, since these watches take firmware either wirelessly through Samsung's NetOdin protocol or over USB through the standard Odin tool, sometimes requiring a cable soldered directly to internal pads. Yikes. The project's official porting tracker is candid about where things stand: the Samsung Gear S2, S2 Classic, and S3 might be supported by AsteroidOS eventually, but they will need more work than other watches on the list. This isn't unique to AsteroidOS or even to Samsung. Across the broader modding community, there's a long-running complaint that manufacturers satisfy the letter of the GPL by publishing kernel source that doesn't actually match what shipped on the device, which leaves developers reverse-engineering drivers instead of building from a clean baseline. Will it be done sometime? Progress is real, but it's measured in years, not months There's genuine momentum behind AsteroidOS, just not necessarily where Tizen owners need it most. The project released version 2.0 nearly eight years after its first stable release, and the new version expanded hardware support meaningfully. It now covers Fossil's Gen 4, Gen 5, and Gen 6 watches, the Huawei Watch and Watch 2, several Ticwatch E and Pro models, the Oppo Watch, and the 2015 Moto 360, alongside partial support for a handful of other models. Most of those, notably, are Wear OS devices where the libhybris approach already works. Still, there are signs the Tizen side is inching forward. The Samsung Gear 2 is now the project's first watch supported through a mainline Linux kernel, meaning it runs without needing libhybris at all, and the Asus ZenWatch 2 has picked up very basic support running on a mainline kernel too. That mainline-kernel approach is exactly the strategy being applied to the Gear S2 and S3, so every improvement made for one Samsung watch has a decent chance of transferring to the others. AsteroidOS remains, by most accounts, the only large-scale effort focused specifically on repurposing existing smartwatch hardware rather than building new devices around open software, which means its pace effectively sets the pace for the whole ecosystem. Keep in mind that none of this happens on a corporate roadmap. It's contributor time, old hardware datasheets, and a lot of trial and error on watches Samsung has already stopped thinking about. A working Tizen build on a Gear S3 is plausible within the next year or two based on current porting activity, but there's no firm date, and watches like the original Gear S2 may simply run out of willing contributors before they run out of battery cycles. An old platform's afterlife depends on volunteers, not Samsung Samsung's Tizen watches aren't dead, just abandoned by their maker. Whether they get a real second life now rests on a small, unpaid community reverse-engineering hardware Samsung never intended anyone outside the company to touch.

item.title: Hurricane Marie: What to expect in SoCal this weekend and how to plan accordingly
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 4.72
Hurricane Marie: What to expect in SoCal this weekend and how to plan accordingly - Click here to listen to this article - Here is how Hurricane Marie could affect Labor Day weekend in Southern California: Impacts Forecasters expect a 6- to 8-foot south swell, bringing strong surf and rip currents to beaches and a chance of rain, thunderstorms and a return to muggy weather as thousands of people flock to the coast to celebrate the long weekend. Timing The National Weather Service said higher tides would begin Saturday but peak Monday and Tuesday, with tides topping 7 feet. Humidity The storm is expected to bring back that muggy weather California experienced late last month, with humidity levels ranging from 35% to 50% over the weekend and temperatures in the mid-80s along the coast. Rain There’s also a chance of light rain, measuring up to a quarter of an inch, arriving by Sunday across the region, and a 5% to 10% chance of thunderstorms, according to the weather service. Flooding risk The south swell is also coinciding with a period of evening high tides, which could result in an “increasing chance of moderate coastal flooding” in low-lying areas including Avalon, the Alamitos Peninsula in Long Beach, Malibu and Point Mugu, according to the weather service. Guidance Officials say Hurricane Marie will never get close to the California coast. The closest the storm’s core will get to Los Angeles is 800 miles away. So the storm does not necessarily mean people will have to change weekend plans. “Temperatures will not be overly warm, but it’s a holiday weekend and a warm time of year, so we’re expecting a lot of people are planning beach trips and family events. We’d encourage people, if you are planning a beach trip, to swim where there’s a lifeguard and be aware of rip currents,” said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Oxnard. “If you’re planning an outdoor event and your tolerance for rain is very low,” she added, “we’d encourage people to look into alternate plans.”

item.title: Firefighters rescue man trapped for hours inside San Francisco garbage truck
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 4.34
Firefighters rescue man trapped for hours inside San Francisco garbage truck - Click here to listen to this article - - Firefighters in San Francisco spent two hours rescuing a man trapped in a garbage truck. - The driver called 911 after hearing yelling from inside the truck. Firefighters rescued a man from a garbage truck in San Francisco. The trapped man was discovered when the driver of the Recology commercial collection truck was emptying a dumpster Wednesday at a hotel on the 100 block of Mason Street and heard yelling, according to Robert Reed, a spokesman for Recology. He immediately shut off the truck to investigate and realized that the yelling was coming from inside the body of the vehicle, Reed said. The driver opened a hatch on the outside of the truck and was able to speak briefly with the man who had become trapped inside, Reed said. The driver then called 911. It’s unclear what the man was doing inside the dumpster when the driver picked it up and emptied it into the back of the truck. The San Francisco Fire Department speculated that he might have been scavenging inside . When the waste management company’s commercial collection drivers pick up dumpsters, they first lift them up and intentionally shake them in an effort to confirm that no one is inside, Reed said. When firefighters arrived, they opened the rear end of the truck and used pike poles to remove the garbage by hand, said Samuel Menchaca, a public information officer with the Fire Department. Video the department shared on social media showed firefighters standing atop a mound of garbage in the street as paramedics stood by with a gurney. The driver used the compactor once before realizing someone was inside, Menchaca said. Fearing the man suffered crush injuries, paramedics reached his arm through the trash and administered medication through an IV as the two-hour rescue stretched on, he said. The man, who was conscious when he was removed from the truck, was taken to a hospital. His condition as of Thursday was unknown. Menchaca said he’s encountered people trapped in dumpsters during his 10 years with the Fire Department, but crews usually can rescue them with a ladder. This was considered a technical rescue — one that required special tools and skills — because the man was buried deep in the truck and was unable to get himself out. It was also uniquely hazardous because waste in dumpsters can include items such as knives, glass, needles, batteries and vermin, Menchaca said. One firefighter suffered a laceration injury and was taken to a hospital in stable condition, he said.

item.title: 1 dead, 4 injured after driver, 91, crashes car in Trader Joe's parking lot, police say
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 3.28
1 dead, 4 injured after driver, 91, crashes car in Trader Joe’s parking lot, police say - Click here to listen to this article - One person was killed and four others injured after a 91-year-old woman drove her car into a group of pedestrians in a Trader Joe’s parking lot near the Grove on Thursday afternoon, authorities said. The Los Angeles Fire Department responded at 1:21 p.m. to a report of a vehicle crashed into a stand in a parking lot near the intersection of 3rd Street and Fairfax Avenue. One person was pronounced dead at the scene, and four others were transported to a hospital for treatment, according to the Fire Department. The Los Angeles Police Department is investigating the incident. Helicopter video by KTLA showed Los Angeles Fire Department paramedics treating the injured. A white canopy was set up over the body of the person who was killed, while a white sedan with front-end damage could be seen pinned against a partially crushed structure. Witnesses told the TV station that the driver lost control of her car upon entering the lot, hit a parked vehicle and then swerved into a group of people before crashing into a parking attendant stand. Firefighters could be seen wheeling an older woman in a wheelchair. Information on the identity of the person killed was not immediately available. Mayor Karen Bass said in a statement that she was deeply saddened by the incident and that her office deployed members of its crisis response team to assist. This volunteer-based program provides emotional support and resources to families affected by traumatic incidents. “My heart goes out to everyone impacted,” Bass said. “I thank the brave first responders who were on the scene quickly to render aid.”

item.title: $10 million in Adidas and Nike streetwear found at Arcadia warehouse, all fake, authorities say
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 3.22
$10 million in Adidas and Nike streetwear found at Arcadia warehouse, all fake, authorities say The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said it uncovered a bulk shipment of counterfeit Adidas, Nike and other branded streetwear at a port of entry in early August. Last week, deputies served a search warrant at the commercial warehouse in Arcadia where the shipment was addressed and found more than 25,000 units of counterfeit branded streetwear with an estimated retail value of $10 million, according to a Sheriff’s Department news release. The department had initially intercepted and inspected the shipment at the port based on a tip received by its counterfeit and piracy enforcement team, the department said in the release. Deputies did not make any arrests at the time they served the search warrant. According to sheriff’s officials, the owner of the business operated out of the warehouse is a suspect and the investigation is ongoing.

item.title: No tracker tag? Gemini can now store item locations right in Find Hub
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.82
What you need to know - Gemini can now remember where you left important items, even without a tracker. - You can tell Gemini where you stashed an item or snap a quick photo, and it logs the detail directly to Find Hub. - Then, ask Gemini where your item is later, or view all saved locations in Find Hub's new memory tab. Google’s September Android Drop is introducing a handy upgrade to Find Hub that allows Gemini to remember where you left important items, even if those items don’t have a tracker attached. With the latest change, you can tell Gemini where you put an item instead of using a Bluetooth tracker to find it later. For example, you could say, “Hey Google, remember in Find Hub that I put my passport in my bedroom drawer” and optionally attach a photo for additional context. Gemini then saves that information in a dedicated “remembered items” tab in Find Hub so you can easily get back to it again by just asking where it is. This feature plugs a hole in Google’s current tracking setup. While Find Hub is ideal for tagged belongings, there are plenty of things you routinely misplace — such as passports, spare keys, documents, or other small essentials — that aren’t worth attaching a tracker to. This new feature essentially provides a lightweight memory layer for those items. The feature will be rolled out to Android 16 and newer devices in countries where Gemini and Find Hub are supported. Google says it will be available soon. This is just one part of the September Android Drop, which also includes enhancements such as Motion Assist to help alleviate motion sickness and new upgrades to Google Messages. However, for those of us who spend far too much time looking for lost items, this new Gemini feature may be the most impactful update of them all. item.title: Qualcomm invests in Ultrahuman's future of human computing for our health
item.description:

What you need to know - Ultrahuman announced that it has raised $70 million, thanks to investments from Qualcomm Ventures, Labcorp, Alpha Wave, and more. - The company says these investments will help push its desires to create a world where human computing helps us and our health. - Ultrahuman says it wants computational platforms that can understand the human body, delivering important, crucial pieces of actionable intel. This afternoon (Sept 3), Ultrahuman announced another substantial investment from several companies. The announcement comes at a time when Ultrahuman wants to push the envelope for human computing. A press release reveals that Ultrahuman has received $70 million in investment funding from Qualcomm Ventures, Labcorp, Alpha Wave, Blume, Nexus, Alteria, and more. As stated before, human computing is where Ultrahuman is placing its focus. Moreover, Ultrahuman states this investment will help it shift from "a wearable health company into a human-computer interface company built around the body." Ultrahuman highlights several features daily users will know well: Jade AI, its smart rings, and M1/M2 Live continuous glucose monitoring. Through AI and newer computing systems, Ultrahuman wants more proactive, smart features that deliver true aid. The company discussed how it's continued to evolve the smart ring form factor with science and computational platforms. Ultrahuman drew attention to Pulsomics, which was launched this year. This research platform aids its software and smart rings with the tools required to turn the body's complex signals and information into actionable intel for the user. Power ahead with intel that means something The investments Ultrahuman has received in September will help continue the work it's trying to complete. The company describes it as a feature that brings "specialised health capabilities" to the platform. Take Ultrahuman and Les Mills' partnership from April. It brought workout sessions that rivaled what you'd find in a traditional studio right to your phone. The app would also take advantage of your biomarkers to understand key data, so you know when to push yourself and when to let off. item.title: Google Health's late August update adds more manual workout logging freedom
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.42
What you need to know - Google Health is rolling out v5.07 to Android and iOS users late this week, bringing a major update to manual workout logging. - Users can now "add or adjust" their metrics much easier, and any changes will appear in their post-workout summaries much quicker. - Other updates this week include trail run and incline data in "Running Distance" totals, a fix for Maps in the Health app, and more. Google Health is rolling out one more update late in August that's just what the doctor ordered for fitness users. The company detailed v5.07 in a community post for the Google Health app this morning (Aug 28). This update is rolling out for Android and iOS users late this week, bringing three important "Activity and Fitness" updates. These improvements concern the Health app's manual workout logging capabilities. Google says users can now "add and adjust more metrics when logging an exercise manually." Any edits made should now appear more quickly in your workout summary. What's more, Google Health now lets users add more metrics and workout information when switching from pool swimming to an open swim exercise. If you're taking things outside, the patch notes state the maps experience has been upgraded. Users should experience faster loading times and "smoother rendering." The patch also solves a bug where some users wouldn't see a map after finishing a run or a long walk. Similarly, the patch this week brings trail runs and incline runs into your "Running Distance" totals. For weight trackers, Google highlights its work in bringing more clarity to trends. Users should be able to notice changes more easily in the weight graph. Lastly, a connection problem between Health Connect and certain Android phones has been fixed. Consistency is key This update falls right in line with Google's Nutrition Logging update. It's that ability for users to add the metrics that matter. The details that matter. Its devices and app do a good job of capturing the majority of what we need, but what about those minute details? What if something needs to change? The program's not going to do that. Placing that ability in the user's hands is always a plus. The consistent Google Health updates continue, even into the final days of August. The last major patch that turned heads was the app's Nutrition Logging patch. This arrived in v5.04, in which Google introduced "custom foods." The purpose was to give users a personal touch behind how they log the meals they've eaten. Users can now "create, edit, and delete" their nutrition logs with more freedom. However, while useful, Google Health added another feature: Quick Logging. The company designed this to be an alternative to the traditional Nutrition Logging approach. Users don't have to search or add the specific name of what they've consumed. Instead, all they're required to add is the meal's calories and macronutrients. Google also added Naps in the Today tab and a Cycle Health update, making it easier for users to track long-term trends. item.title: Lumus, Quanta reach licensing agreement for next-gen waveguides for AR glasses that may turn the tide
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.19
What you need to know - Lumus is expanding its partnership with Quanta this week, which brings a licensing agreement between the two companies for next-gen waveguides. - Lumus states Quanta will manufacture its next-gen waveguides: the Z-30 2.0, A-Lens 30 (30-degree FOV), and A-Lens 50 (50-degree FOV). - The company was at CES 2026 where it stated it's future for waveguides for AR glasses will be "thinner, lighter, and easier to produce." This morning (Sept 1), Lumus, a developer of waveguides for several big-name brands, announced a major partnership expansion. In a press release, Lumus announced that it has expanded its partnership with Quanta Computing. This expansion sees the two companies reaching a licensing agreement "to manufacture three new geometric waveguides for AR glasses." The post states Lumus is developing three new waveguides: the Z-30 2.0, A-Lens 30 (30-degree FOV), and A-Lens 50 (50-degree FOV). Thanks to the new licensing agreement, Quanta will handle manufacturing. What we can expect from the Z-30 2.0 is a 30-degree FOV "in a thinner, lighter optical engine." Lumus adds that its latest technology increases the display's brightness, alongside direct prescription lens bonding. The two new A-Lens waveguides (30 and 50) are Lumus' "lower-cost" production solutions. The next-gen A-Lens waveguides are reportedly cutting down the weight and thickness by 50%. However, Lumus states it maintained its image quality and efficiency with this upgrade. This is an ongoing trend that Lumus is trying to introduce into this advancing world of AR glasses. Trimming down waveguide weight and thickness is key, but so is image quality, brightness, and cost. Earlier today, Lumus' CEO, Ari Grobman, said, "Our relationship with Quanta has always been built around solving the practical challenges of bringing advanced AR optics into mass production. This agreement allows us to bring our next generation of lower-cost waveguides into manufacturing with a partner that understands both the technology and the production requirements behind it." Here comes the future, and Lumus is leading it As mentioned before, Lumus creates waveguides for several brands, even for Meta and its Ray-Ban Display Glasses. Earlier this year, Meta announced that it was doubling the production of its Ray-Ban glasses to meet demand. This was something Lumus echoed in its press release this morning. The demand for smart glasses continues to rise, but there's room for improvement. Its work to reduce the weight and thickness of its waveguides for AR glasses is one such upgrade. Additionally, the lower-production-cost A-Lenses are designed to help bring more products to consumers. We'll have to see how things pan out going forward. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android On a related note, Lumus was at CES 2026. This major tech event is where the company first stated what its plans were for the future of AR glasses. Lumus said, "That's the future for us—making these waveguides thinner, lighter, and easier to produce." Its announcement today further echoes that sentiment. item.title: Google adds shared Keep notes and custom themes to Messages
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.81
What you need to know - Google Messages gets two standout updates, including Custom Chat themes and Google Keep integration as part of the September Android Drop. - You can tap the plus button to add a Keep note, letting everyone view, edit, and contribute without leaving the conversation. - Personalize individual chats using curated wallpaper collections (like Animals, Landscapes, or Space) or your own gallery photos. Google's September Android Drop is here, and while there’s a lot to go over, two features for Google Messages are stealing the spotlight: custom chat themes and seamless Google Keep integration. Beginning today, you will be able to bring a Keep note directly into a Google Messages conversation by tapping the plus button. This lets everyone in the chat view, edit, and add to shared notes, whether you're building a grocery list or planning a vacation. The idea appears to be to turn your Messages conversations into the place where plans are actually made. This might be particularly handy for group chats, where information can get lost in the flood of messages. Google is also rolling out Chat theme, which lets you set different backgrounds and color treatments for individual conversations. Google has curated collections of wallpapers to choose from — including Animals, Landscapes, Space, and more — or you can upload your own photo from your gallery. Google recommends everything from a latte theme for a coffee buddy to a beach photo for a vacation group chat. Messages automatically matches the chat bubble colors. This is much more than the simple “Change colors” option we saw back in 2024. It’s rolling out now in Google Messages. Remember, these customizations are just for you, so that beach photo you set for the vacation chat isn’t going to show up on anyone else’s phone. Google actually announced these custom backgrounds and themes a few days ago, in a post to the Google Messages Community, so the September Android Drop is another confirmation that the feature is coming. What you need to know - At IFA 2026, the Moto Watch Ultra was announced with Wear OS, a partnership with Polar for fitness, on a 46mm stainless steel body and a 1.5-inch OLED display. - The continued Polar partnership adds various sleep features like "Serene" for breathing exercises and Nightly Recharge and Sleep Plus Stages for sleep score and more. - The Moto Watch Ultra will be available on September 10 for $349. That's not all Motorola has prepared this midweek. The Moto Watch Ultra was debuted at IFA 2026, expanding the company's wearable portfolio. The Watch Ultra uses Google's Wear OS, incorporating the Play Store and Moto's AI, Qira. However, the major highlight with the Moto Watch Ultra is Motorola's continued partnership with Polar. Polar excels at wearable sports and fitness, and it's bringing that prowess to the Moto Watch Ultra. For its wellness features, the Watch Ultra sports "Serene." This breathing exercise mode delivers real-time "biofeedback" to help the user calm their breathing and reach a more optimal rhythm. Nightly Recharge and Sleep Plus Stages help users understand their recovery and sleep score. If you're looking to get more active and track your progress, Polar's involvement brings a breadth of features. Consumers will find expected features like Activity Goal, Activity Score, and Active Intensity Zones. What's more, Smart Calories delivers an overview of your daily calories burned, alongside an Inactivity Alert and Energy Sources (metabolic insights). The Moto Watch Ultra offers a 1.5-inch OLED display on a 46mm stainless steel body. Inside, you'll find Qualcomm's Snapdragon W5 Plus Gen 1 SoC. The Watch Ultra is said to last two days with "active use" with its AOD (always-on display) disabled. Consumers can choose between the "breathable" silicone band (PANTONE Black Beauty or PANTONE Mountain View) or the leather strap (Black Beauty or Nuthatch). Not bad Elsewhere, Motorola highlights the "Running Coach." As it sounds, you can expect a guided experience for new and veteran runners (walking, too). The Watch Ultra will expand to more places, such as T-Mobile, Metro by T-Mobile, AT&T, Xfinity Mobile, and Consumer Cellular, "in the coming months." Android Central's Take I'm pleasantly surprised by the Moto Watch Ultra. Motorola already has what you'd consider a "basic" watch. It misses the Ultra tag. The design is fairly simple, very watch-like. The Watch Ultra feels cleaner to me. I also think the Polar partnership is a huge win for Motorola to continue with the device. I already think I hear my colleague Derrek Lee putting one on his wrist and heading outside. item.title: Android 17 QPR2 Beta 4 is shaping up to be Google’s best beta yet
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.78
What you need to know - Android 17 QPR2 has officially hit Platform Stability with Beta 4, meaning APIs are locked and the update is in its final stretch focused entirely on system polish and bug fixes. - Google fixed several Pixel pain points, including overheating, unexpected reboots, gesture navigation, battery-limit charging, Recents, Bluetooth audio, and screen-recording issues. - Hardware support gets attention, too, with fixes for USB-C XR mirroring, 3D smart-glasses displays, and low-light Face Unlock. Google’s Android 17 QPR2 beta cycle is moving into its final stretch. Beta 1 was released on July 20, with Beta 2 following on 3 August and Beta 3 only 11 days later. Now, Beta 4 has arrived with a long list of fixes, and more importantly, Android 17 QPR2 has reached Platform Stability. That milestone means Google has locked the API surface for the release, giving developers a much more stable target for testing apps ahead of the update reaching users more broadly. QPR2 is a pretty small SDK update that has no planned behavior changes, so this build is much more about polish, stability, and fixing things that could make a Pixel frustrating to use. Critical bug fixes And there are a lot of things to fix. As per the changelog, Beta 4 resolves a bug in thermal management that could cause overheating and reboots. Another solution is for the 80% battery limit feature that takes way too long to finish charging the last 2%. Google has also fixed broken gesture navigation and a transparent status bar that could appear after full-screen video with specific display-cutout settings enabled. You'll see that polish in everyday Pixel features as well. The search in the app drawer may stop accepting text input. Bluetooth call audio may be routed incorrectly through the phone speaker. The Recents screen may freeze or visually clip app cards. Google also fixed a bug with screen-recording audio that could cause microphones to be unavailable to apps such as Gboard and Gemini until a reboot. There’s some interesting hardware cleanup, too. Beta 4 brings back screen mirroring for USB-C XR glasses and fixes blank screens in 3D mode for connected smart glasses. It also solved Face Unlock issues in low-light conditions that would take users straight to a PIN. Android 17 QPR2 is also beefing up the protection against call-forwarding scams by limiting some USSD-based forwarding commands and requiring confirmation when users manually dial them. Positive user feedback Reddit users who own Pixels are giving surprisingly positive early feedback. One Pixel 9a owner called Beta 4 the most stable QPR2 build yet, with the lag gone and performance noticeably improved. Another Pixel 8 owner said that the phone now feels "fast." Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Beta 4 isn’t perfect, though. Some testers complained about oversized text and a lower display resolution after installing the update, though one user said a reboot fixed everything. At least one tester also states that a Bluetooth routing issue for incoming calls has persisted across all four QPR2 betas, with them having to manually select the Bluetooth audio source. Beta 4 is rolling out to a wide range of Pixel phones and tablets, with Pixel 11 support listed as “coming soon” for now. Some early beta testers on Reddit said a download of about 671MB on a Pixel 9 Pro XL, with a few rollout quirks and some confusion on the update screen. If you're already a Pixel owner and are enrolled in the beta, you'll get the update over the air. Just know that if you leave the program after installing Beta 4, it can wipe your data. What you need to know - The Google TV Streamer has jumped from $100 to $150 at the Google Store and Best Buy. - Retailers including Amazon may still have older stock at the original price, but supplies could disappear quickly. - The Nest lineup also gets across-the-board markups, with all five Nest cameras and doorbells seeing price increases of $20 to $50. If you've been holding off on picking up Google’s smart home hardware, your hesitation just got a lot more expensive. The tech giant has quietly increased prices across its streaming and security hardware lineup. The Google TV Streamer arrived in 2024 for $100, replacing Chromecast as Google’s flagship streaming box. It was also pretty easy to find below that price, with holiday discounts knocking a few bucks off. Now, Google has quietly bumped up the device’s price by $50 to $150, as spotted by 9to5Google. Google mentions increased component costs, with the Streamer’s 4GB of RAM and 32GB of storage making memory costs a likely factor behind the increase. Other recent Google hardware has already been under the same broader cost pressures. The Nest lineup is taking a hit, too. Google has increased the price of all five of its currently available cameras and doorbells by $20 to $50. Both the wired and battery Nest Doorbells now cost $200, up from $180. Interestingly, the Nest Cam with Floodlight bundle is still priced at $280, and the Nest Hub, thermostats, and the new Google Home Speaker remain unchanged for now. item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra with hacking risks in check
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.37
What you need to know - GPT-6 Astra is the first OpenAI model to hit the "critical" cybersecurity threat level, but deployment is moving forward with significant safeguards in place. - It is currently limited to defensive tasks like secure code review. Advanced capabilities like exploit creation are blocked for now, but trusted users in the Daybreak program will eventually get access to complex workflows. - Astra drastically outperforms GPT-5.6 Sol, hitting a perfect 100% on ExploitBench and 42.4% on ExploitGym. OpenAI just released GPT-6 Astra, and it’s the company's first model to reach the “critical” threat level in the company’s Preparedness Framework for cybersecurity. Despite these unprecedented security risks, OpenAI is moving ahead with the deployment. That doesn't mean GPT-6 Astra is being rolled out as an unrestricted hacking tool. The version rolling out now will do defensive work such as secure code review and patching, but will not entertain more advanced requests like creating proof-of-concept exploits, OpenAI says. The company adds that it intends to relax some of those restrictions with its Daybreak program for trusted users, ultimately supporting workflows such as vulnerability validation, malware analysis and detection engineering. So, how did we arrive at this point? OpenAI had to severely lock down its development pipelines after the recent mess where rogue AI agents hacked the Hugging Face platform. Astra is a huge step up from GPT-5.6 Sol in capabilities. Massive performance leap In OpenAI’s testing, the new model scored 100% on ExploitBench, compared to 78.5% for GPT-5.6 Sol. It also scored 42.4% on ExploitGym against 30.3% for its predecessor. More worrying, Astra uncovered and took advantage of two new zero-day vulnerabilities in the course of testing, which OpenAI says it is reporting to the appropriate maintainers. OpenAI explains that GPT-6 Astra is built on improvements to pre-training, reinforcement learning, alignment, and computer use. It can run software, surf the web, write code, and complete multistep tasks. OpenAI says its OSWorld 2.0 testing shows it’s about 47% faster per task than GPT-5.6 Sol, while scoring 72.6% vs 65.7%. The company says it has responded with stronger jailbreak resistance, broader monitoring, encrypted model checkpoints, tighter access controls, and misalignment monitoring across tool-using deployments. Astra also outperformed Sol in remaining within authorized boundaries. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android But one big weakness that OpenAI does acknowledge is that it’s actually a lot harder to monitor. Internal testing indicated that GPT-6 can actively influence its own "chain of thought” reasoning to avoid leaving incriminating evidence. In adversarial situations, the model has even sandbagged its performance to fly under the radar and avoid internal monitors. For developers, Astra costs $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, with an accelerated API at twice the normal price. It’s rolling out now to a limited number of people before it’s available to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise users and the API and Amazon Bedrock. item.title: Meta just closed another loophole that could let its smart glasses record discreetly
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.41
What you need to know - Meta's latest smart glasses update stops video recording if someone covers the capture LED after filming begins. - The update closes a loophole that previously allowed users to start recording first and then cover the LED afterward. - Meta says several businesses offering capture LED tampering services have already shut down following its changes. Meta has started rolling out another update for its AI glasses that closes yet another loophole that allowed users to record discreetly while keeping the capture LED covered. Earlier this year, Meta took several major steps to address privacy concerns surrounding its smart glasses. The company rolled out a mandatory update for its Ray-Ban Meta, Oakley Meta, and Meta AI glasses that prevented the camera from recording if the capture LED had been tampered with or covered. Meta said the change was designed to make sure people around the wearer can clearly tell whenever the glasses are capturing photos or videos. Now, the company is rolling out another update that closes a loophole in that system. Meta VP Alex Himel shared on Threads that the new update will stop video recording if someone covers the capture LED after recording has already started. Until now, users could apparently get around Meta's protection by starting a recording while the LED was visible and then covering it afterward. With the latest update, doing that will automatically stop the recording. Himel added that Meta will continue rolling out updates like this to make sure the capture LED can "reliably alert bystanders" whenever photos or videos are being captured and saved to someone's gallery. Meta also claims that its efforts against LED tampering are already having a deterrent effect. According to the company, several businesses that previously offered services to disable or cover the capture LED on Meta's smart glasses have already shut down. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android In fact, the company has also launched an awareness campaign explaining what the capture LED actually means. With AI glasses quickly becoming a much bigger product category, Meta says not everyone is familiar with the light or knows when someone is recording. The company now seems to be heavily marketing these new privacy protections in an effort to build back some of that trust. In addition to these changes, Meta says it has removed accounts from its platforms that engaged in this behavior, alongside posts that provided instructions or advertised services for tampering with the capture LED. Honestly, it's pretty sad that things have reached this point. In my opinion, protections against something as obvious as covering the recording light should have been built into these glasses from the beginning. But nonetheless, Meta is finally closing these loopholes, and hopefully, it makes discreet recording with its smart glasses much harder going forward. item.title: Google Messages just became a lot more fun with new chat themes, but it could learn a thing or two from Apple Messages
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.18
Google has been steadily improving its Messages app over the years, especially since the advent of RCS. We've been seeing some fun features arriving in the app, such as Voice Moods and Selfie GIFs. However, until now, customizing your chat look has been limited to just changing the color of your chat bubbles, and even that was pretty limited. Now, Google has introduced new chat themes, which can fully transform your conversations. It lets you pick from a selection of photos (or you can upload your own) as a background and even changes the color of chat bubbles to match. It's actually a pretty fantastic upgrade to the Google Messages experience that makes it feel much more fun, although I do think it went a step further. I'll walk you through changing your chat theme in Google Messages and explain why I want a little more. How to change your chat theme in Google Messages 1. Open a message. Tap the three dots in the top right corner of your chat. 2. In the overflow menu, tap Chat theme. 3. Select from among the provided themes or tap Choose a photo to upload an image from your gallery. 4. Select a photo from within a theme or within your gallery. Tap Next. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android 5. Choose a color combination in the Colors row or stick with the automatic selection. You can preview your theme and colors in the image above. 6. Tap Apply to save your theme to the chat. Enjoy your new chat theme! Chat themes are fun, but... Chat themes are something I've been wanting in Google Messages for some time. On the one hand, I like the relative simplicity of the app, but on the other hand, it can feel quite monotonous with the simple black or white background. Changing chat bubble colors were a nice way to break up some of that monotony, but they were limited to just nine color options and none of them were particularly good. Chat themes is a great step forward, and in some ways, makes Google Messages feel as fun as Backgrounds on Apple Messages. However, there are a few things I think Google could have implemented to make this a much more full-featured experience. It feels like a missed opportunity that Google didn't implement Nano Banana in any way whatsoever. Gemini is already integrated into Google Messages, letting you chat with the AI or remix images shared in a chat. I would have loved to see an option to generate a background on-device with Nano, similar to how iPhones let you describe or edit preloaded backgrounds with Apple Intelligence. I also think Google could take chat themes a step further by having them sync across devices. Right now, when using Chat themes, you'll notice at the top of the page that "only you will see these changes." That means once you apply a theme, it will show up for you but not for the recipient. On the one hand, I get it, because your friend may pick a theme that you find annoying, inappropriate, or just don't like. However, even Apple Messages syncs backgrounds for both users across iPhones, and some apps like Instagram and Facebook Messenger also sync chat backgrounds (though with a limited selection), which has led to some fun surprises and "fights" over which one to keep. As one friend puts it, it would be fun swapping a background "and seeing how long it takes someone to notice." Perhaps Google can add a toggle that lets the person changing it sync their background choice across devices, while letting the recipient either keep it or select their own without syncing it back. Finally, I've noticed a weird bug that freezes the Google Messages app when I tap a theme but don't apply it, then exit back to the chat. Fully exiting the Google Messages app will bring things back to normal. My colleague, Nick Sutrich, has also noticed this, though it doesn't seem to occur for everyone; a friend hasn't experienced this behavior. I do notice, however, that when he swipes back, he's met with a dialog asking if he wants to leave the page without saving the changes. That only appears for me when I opt to reset the background to default and try to exit without saving. It's a relatively small bug that Google can hopefully fix soon. Derrek is the managing editor of Android Central, helping to guide the site's editorial content and direction to reach and resonate with readers, old and new, who are just as passionate about tech as we are. He's been obsessed with mobile technology since he was 12, when he discovered the Nokia N90, and his love of flip phones and new form factors continues to this day. As a fitness enthusiast, he has always been curious about the intersection of tech and fitness. When he's not working, he's probably working out. item.title: Cisco patches three critical vulnerabilities as part of 'comprehensive internal security review'
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 6.09
- Cisco patched eight IOS XR flaws, including three critical (CVE‑2026‑20274, CVE‑2026‑20279, CVE‑2026‑20212) - Vulnerabilities allow unauthenticated exploitation, improper access control, and crafted input execution - No abuse reported; patches urged, with iACL workarounds for Nexus 9000 devices using Silicon One ASIC Cisco patched eight vulnerabilities affecting its IOS XR operating system, including three critical-severity ones. It urged its customers to apply the patches as soon as possible, even though it stressed that there is no evidence any of these were abused in the wild. The company detailed its findings in two advisories published on the same day - September 2. In the first one, it disclosed seven vulnerabilities, including two critical-severity ones: CVE-2026-20274 and CVE-2026-20279. Both carry a severity rating of 9.8/10 (critical). The former is an improper control of a resource during its lifetime flaw - a network-based, low complexity, vulnerability that requires no authentication or user interaction to be exploited. The latter is described as an improper access control vulnerability that can lead to the same consequences. Fixes and mitigations These flaws, along with five others, affect all releases of Cisco IOS XR Software, including Cisco IOS XR7 (LNT) Software, regardless of device configuration, the company explained. There are no available workarounds, and installing the provided patch is the only way to mitigate the risk. The third flaw, disclosed in a separate advisory, is tracked as CVE-2026-20212. Successfully exploiting this one allows attackers to connect to an affected device and send crafted input that could be executed as code, without root privileges. “The exploitation of this vulnerability could also cause the S1HAL process to crash, which could cause the device to reload,” Cisco explained. This bug affects Cisco Nexus 9000 Series Switches if they include a Silicon One ASIC, the company stressed. A possible workaround is to use infrastructure access control lists (iACLs) to allow only required management and control plane traffic that is destined to the affected device. There is also the option of iACLs only being used to explicitly deny all TCP packets that are destined to a locally configured IP address with a destination port of 43210 or 43211. item.title: Why did FulcrumSec hackers try to extort Manchester Airports Group, and what happens now the data is leaked? The experts weigh in
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 6.00
Following the aftermath of the Manchester Airports Group cyberattack - where hackers made off with the data of 8.7 million people - the hackers have now posted the entire database for sale on the dark web. The group behind the attack, FulcrumSec, attempted to get Manchester Airports Group (MAG) to pay for the security of the database, promising that it wouldn’t be released if the company paid a settlement. But as all companies should do when faced with extortion, MAG didn’t play ball. Now FulcrumSec wants to try and maximise the damage of the cyberattack, and has listed the database containing email addresses, phone numbers, vehicle registrations and postcodes online in the hopes a fellow hacking group will find value in the data. What happens when extortion fails, and why didn’t MAG pay? In the past, when companies faced ransomware attacks or data breaches, they would sometimes quietly pay the hackers for their silence. Companies feared serious reputational harm and loss of business would cost more in the long run than the perpetrators were asking for. But this created an incentive for hackers to carry out more attacks. After all, if companies aren’t kicking up a fuss about being hacked or reporting the attack to the authorities, hacking groups can launch more attacks on other companies that are completely unaware of their tactics. In order to counter this, authorities and cyber experts from around the world issued guidance that under no circumstances should companies pay for the safe return of their data. By removing the incentive from ransomware attacks and data breaches, the hope is that hackers will get bored or not see enough ROI, and therefore stop. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! But the 500GB database of data on over 8.7 million people is ripe pickings for other cybercriminals looking to launch highly specific phishing attacks or scam campaigns. While FulcrumSec may not make any money from the attack, they can seriously enhance the damage of the attack by offering the data for free for others to use. A successful scam or phishing attack can steal banking and financial details, allowing other groups to steal even more money off the back of the attack. Expert perspectives on MAG extortion and customer data - Dray Agha, senior manager of security operations at Huntress: While Manchester Airports Group followed official guidance by refusing to pay the ransom, the release of 8.7 million records creates an immediate risk for passengers. We expect other criminals to use this freely available database of vehicle registrations, postcodes and contact details to craft highly convincing phishing attacks. Anyone who has used parking, lounges or Wi-Fi at these airports must treat unexpected messages about their travel with extreme caution. - Muhammad Yahya Patel, vCISO and cybersecurity advisor for EMEA at Huntress The "free release" model is deliberately designed to maximise harm and reputational damage as a warning to the next target. Publishing almost nine million records for free isn't just punishment for MAG it's a marketing campaign aimed at every other organisation watching. Pay up, or your customers' data gets handed to every fraudster and scammer on the internet at no cost. Refusing to pay a ransom is the right call. But nearly nine million people are now paying a different price for a decision that was never theirs to make. - Danny Jenkins, Co Founder & CEO at ThreatLocker Unfortunately, once data is made public, it can’t be hidden again. The most important thing consumers can do is focus on basic cyber hygiene. Use a unique password for every website, learn how to identify phishing scams, and monitor your credit report. Be highly suspicious of emails that create a sense of urgency, offer something that seems too good to be true, or ask you to reset your password. When in doubt, look up the phone number for the alleged sender yourself, rather than using a number provided in the email, and call to confirm whether the communication is genuine. - Brian Higgins, security specialist at Comparitech: Whilst the airports breached in this attack don't appear to have had any financial data compromised the risk to affected or associated customers is very real. With so much other information freely available in the wild it is vital that airport users stay highly vigilant for some time to come. Any and all unsolicited contact; whether online, by telephone or even home visit approaches, should be viewed as suspicious. Never engage until you've taken time to check credentials/veracity etc. Research advice from trusted sources like the NCA or Information Commissioner and share it with your family and friends. Look for ways to increase digital and physical security like two factor authentication on Apps and devices or Smart Home tech. When this breach was first reported by the Manchester Evening News the comments were quite telling. Affected parties were quick to identify potential vulnerabilities over and above the breach of financial and banking details. Home addresses, vehicle registrations and time spent away from home all add up to some excellent opportunities for criminal exploitation, not to mention the usual follow-up phishing campaigns common in this type of incident. As AI makes data aggregation swift and easy consumers are waking up to the fact that criminals can monetise successful breaches in increasingly inventive ways. It’s no longer enough for data owning organisations to advise post-attack vigilance and turn to their backups. Victim communities rightly expect better protected networks and systems over and above established norms. As the marketplace grows less fearful and more angry when breaches are made public we may see more emphasis on cyber crime prevention which can only be a good thing. - Denis Calderone, CTO at Suzu Labs: The 8.7 million number is attention-grabbing, but it deserves some context. MAG has confirmed that the vast majority of those records are email addresses collected through airport WiFi sign-ups. A much smaller subset includes phone numbers, vehicle registrations, and postcodes from customers who actually completed parking or lounge bookings. No payment data, no passwords, no passport information. So despite this affecting airports, which is obviously a sensitive subject, the actual data sensitivity for most affected individuals is relatively low. What's more interesting to us from a technical standpoint is the attack path. MAG told The Register that attackers compromised one of their internal systems and then went on to steal files from a database hosted by a third party. That's a pivot upstream into a data provider, not downstream into operational systems. What remains unclear is whether the data was exfiltrated directly from that third-party environment or whether it was pulled back through MAG's network first. That distinction matters for understanding where detection controls failed and who was responsible for monitoring the egress. The UK's Civil Aviation Authority has a Cyber Assessment Framework for Aviation, developed with the NCSC, that mandates strict separation between IT systems and operational technology. We don't know whether MAG was formally operating under that framework at the time of this incident, but I would be very interested to find out. Because the segmentation appears to have held here. Flight operations, baggage handling, terminal systems, etc., all were unaffected. The lateral movement went upstream toward a data provider, not downstream toward the systems that keep planes in the air. - Seemant Sehgal, CEO and Founder at BreachLock: This data was initially collected because passengers needed a login, and somewhere along the way, the sensitivity of what was accumulating in that database stopped getting the same scrutiny as the network itself. Vehicle registration details, postcodes, and contact information across three major airports are a profiling dataset, and whoever held it for ransom understood its value better than the organization storing it did.
