item.title: A N.Y. hospital tried to close its birthing center. This city united to fight back
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Science Score: 4.74
A N.Y. hospital tried to close its birthing center. This city united to fight back TROY, N.Y. — Like many residents of this aging industrial city on the Hudson River, Starletta Washington was stunned when she heard Troy's last remaining hospital planned to close its birthing center. "It was devastating," said Washington, who heads the local YWCA. Washington was born at the hospital and had her children there. She couldn't believe families would now have to get to a hospital half an hour away or face the prospect of an emergency delivery. "Nobody else was going to be born in the city of Troy unless they were born on a city bus, in the back of a cab, or, disgustingly, on the side of the street?" Washington said. "Blew my mind." Troy wasn't the first community to face this prospect. Since 2010, hospitals have closed hundreds of maternity units as cities and towns shrink and hospitals consolidate into larger systems. Troy found a more hopeful ending. Elected officials from both major parties joined patient advocates, mothers, midwives, doulas and community leaders like Washington to challenge Trinity Health, the large Catholic health system that owns Troy's hospital and birthing center. The campaign even united Planned Parenthood and the Catholic diocese. "Whether you were Republican or Democrat, or if you didn't vote, it literally brought everyone together," said Carmella Mantello, the city's Republican mayor. "Everyone just said, 'We can't let this happen.'" Throughout the country, healthcare remains a flash point as politicians square off ahead of November's elections. But in many places, Americans are also quietly finding common ground. In this small city, citizens were brought together by frustration over large, corporate health systems that can seem to put profits over patients. And they resolved to work together to keep critical medical services in their community. A community institution Babies have been delivered at Samaritan Hospital on a hill above Troy since this city's once bustling factories produced most of America's shirt collars a century ago. More recently, Samaritan's Burdett Birth Center had become a model for patient-focused care. Midwives and doulas work alongside OB-GYNs and support mothers who want to avoid a delivery by cesarean section unless necessary. Patient safety advocates have pushed for years to reduce surgical deliveries, which can lead to complications. At Burdett, only about a quarter of newborns are delivered by C-section, compared with about a third statewide, according to 2025 hospital data. Burdett also had fewer preterm births and fewer babies with low birth weights. "I wouldn't go anywhere else," said Lidia Zambrano-Madera, who gave birth to both her children at Burdett with the help of a midwife. For Zambrano-Madera, who recently opened a children's play center in Troy, Burdett offered another advantage: It was just five minutes from home. But three years ago, Trinity Health, a multibillion-dollar Michigan-based hospital system, said the birth center was losing money and would close. Families from Troy and surrounding Rensselaer County would have to deliver at another Trinity hospital in Albany, up to a half-hour's drive away. The hospitals are branded under St. Peter's Health Partners in the Albany region. "We've been frantic about trying not to cut the care at the bedside," said Steven Hanks, a physician who oversees Trinity hospitals in New York and New England. "But, you know, you get to a point where you can only consolidate so much. You can only spread people so thin, and then you have to start taking harder looks at your actual services." Corporate backlash Trinity's plans — news of which broke in a local newspaper — came without warning, surprising the obstetrical staff and community leaders. They set off a firestorm. Within days, midwives, mothers, community leaders and politicians held a rally at the YWCA in downtown Troy. Others would follow. Volunteers led by doulas and midwives made T-shirts and handed out pink "Save Burdett" signs at the local farmers market. Activists were outraged that the hospital hadn't adequately assessed the impact of the closure, particularly on low-income families. They conducted a community survey that found 1 in 4 Troy residents didn't have access to a car and would have trouble getting to Albany. The campaign drew on deep connections that many residents had to Burdett. "They realized what a gem Burdett is, and what a great community service they provide," said Jessica Hayek, a doula and birth educator who helped lead the campaign. Hayek and others also tapped into deep-seated frustration with Trinity, a healthcare behemoth that operates 91 hospitals and last year recorded more than $25 billion in revenue and a healthy operating margin that topped 5%. "Trinity Health is in the Midwest, and they are not in the community," Hayek said. "So when you're looking at just the numbers from an office in the Midwest somewhere, they're not looking at the benefit that this place has on the community." Hayek describes herself as a liberal Democrat. But Trinity's focus on its bottom line also irked many Republicans, including Mantello, who was the City Council president at the time. "The whole hospital scene has changed," Mantello said. "It was very personable. You had nurses and doctors who were able to give more care and spend more time with patients." Now, by contrast, many hospitals have what she described as a "more corporate type of atmosphere." Even the Catholic bishop decried the planned closure of the birthing center as out of step with the values of his faith and the hospital system's. "Nothing is more central to the Catholic healthcare mission than supporting life and all those who bring it into the world," Bishop Edward Scharfenberger said after Trinity announced the closure plan. Scharfenberger has since retired. A bipartisan solution Despite the backlash, Trinity Health executives for months insisted they had no choice. The system even sued the state to push through the closure. Ultimately, though, powerful state officials, including New York Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat, joined the fight to save the birthing center, launching an investigation into the proposed closure and hosting a daylong hearing in Troy. State Assemblyman John T. McDonald III, a Democrat who represents Troy, worked with Republican elected officials, including the county executive and the state senator representing Troy, to secure $5 million in state funding to help keep Burdett open. "You had a Democrat and a bunch of Republicans all working together on the same issue," McDonald said, "because, at the end of the day, our job is to listen to what the public has to say." Nearly a year after announcing the closure, Trinity reversed itself and said Burdett would remain open. Lois Uttley, a New York City-based researcher and activist who has worked with communities facing hospital consolidation, said Troy's success reflects a growing bipartisan suspicion of big corporate healthcare organizations. "The executives of these health systems will tell the community that joining a big health system will be good, that the quality of care will improve, that efficiencies will mean they can keep the costs low," Uttley said. "But what I have seen over the last 30 years of work is that those promises often are broken." As hospitals close or downsize, she said, communities are catching on. "They're becoming more skeptical." There's another, more hopeful lesson in Troy's success, said McDonald, the state assemblyman. "If we take down our swords," he said, "and put out our arms, maybe we can get something done." KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

item.title: Why too many women are prescribed antibiotics for UTIs they don't have
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Science Score: 4.35
Why too many women are prescribed antibiotics for UTIs they don't have Maria Uloko sees the same scenario in her urology practice in Los Angeles every day: A woman has been diagnosed with recurrent urinary tract infections (which means she's had at least two in six months or three in a year), taken repeated rounds of antibiotics, and feels confused as to why the infections keep coming back. Then, Uloko tells these patients something that often feels both revelatory and frustrating. "Most of them don't actually have UTIs, even though that's been their diagnosis time and time again," she says. "In fact, millions of women are being treated for UTIs they may not actually have." Uloko is the co-author of a recent study published in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that backs this up. She and her fellow researchers reviewed the medical records of 253 women with recurrent UTIs and found that just 15% showed evidence of problems that were limited to the bladder or urinary tract. The remaining 85% had signs of hormonally driven inflammation of the vulvar region and 75% had pelvic floor dysfunction. These conditions produce identical symptoms as UTIs — burning with urination, urgency, frequency, and/or lower abdominal pain — but require different treatment. "What we found is that in women with recurrent UTIs, the majority didn't have a bladder problem at all; they had a vulvar problem," says Uloko. Uloko's study provides insights that could help patients with urinary tract symptoms, says Melissa Kaufman, professor and chief of the division of reconstructive urology and pelvic health at Vanderbilt University Medical Center who was not involved in the research. "These findings will accelerate our discipline's investigations into a comprehensive unifying hypothesis to more precisely optimize care," she said via email. Why are these vulvar conditions getting missed? One reason is the current diagnostic process for UTIs. When a patient comes in with classic UTI symptoms, the first thing most clinicians order is a screening test called a urinalysis, which detects the presence of inflammation — not bacteria. To determine whether there's a bacterial infection, that urine must be cultured. What's more, that urine sample must be a "clean catch," which requires thoroughly cleaning the urinary tract opening and surrounding areas and collecting only the midstream of urine, something not all patients are instructed on how to do, says Kaufman. "But because patients are suffering in real time, clinicians often start them on a broad-spectrum antibiotic right away if that urinalysis comes back positive and adjust the medication if needed once the culture comes back," says Uloko. There's also a lack of training among medical professionals, says Uloko, adding that doctors are taught that when a patient presents with classic UTI symptoms, it should be considered a UTI until proven otherwise. "We do the urinalysis, send the culture, start the antibiotic, and for the patients who get better, amazing," she says. For the patients who don't get better, the cycle continues "because the doctor, who hasn't been taught how the vulva relates to urinary, colon, and sexual health, doesn't know what else to do." Overlooked causes of UTI-like symptoms The truth is that lower urinary tract symptoms that may look and feel like a UTI can be caused by things other than bacteria, says Lindsey Burnett, a urogynecologist, assistant professor at the University of California, San Diego, and co-author with Uloko on the study. For example, a loss of hormones to the vulvar tissue can cause inflammation, a condition called hormonally mediated vestibulodynia. This can happen due to natural physiological changes to hormones that happen during breastfeeding and menopause. It can also happen if you're taking medications that impact hormones. For example, oral birth control is one of the most commonly prescribed anti-androgen medications that can disrupt the hormonal balance in the vulvar tissue and cause inflammation that prompts UTI-like symptoms. Other commonly prescribed medications that can cause vulvar inflammation include medications for acne (such as isotretinoin, sold as Accutane) and hair loss (such as minoxidil, sold as Rogaine); oncologic treatments for breast, ovarian, and/or uterine cancer (such as aromatase inhibitors and selective estrogen receptor modulators); and hormone therapies for endometriosis or fibroids. The genitourinary syndrome of menopause, or GSM, a collection of symptoms caused by the decline in estrogen and other sex hormones during menopause, can also affect the tissues of the vagina, vulva, bladder, and urethra and cause UTI-like symptoms. Chronic inflammation due to GSM can also prompt the pelvic floor muscles to go into a state of reactive guarding, says Uloko, which can make them hypertonic (too tight) and can further disrupt bladder function. Things get even more complex when you consider that these hormonal changes can also alter the balance of good and bad bacteria in the urinary tract and vagina. When levels of hormones like estrogen and testosterone are disrupted, the good bacteria decline, which puts patients at risk for developing bacterial UTIs, says Uloko. "So now you have a patient who is testing positive on urinalysis, sometimes growing actual bacteria on culture, receiving antibiotics, getting temporary relief mostly because of the anti-inflammatory properties in antibiotics, and then cycling right back into symptoms because the underlying hormonal and vulvar dysfunction was never addressed." What to ask your doctor to make sure you're getting the best care If you suspect your recurrent UTIs may be caused by a vulvar issue that has yet to be diagnosed, ask your clinician a few key questions: Was my urine culture positive for bacteria? Remember, the first test typically given to patients who present with UTI-like symptoms is a urinalysis, which tests for inflammation — not a bacterial infection. Could my symptoms be due to hormone changes affecting my vulva due to medications I'm taking, or the menopause transition? There are many conditions that have overlapping symptoms with lower urinary tract symptoms, but getting an appropriate diagnosis for the condition causing your symptoms "requires that someone have the wherewithal and the care to screen and diagnose appropriately in women," says Kaufman. This can be surprisingly difficult to find. The antidote is to arm yourself with knowledge and name it at your next appointment. You might say to your clinician, "I read that taking the birth control pill could impact my hormones in such a way that it causes vulvovaginal symptoms that could mimic common UTI symptoms. Can we talk about this being a potential factor in my case?" Uloko recommends that patients print the research and bring it to their appointment. "If you've asked directly and collaboratively, 'Have you considered this angle for my recurrent UTIs?' and you're dismissed, ask the clinician to document the refusal in your chart, in writing," she says. "This changes behavior and leaves you a record." Have my vulvar tissue and pelvic floor been examined? Vulvovaginal health and pelvic health are just as important as bladder function and should be evaluated, says Burnett. "I can't tell you how many patients I see who have spasms of their pelvic floor muscles, and that's probably what's causing their urinary symptoms." Unfortunately, many clinicians aren't comfortable doing even a basic physical exam of a woman's pelvis, says Kaufman. "It's a simple exam to look for diagnostic changes around the vulva and openings to the vagina and urethra — one that doesn't even have to involve a speculum or a pap smear," she says. "And it's too often a barrier to treatment for many of these conditions with symptoms that mimic a UTI." If you don't think your primary care doctor is doing an adequate physical exam or answering your questions, make an appointment with a specialist. Start with a urologist, who has specialized training in treating UTIs and understands that the bladder is part of an interconnected genitourinary system. Other good options include a urogynecologist, gynecologist, or Menopause Society-certified practitioner. Am I a candidate for vaginal estrogen or DHEA? The American Urological Association has published guidelines for multiple conditions that can all present with UTI-like symptoms — overactive bladder, recurrent UTIs, and GSM — and they clearly state that low-dose vaginal estrogen or DHEA is an effective treatment. "There are a number of randomized control trials and systematic reviews that demonstrate that low-dose vaginal estrogen reduces the risk for recurrent urinary tract infections in perimenopausal and post-menopausal women," says Kaufman, one of the authors of the association's guidelines. You can even bring these guidelines with you to your next healthcare visit to jumpstart the conversation with your clinician. "As urologists, we do a pretty good job of the urinary part of the evaluation — the bladder, ureters, and kidneys," says Uloko. "Where we fall short is the genital part, and that requires a much broader understanding of the pelvic ecosystem as a whole — the hormonal environment, vulvar tissue, and pelvic floor musculature, all influencing each other and all capable of producing symptoms that look exactly like a UTI." Meghan Rabbitt is a journalist and author of The New Rules of Women's Health.

item.title: Exclusive: Meet the inaugural winner of Fat Marmot Week
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Science Score: 3.29
Exclusive: Meet the inaugural winner of Fat Marmot Week Annnnd there's a winner in the first-ever Fat Marmot Week! The competition was among eight yellow-bellied marmots in Colorado vying to gain the most weight before winter hibernation. The Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory's Marmot Project hosted Fat Marmot Week as a way to hype up these cat-sized alpine rodents, in the face of cuts to research funding. Yellow-bellied marmots hibernate to survive the snowy high-mountain winters. They curl up, lower their body temperatures, and slow their breathing. They spend more than half the year like this, relying on their stored fat. Thus: Fat Marmot Week. Marmot enthusiasts were encouraged to cheer on Dawn, G, Dan's Hat, Citroen, Open Kite, 1, Dandelion, and Stonehenge as they spent the month of August bulking up. Weekend Edition had the honor of exclusively announcing the popular vote winner — the marmot that the public crowned as the fattest of them all. Congratulations to Dawn! Your chunky champion is a father who the RMBL says "enjoys the taste of rocks." The Marmot Project also announced that Dawn was the competition's "true" winner on Saturday, based on researchers' estimation of the animals' actual size. Clocking in with a 4.5lb weight gain for a total of 13lbs, congratulations to Dawn for gaining the most weight! Weekend Edition staff also held an informal vote, picking Stonehenge, a resilient mother who lost her litter to a hungry badger earlier this year. The competition was inspired by Alaska's Fat Bear Week — when more than a million people cast votes for the chonkiest brown bear. Fun fact: Marmots are the biggest true hibernators in the world. Bears do not hibernate, they go into a sort of deep sleep called "torpor." The Marmot Project has been researching these rodents since 1962. It's one of the longest-running projects studying individually tagged mammals in the wild. "These long-term studies provide us the insights to understand how organisms, plants, animals, whatever, respond to a changing environment," said Dan Blumstein, a professor at UCLA who runs the Marmot Project, in an interview with NPR's Ayesha Rascoe earlier this month. Fat Marmot Week is not the only way that the project is creatively working to restore lost funds. Blumstein opened an OnlyFans account, OnlyMarms, promising "uncensored marmot content" to subscribers. At the beginning of August, OnlyMarms had generated about $4,000 for research funding. Blumstein hopes the hoopla around Fat Marmot Week will boost donations. "We have some funding for next year, but after that, it's looking very dire," Blumstein said.

item.title: What's the secret ingredient in these cookies? Plastic
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Science Score: 3.09
What's the secret ingredient in these cookies? Plastic New research at the American Chemical Society meeting showcased a potentially edible cookie made out of — plastic! MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST: This next story is about taking plastic and converting it into cookies - yes, cookies. This is a process that might help deal with pollution and other problems. NPR science reporter Ari Daniel reports. ARI DANIEL, BYLINE: Transforming plastic into a snack may sound a little tough to swallow. But Lahiru Jayakody, a synthetic microbiologist at Southern Illinois University Carbondale, says just think of a cow. LAHIRU JAYAKODY: Can you eat grass? No. But cow take the grass and it produce milk. We use milk to make many, many different product. DANIEL: In other words, living creatures are like chemistry labs, converting raw ingredients into new materials. Microbes excel at this kind of thing, so Jayakody decided to try genetically engineering yeast to digest plastic, specifically the kind often used in water bottles and food packaging. Ph.D. student Sandhya Jayasekara first took the intact plastic, along with ground-up corn husks and stalks, and broke it all down into simpler molecules. SANDHYA JAYASEKARA: So that those molecules are available as a food for the yeast. DANIEL: She then gave it to the yeast, which processed this mix of disintegrated plastic and corn to make a gluey protein paste, which Jayasekara mixed with vanilla and beta-carotene that were produced by other yeast and different food ingredients, like oatmeal. A 3D food printer then turned that slurry into small cookies. Here's Lahiru Jayakody. JAYAKODY: There is no micro- or nanoplastic embedded into this cookie. So you are not eating plastic. DANIEL: Nor has anyone actually eaten the cookie yet. There are still safety tests to be done. The process is pricey, uses a lot of energy and not much of the plastic makes it into the final cookie. JAYAKODY: This is a proof of concept, right? JAYASEKARA: Kind of a beginning of a journey. DANIEL: Still, the researchers say they hope the cookies may, at some point, be made from plastic waste on-site in extreme or difficult environments, like outer space or disaster zones. This work was presented at the American Chemical Society meeting in Chicago last week. PAMELA SILVER: I think the concept is right on the mark. DANIEL: Pamela Silver is a synthetic biologist at Harvard Medical School who wasn't involved in the research. She says the idea of turning plastic into food isn't new. The real barriers to making it a reality tend to be scalability, cost and texture. SILVER: Texture comes from fats. So in all the foods you eat - meat, cheese, everything you eat - it's the fat that makes you enjoy it. DANIEL: There's not much fat in these new plastic-derived cookies, but Silver welcomes this kind of thinking, which may one day provide a sweeter solution to a less-than-palatable problem. Ari Daniel, NPR News. (SOUNDBITE OF RAPSODY SONG, "ASTEROIDS") Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information. item.title: Meta's multi-billion settlement launches the next phase of national tech regulation
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Technology Score: 3.81
Meta's multi-billion settlement launches the next phase of national tech regulation Meta's settlement with states in a child safety case this week had a big payout, but the attorneys general have their eyes on a bigger prize: national regulation of social media companies. SCOTT SIMON, HOST: When Meta agreed to settle a landmark child safety case this week, it said it would pay up to $17 billion in penalties. That's among the largest settlement payouts by any company in U.S. history. But that's not what the state attorneys general who brought the case were excited about. Here's California's AG Rob Bonta. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) ROB BONTA: It's not about the money, although the money is important and significant. The lead here is the injunctive relief. SIMON: By injunctive relief, he means changes Meta has to make to its platforms so they're considered safer for teens, changes the company has resisted and that Congress hasn't been able to achieve through legislation. NPR tech correspondent John Ruwitch joins us now. John, thanks for being with us. JOHN RUWITCH, BYLINE: Sure thing, Scott. SIMON: Before we get into this legal strategy, what kind of changes did Meta agree to? RUWITCH: Sure. So this case was a reaction to widespread concern that social media can be unhealthy for kids and has fueled a teen mental health crisis in America. The states argued in their case that Meta designed Facebook and Instagram to be addictive to kids. It knew they were getting exposed to dangerous content and lied about it to the public. So in the settlement, Meta agreed to make changes to its platforms that aim to better protect kids from addiction. That includes time limits on daily use, blockers at night and during the school day, no access to beauty filters, no information for minors about how many people like their posts. The idea is that teens would be on these platforms less. SIMON: Why is this the focus for these state AGs rather than the money? RUWITCH: Yeah. Look, the money is going to be used to fund things like mental health programs and after-school activities. That's all meaningful. But the AGs are trying to do something that's much bigger. Part of this settlement is an effort to get three other big social media platforms - Meta's main competitors - to sign on to similar use restrictions for kids. Those platforms are YouTube, TikTok and Snap. They were not involved in this specific trial, but they've been named in all kinds of other lawsuits that are related to kids and mental health. We reached out to these companies for comment but haven't heard back. For Meta, having them agree eventually to the same rules would level the competitive playing field and make sure that its users don't just migrate to other platforms with looser rules. For the AGs, it's part of a pretty interesting gambit. SIMON: What is the gambit? RUWITCH: Yeah. The AGs aren't just enforcing the law here. They're trying to create a regulatory regime around social media companies where there isn't one right now. I asked William Tong about this. He's the AG for Connecticut, which was part of the case, and I wanted to know why the state attorneys general are being so aggressive in pushing these changes to how social media companies operate. WILLIAM TONG: It's in large part because there are large areas of American life that require action or require protective action to keep people safe where Congress has not been effective. RUWITCH: Basically, they're using litigation to replace legislation. Now, to be fair, some states have put in place regulations, but at a national level, most attempts have failed. Timothy Lytton, a law professor at Georgia State University, says that is in part because Big Tech is rich and powerful and has been very successful in lobbying against regulation. TIMOTHY LYTTON: And so that's why you see, I think, attorneys general stepping in where legislatures and governors have not been willing to go. RUWITCH: He says they're acting as a kind of insulated counterbalance to the politics of it all. And it's worth noting, the AGs in this case were a bipartisan group. SIMON: That is interesting in these times. How do you rate their chance of success in reining in these social media companies? RUWITCH: Well, a lot has to fall in place for that to happen. We don't know yet, for instance, when or how these other companies are going to fall in line or if they will. Experts say the attorneys general are signaling - in this case and others - that they don't want to destroy these social media companies with crushing penalties but instead want to work with them. But this settlement contains an implicit threat. Here's Timothy Lytton again. LYTTON: Everybody in this particular industry is now on notice that if you don't exercise the kind of restraint that Meta is now starting to agree to, that you can probably expect to see some sort of legal action. RUWITCH: He says the case raises public pressure on legislators to move on the issue. People are really mad about this. But he says meaningful regulation in America actually often comes through litigation like this. It's a feature of our system, not a bug. SIMON: NPR's John Ruwitch. Thanks so much. RUWITCH: You're welcome. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information. item.title: 2 trapped workers rescued from a hydropower tunnel 9 days after Nepal floods
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Score: 3.27
Rescuers pull 2 trapped workers from a hydropower tunnel 9 days after Nepal floods KATHMANDU, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal pulled two workers alive from an underground tunnel at a hydropower plant Friday, raising hopes of reaching dozens of others believed to be trapped nine days after deadly floods swept away villages and submerged the Himalayan region in mud and debris. Search teams first heard voices from inside the tunnel in the morning, allowing them to locate the two men, Nepalese lawmaker Shri Ram Neupane said. Images showed a rescuer carrying one of the workers, covered in mud, on his back, while soldiers on either side helped. One of those rescued said more people are alive inside the tunnel, according to army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet, and the search is ongoing. "I can't explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to god," Amir Maharjan, the brother of one of those rescued, told The Associated Press. Basnet confirmed the first trapped worker's rescue, and Neupane posted about the second on his Facebook page shortly after. Both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu, and Maharjan said his family was on its way there. One of the survivors was in critical condition, according to a statement from the prime minister's office. Officials identified the men as a mechanical foreman and a mechanical supervisor. They were rescued from a tunnel at the Trishuli 3A plant. About 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in various tunnels, according to authorities. About 115 are believed trapped in the tunnel at Trishuli 3A alone, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal. Nepal's Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina wrote on his Facebook page that officials "are waiting for the rescue of more and more people." At least 1,287 people were killed in the Aug. 26 floods, likely caused by a glacier collapse, and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal's disaster management agency. China said Friday 31 people were killed and 531 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, according to Chinese official news agency Xinhua. Nepal's disaster agency estimated Friday that flooding caused at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees ($2.5 billion) in damage to infrastructure and property.

item.title: GPT-6 Astra Is Here: What You Need to Know About ChatGPT's New Model
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 7.08
OpenAI is rolling out GPT-6 Astra, the latest model to come to ChatGPT, following a self-imposed delay to help ensure its security features are used responsibly. OpenAI calls Astra the “world’s most intelligent and aligned model," claiming it's state-of-the-art for browsing, computer use, cybersecurity, software engineering, science, and professional work. AI companies tend to hype up every model release, however, so we'll have to see how it performs in practice. GPT-6 Astra is rolling out to organizations in OpenAI's Daybreak program, with a release coming for paid subscribers on Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise plans in the next few days. OpenAI has not yet clarified whether free users will be able to access GPT-6 Astra, but if it follows its previous rollouts, free access with limits may come at a later date. The rollout got off to a "messy" start, CEO Sam Altman says. Those who couldn't access it will get "one banked reset for every day you don't have access to Astra on your paid ChatGPT plan, starting today," OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux tweeted last night. "Team is moving mountains to give access as fast as we can." The Astra model outperforms OpenAI's previous releases, with benchmarks showing it beats competitors such as Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 and Google’s latest Gemini 3.8 Flash across a range of intensive tests. GPT-6 came out on top in benchmarking results for ARC-AGI-3, which tests the ability to solve unfamiliar problems; FrontierMath Tier 4 (v2), for mathematical problems; Terminal Bench 4.0, for coding; and Agent's Last Exam, for agentic features. OpenAI says the tool is better for agentic work than previous models, with what it calls “substantial improvements in understanding user intent and model behavior,” allowing you to delegate tasks more effectively and be confident the model won’t misunderstand you. It also claims agents will have improved decision-making when a prompt doesn’t clearly explain a task, meaning you're less likely to receive incorrect information. GPT-6 is also said to be faster than ever for browser and computer work. OpenAI confirmed previously announced plans to limit the cybersecurity features within GPT-6 Astra, citing concerns that its advancements could be used by bad actors to launch sophisticated attacks. “Astra will refuse to comply with more advanced cybersecurity tasks such as creating proof-of-concept exploits for vulnerabilities," it says. Instead, it’s letting its select Daybreak business partners begin experimenting with the full tool, allowing each to use Astra to identify flaws in their own systems before patching them. This comes after in-development models, unrelated to Astra, were found to have broken containment and hacked another AI platform, Hugging Face, last month. OpenAI slowed the development and rollout of future models to strengthen security measures after the incident. In a press briefing attended by The Guardian, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said he believes this is the start of the artificial general intelligence (AGI) era, a term used to describe the moment when AI can surpass human intelligence across cognitive tasks. “If we fast forward a couple of years, and we look back and say, when was it really that AGI was created, I think it’s going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model," he said. “I think it’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era," he added. Altman, however, recently told the Sources podcast that “At best, [AGI is] a very poorly defined term. I was going to say it’s like an irrelevant marketing term.” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang appears to agree. “For many tasks, we could say that we have already achieved AGI. I think all of those milestones...are kind of senseless at this point,” Huang said in an earnings call last week. Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems. item.title: Lenovo Refreshes the Desktop for the AI Era, From Living Rooms to Offices
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.38
At IFA 2026 in Berlin, Lenovo unveiled a revamped desktop portfolio engineered for the agentic AI era. The new lineup spans high-performance modular mini-clusters for enterprise power users to lifestyle-driven PCs for the modern home, headlined by three business-focused ThinkCentre models and a redesigned consumer IdeaCentre All-in-One. Living Room Refresh: Lenovo IdeaCentre AIO i Gen 11 The centerpiece of Lenovo's desktop announcements is the Lenovo IdeaCentre AIO i Gen 11, a sleek all-in-one desktop designed for the modern home with a clutter-free design and intuitive smart features. Like most AIO desktops, this one uses a streamlined desktop design that eliminates the need for an extra bulky tower. Available in Pantone-curated finishes, including Dreamy Violet, Radiant Coral (light red), Zen Green, and Chill Blue, Lenovo aims to make this all-in-one a style piece for contemporary living spaces rather than just another utilitarian home PC. The all-in-one IdeaCentre comes in two sizes: a 23.8-inch or 27-inch Full HD display, featuring up to 120Hz refresh rates and 350-nit peak brightness. The display has an adjustable stand providing -5 degrees to 15 degrees of tilt and 30mm of height adjustment, letting you raise and tilt the display just how you want it, and even making things more eye-friendly with a dedicated ebook reading mode that helps reduce blue light and eye strain. AI-powered adaptive lighting modes during boot-up, general use, and music playback turn the system lighting into interactive visual feedback. The visuals are matched by an integrated Harman audio system providing clean, vibrant sound. The desktop runs on an Intel Core Series 3 "Wildcat Lake" processor, delivering up to 40 trillion AI operations per second (TOPS), and up to 32GB of RAM on the 27-inch model, with dual SSD slots for expandable storage. Six USB ports, an HDMI-in and HDMI-out combo connection, a conveniently positioned headphone and microphone combo jack, optional wireless charging in the base for seamless smartphone power, and an optional 5-megapixel IR camera with a physical privacy shutter provide the flexibility to connect and work the way users prefer. Multi-Agent AI Engine: ThinkCentre X Ultra First up on the business desktop list is the ThinkCentre X Ultra, a 1.6-liter ultra-compact desktop engineered specifically for localized, multi-agent enterprise AI workloads. The system is powered by up to an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 processor with a 55 TOPS NPU. In many ways, it's Lenovo's take on the AMD Ryzen AI Halo, with additional attention paid to enterprise needs. Equipped with up to 128GB of onboard LPDDR5X memory and integrated AMD Radeon 8065S graphics, it is built to run complex local AI models. Adaptive lighting provides real-time visual status and activity feedback, making it easy to monitor progress while an agent works independently. Lenovo also built this one for scale, featuring a cluster-ready architecture that lets you combine up to four X Ultra units into a unified platform via 10GbE RJ-45 LAN. By sharing processing across systems and storing data on up to two 4TB M.2 Gen5 Performance SSDs, clustering drastically expands the compute and memory footprint to handle large models and demanding multi-agent tools. Beyond its AI performance, this enterprise-ready machine comes equipped with Lenovo ThinkShield security. Connectivity options include dual Thunderbolt 4 ports, 10GbE RJ-45 LAN, DisplayPort 2.1, and HDMI 2.1. Commercial Workhorses: ThinkCentre M75q Tiny & M75s SFF Finally, Lenovo has a pair of compact ThinkCentre desktops, with the ThinkCentre M75s, a small-form-factor (SFF) tower for those who need traditional desktop expandability, or the mini-PC-sized ThinkCentre M75q Gen 6 Tiny, which is tailored for even more space-constrained environments, with the device so small it can be mounted to the back of a display or the underside of a desk. Both systems leverage dedicated 50 NPU TOPS using the AMD Ryzen AI 7 PRO processor series, which is built to handle both enterprise workloads and AI PC features with compact efficiency. Top specs, despite the difference in size, are similar across the two systems. Both are configurable with up to an AMD Ryzen AI 7 Pro processor, with integrated AMD Radeon 860M graphics, or the larger ThinkCentre M75s Gen 6 can also be bumped up to a discrete AMD Radeon RX 6400 8GB graphics card. Both systems can fit a pair of 2TB SSDs, with the larger M75s SFF desktop supporting Gen 5 SSDs and adding a slot for up to a 2TB 3.5-inch SATA HDD. Lenovo ThinkShield protection comes standard on both systems, while the self-healing BIOS is offered only on the M75s. The M75's compact tower has added expansion options with 1x PCIe x16 Gen4 slot and 2x PCIe x1 slots. The Tiny M75q mini PC offers multiple power options, with adapters available for 65W, 90W, or 135W. If you're saving space with that mini PC design so you can fit an extra monitor or two on your desk, you are in luck, because the M75q Gen 6 Tiny supports up to four displays. Pricing & Availability: New Desktops Drop This Fall Lenovo will roll out its new desktop portfolio in staggered waves starting in autumn 2026. The consumer-focused IdeaCentre AIO i Gen 11 will begin selling in November 2026, starting at $939.99 for the 24-inch model and $1,149.99 for the 27-inch model. The ThinkCentre M75q Gen 6 Tiny arrives first in September 2026, starting at $1,379, followed by the ThinkCentre M75s Gen 6 Small Form Factor, launching in October 2026, with a starting price of $1,489. The AI-focused ThinkCentre X Ultra hits enterprise channels in November 2026, starting at $3,699 for the entry configuration. About Our Expert From the laptops on your desk to satellites in space and AI that seems to be everywhere, I cover many topics at PCMag. I've covered PCs and technology products for over 15 years at PCMag and other publications, among them Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, and TWICE. As a hardware reviewer, I've handled dozens of MacBooks, 2-in-1 laptops, Chromebooks, and the latest AI PCs. As the resident Starlink expert, I've done years of hands-on testing with the satellite service. I also explore the most valuable ways to use the latest AI tools and features in our Try AI column.

item.title: CSI: Living Room? Dyson's New $1,200 Robot Vacuum Uses UV Light to Hunt Down Invisible Stains
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.95
BERLIN–Maybe I've been watching too many murder shows lately, but Dyson's latest robot vacuum reminds me of a detective. Unveiled at IFA, the Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV uses an ultraviolet LED to find invisible stains on your floor, like something out of "CSI: Crime Scene Investigation." "Specifically, [it can detect] real nasties, things like pet urine, spilled milk, alcohol, beer," Dyson engineer Guy Turner told me. "As they dry on the floor, they become transparent; they're really hard to see." The UV light causes those invisible dried stains to fluoresce, or glow. The Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai, introduced last year, uses a green laser to detect invisible dust, but the R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV is the company's first model to use UV light as well. After locating such gunk, the robot uses a roller mop on the bottom to wash it away. While rare, this feature isn't entirely new. The Shark PowerDetect UV also uses ultraviolet light to seek out otherwise imperceptible stains. Dyson's R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV has already received FCC approval, and is slated to go on sale in the US on Sept. 15 for $1,199. It debuts alongside the Costco-exclusive Dyson R2 Nurovi Wash+Dry ($699), which features triangular mopping pads for thorough corner cleaning, and the vacuum-only R1Nurovi Dry ($549). While Dyson's latest models are unaffected by the foreign robot vacuum ban, the long-term future of autonomous floor cleaning in the US remains to be seen. I asked Turner about Dyson's reaction to the ban, and he said the company, which is based in Singapore, has always taken privacy and data custody "incredibly seriously." "The US is one of Dyson's biggest markets," Turner said. "Of course, we're really committed to bringing all of our new technologies and products to American consumers. We will do what it takes to make sure that happens." I have been with PCMag for more than 10 years, and in that time have written more than 6,000 articles and reviews for the site. I previously served as an analyst focused on smart home and wearable devices, and before that I was a reporter covering consumer tech news. I'm also a yoga instructor, and have been actively teaching group and private classes for nearly a decade. Prior to joining PCMag, I was a reporter for SC Magazine, focusing on hackers and computer security. I earned a BS in journalism from West Virginia University, and started my career writing for newspapers in New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and West Virginia.

item.title: Tesla's No-Steering-Wheel Cybercab Hits Austin Streets
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.94
Tesla on Thursday announced it is adding Cybercabs to its robotaxi fleet in Austin, Texas. First teased back in 2024, Tesla’s Cybercab is a fully autonomous electric vehicle that requires no driver intervention. In the absence of a steering wheel and pedals, the AV uses “camera vision and sensors to intelligently and safely navigate city streets, highways, complicated intersections, and parking lots,” Tesla says on a support page. It appears select customers in Austin can now choose between a Cybercab and Model Y when booking a ride via the Robotaxi app. Availability, however, may be limited as only 45 of Tesla’s 314 robotaxis operational in Texas are Cybercabs, The New York Times reports. Tesla says Cybercabs can be used for errands, commutes, and other purposes. Once the car arrives, its butterfly doors will automatically open as you approach it. You’ll also find options to enter the car, start a ride, or open its trunk, spacious enough for luggage, wheelchairs, golf clubs, and scooters, on the Robotaxi mobile app. Inside the car, you’ll find two bench-style seats at wheelchair height for easy entry and exit. At the center, you’ll see a giant 22-inch touch screen with access to entertainment and connectivity features, including music and gaming apps. From the mobile app, you can also adjust climate and media settings, and save them to your profile for future trips. Soon, these cars will also be equipped with V5 Starlink hardware for satellite connectivity. Initially, Tesla expected to sell the Cybercab to private owners and rideshare companies for about $30,000, but the sale of a car without pedals and a steering wheel has yet to receive regulatory clearance. You can still fill out an interest form on Tesla’s website, though. For now, Cybercab remains limited to Tesla’s robotaxi service in Austin. The company also offers robotaxi rides in Model Y vehicles in Dallas, Houston, and Miami. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Major AI Outage: Grok Trouble Blamed on Outage at Memphis Data Center
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.83
UPDATE 4 p.m. ET: SpaceXAI apologized to users and compute partners for the Grok outage, blaming "an outage at our Memphis compute center this morning." It says, "all systems have now been restored and are functioning nominally." Queries on Grok are now going through for us. UPDATE 3:15 p.m. ET: Claude appears to be back now. "All systems operational," the status page says. On Grok, however, we are still getting "Grok was unable to reply" errors. UPDATE 1:25 p.m. ET: OpenAI's status page now says it's fully operational. "We’re not aware of any issues affecting our systems." Reports on Downdetector have also dropped, and the chatbot is responding to queries. Gemini also appears to be up and running. Grok, however, is currently displaying a warning that says it's "experiencing issues," and warns that "Some features may be slow or unavailable." It's telling people to check status.x.ai for updates, but the page doesn't currently show any service disruptions. On Claude, we're getting "This response didn't load" to any queries. Original Story: If you’re trying to use AI tools today, you are likely experiencing problems. A widespread outage affecting thousands of users is ongoing across OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini, X's Grok, and other AI platforms. As shown on Downdetector, outages affecting OpenAI services began around 10:30 a.m. ET, ramping up quickly over the past hour. The outage appears to be widespread, with the peak number of reports exceeding 36,000. The OpenAI status page says it has applied a fix and is “monitoring the recovery” after 24 minutes of downtime across ChatGPT and Codex. One PCMag reporter who was experiencing issues says their service returned soon after the fix, but is now working slowly. OpenAI has yet to say what caused the outage. Google Gemini saw a similar spike in reports around the same time, but Google has yet to acknowledge an outage. Another PCMag reporter found that any prompts entered into Gemini returned an error, although reports on Downdetector are significantly smaller, suggesting it isn't impacting all users. Issues with Anthropic's Claude began earlier in the day with a small spike in reports at 8:30 a.m. ET before surging an hour later with more consistent issues. The first problem directly affected Claude Sonnet 5, while a second wave hit many more models, including Mythos/Fable 5.1 and Opus 5. Anthropic says it has issued a fix for its issues, which is now rolling out to users. It says the currently affected models are restricted to Opus 5 and Opus 4.8, with recoveries happening across Fable models and Opus 4.6. X’s AI platform, Grok, also appears to be down, alongside the smaller AI agent service Cursor, with both seeing spikes on Downdetector. Meanwhile, despite reports on Downdetector, Cloudflare says it is not experiencing downtime. “Cloudflare is not experiencing any significant service disruptions at this time. Our services are operating normally, and any reporting that deviates from this is incorrect.” This is a remarkable outage to hit all of these services at once, especially since it doesn't seem to be affecting other businesses outside the AI space. We'll update this article with more information as we hear it. Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems. item.title: Apple Tests iOS 27 Handoff Feature That Supports Same Number on 2 iPhones
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.83
Apple is reportedly testing an iOS 27 iPhone Handoff feature that allows you to switch between two iPhones without changing your eSIM number. The feature was briefly mentioned on a slide during the WWDC 2026 keynote, and an iPhone user recently spotted it on their device, MacRumors reports. On the site’s forum, the same user also shared a video demonstrating how iPhone Handoff works. When available, users can enable iPhone Handoff in Settings > Cellular. While setting it up, you’ll be asked to keep the iPhones close and choose which one retains the main eSIM and which one gets the companion eSIM. Only the main iPhone will be able to modify Cellular Settings from then on. The feature allows you to share your eSIM with another iPhone and switch between them as needed. Each time you unlock an iPhone, a notification will indicate that cellular service has been transferred to the currently active device. A support article for developers also describes an “iPhone quick switch” feature that enables transfer of active services, “such as login credentials and persistent state from a formerly active iPhone to a newly active iPhone.” As with Apple’s original Handoff feature, this should allow you to pick up from where you left off on another device. Of course, Apple doesn’t control all aspects of the iPhone Handoff feature. You’ll be able to use the feature only if your carrier supports it. According to MacRumors, T-Mobile in the US and Deutsche Telekom in Germany might support the feature at launch. We should have more details about it soon. While iOS 27 is still being tested with public and developer betas, the stable version is expected to launch with the new iPhone 18 Pro and the foldable iPhone sometime next week. item.title: LA Schools Join NYC in Blocking Student Access to Generative AI
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.82
From coast to coast, AI is getting a failing grade this academic year. Days after New York City announced a one-year moratorium on AI tools for students through 8th grade, the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) said students will be barred from using AI tools on district-provided devices this academic year. While NYC’s ban leaves some room for high school students to explore the tech with vetted programs, LAUSD seems to have shut off access completely. Students will be able to see Google’s AI summaries on top of search results, but they won’t be able to interact with the AI tool any further, The New York Times reports. The move comes as part of the district’s broader effort to reduce student screen time. Earlier this year, LAUSD banned digital devices for young kids and enforced strict screen limits for others. Some board members were reportedly surprised when the decision was announced at Wednesday’s committee meeting. The ban is temporary, and the committee will make recommendations on AI policy at the end of the school year, an LAUSD spokesperson tells Bloomberg. At both LA and NYC public schools, teachers will be allowed to use AI tools. And students can use AI chatbots on personal devices, so it remains to be seen how effective this will be. The bans arrive amid concerns that a growing number of students are using AI for homework and bypassing the learning process. AI tools are also notorious for providing inaccurate information and entertaining inappropriate conversations. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Don't Want to Pay for Whoop? Screenless Luna Band Costs $149, No Subscription
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.67
Screenless fitness trackers are the new battleground in wearable tech, with recent releases like Garmin’s Cirqa Smart Band and Google’s Fitbit Air arriving to compete with the market leader, Whoop. Now, there's an alternative, and it's cheaper than most of those rivals. The Luna Band comes from smart ring maker Luna. The screenless fitness tracker minimizes distractions while giving you a full picture of your health, tracking activity, sleep, skin temperature, SpO2 (blood oxygen), women's health, Vo2 Max, heart rate variability, and more. The device has a rectangular design and no display, and is attached to your wrist with a nylon strap with a metal frame. Your color options are Aloe Green, Desert Beige, or Onyx Black. Some other sources report the availability of a blue version, but it’s yet to appear on Luna’s website. The device is also water-resistant up to 5 ATM (about 164 feet deep). As it's not powering a screen, Luna’s tracker can offer up to 10 days of battery life from a single charge, which it says takes around 60 minutes. That works through a proprietary charger, which is included in the box. Unlike the Whoop 5.0, the Luna Band doesn’t require a monthly subscription to access features. It’s a flat fee of $149 to buy the tracker, though some of its software doesn't appear to be as advanced as its rivals'. The Luna Band was first unveiled at CES 2026, then entered a limited preorder period, which meant some customers got their hands on the fitness tracker in late July. Now, Luna is ready for a full launch, including immediate availability across the US. You can buy the Luna Band from its official website, with shipping beginning today, Sept. 4. The Aloe Green version will ship on Sept. 7, Luna says. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. item.title: Uber Launches UK's First Robotaxi Service in London, But There's a Catch
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.49
Robotaxis are finally available in the UK. After months of testing, Uber began offering public robotaxi rides in London earlier today. Customers in the city who book an UberX, Uber Electric, or Uber Comfort ride may now be matched with a Ford Mustang Mach-E vehicle equipped with Wayve’s AI Driver tech. Interested customers can accept Uber’s robotaxi offer at no extra cost or decline it and ride in a non-autonomous vehicle as usual. When the car arrives, follow the instructions in the app to open the door and initiate the trip. For safety reasons, Uber’s initial robotaxi trips will have a supervisor behind the wheel, and the company will operate just 15 vehicles in its fleet. More vehicles will be added “thoughtfully over time in line with rider demand, readiness, and regulation,” but if you’d like to increase your chances of being matched with a robotaxi, you can set your trip preferences to AV by going to Account > Settings > Ride Preferences in the mobile app. Approximately 140,000 Londoners have already done so, Uber says. When it comes to the service area, Uber’s robotaxis cover all parts of London but not airports. It’s quite a challenging city for autonomous driving, since the roads are narrower and more irregular compared with orderly grid systems found in many modern cities. "This launch is a major milestone in scaling safe, accessible AV technology in a city with some of the world’s most complex roads," says Sarfraz Maredia, Uber’s head of autonomous mobility. Speaking of airports, Amazon-owned Zoox has extended service to Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas, TechCrunch reports. In late July, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) gave Zoox a temporary exemption, allowing the company to finally begin offering commercial rides. This week, it also launched in Houston and San Diego. Google-owned Waymo, meanwhile, is expected to begin its robotaxi service in London soon. It began testing Wayve’s driving tech last year and may launch public rides in the city this year. Last month, Uber beat Waymo to become the first to launch robotaxi services in Europe with rides in Zagreb, Croatia. The company has committed $10 billion to its AV expansion and is targeting 15 cities by the end of this year. It is already operational in eight. This comes as Tesla is expected to unveil more details about its Cybercab at an event in Austin, Texas, tonight. First unveiled in 2024, the robotaxi is a smaller coupe with two butterfly doors, two seats, and a single band of headlights, similar to the Cybertruck. There's no steering wheel, pedals, or charging port, as it can charge via induction. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. item.title: HTC's New Smart Glasses Offer a Few Imperfect Fixes for the Pervert Problem
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.28
Privacy and smart glasses should go hand in hand, and with the $499 Vive Eagle AI, HTC seems to realize that. It's clear the company wants to avoid the "pervert glasses" stigma that Meta's smart glasses have earned, and it's taking notable steps toward that end, though the built-in camera remains on the Vive Eagle AI. I'm currently testing them, and a full review is coming, but for now, here's what I see with HTC's "privacy-first approach." Addressing and Anonymizing AI Like all AI glasses, the Vive Eagle has built-in voice-activated AI. Interface functions, like activating different features, are handled by HTC's Vive AI, and HTC says your data will not be used to train its AI. Frankly, I think all AI data training should be opt-in, not the opt-out-and-good-luck-finding-out-how-because-we-won't-tell-you approach of a lot of AI systems. Including AI systems you weren't interacting with in the first place, like Twitch. If you want general information beyond the glasses' core functions, the Vive Eagle supports Google Gemini and OpenAI's GPT. They're much larger systems that have basically scraped the entire internet for training data, and will certainly use your interactions as well. Considering how much Google is tied to our internet footprints, there's a reasonable concern that every Gemini-related thing you do with the glasses will be linked to your Google profile. However, HTC says LLM requests through the glasses will be de-identified. The company pointedly says it makes it "harder" to build a profile, but not impossible. Sadly, that's the current reality we live in, and no privacy or security feature is completely bulletproof. Welcome to the data economy. The Vive Eagle is also ISO 27001 and ISO 27701 compliant, which means it meets international standards for securing personal data and ensuring some level of user-side privacy control. The Camera Problem The Vive Eagle has a built-in 12MP camera that lets you take photos and 3K video, and provides translations in 96 different languages. A camera is always handy to have, but it's also the main reason "pervert glasses" has become a common phrase. Creeps, stalkers, and general jerks use camera-equipped smart glasses to surreptitiously record and harass people. To address the problem, HTC added extra privacy and security features to the Vive Eagle. First, its recording light uses multiple sensors to ensure it's always visible when the camera is recording. It will adjust its brightness based on ambient light to be easily seen, and the camera won't work if the light is obscured in any way. A recording light that you can't disable has become standard on major smart glasses with cameras, including Meta's, but I'm skeptical that it can't be circumvented in some way. Second, the camera will not record unless the glasses are being physically worn. This means someone can't take the glasses off and set them to capture from a hidden position. There could also be a workaround there, but it's another good step. Third, the camera will turn off if anyone nearby says "stop filming." That's kind of brilliant in its simplicity. If you know you're being recorded, you can stop it. Again, in theory. The fourth feature is less an anti-pervert-glasses fix and more about general user security improvements. Photos and videos taken on the Vive Eagle stay on the glasses' on-board 32GB storage until you manually transfer them to your phone or another device, and that data can't be accessed if you pair the glasses with a different device. When combined with the ISO 27001 and ISO 27701 certifications, anything you capture on the glasses should be safe from other people. Privacy, Security, and Uncertainty It's good that HTC is up-front and highlighting its privacy and security measures on the Vive Eagle. They aren't remotely guaranteed, since no information security measure is, but it's a start. Still, in an ideal world, we wouldn't have to worry about this at all. Security to prevent individuals from stealing your data is one thing. Preventing unauthorized system access by bad actors has been a vital part of information security for as long as information has existed. Thieves will always exist, so we find ways to deal with the threats. But the concerns about AI glasses go beyond those bad actors to the devices' own manufacturers, service providers, and users. The Vive Eagle doesn't anonymize your AI prompts to keep some random hacker from tracking you; it does that to keep Google and OpenAI from tracking you. HTC comes out and says Vive AI won't use your data for training, even though every major AI firm is using it for training, whether you like it or not. The glasses don't have a "stop filming" kill switch to keep your photos and videos out of others' hands; they have it to keep you from being a creep or stalker with them. These privacy and security features aren't simply necessary to protect us from criminals. They're necessary to protect us from the very services we rely on, and from ourselves (or at least other people using the exact same devices). HTC seems to be doing what it can with the Vive Eagle (besides removing the camera entirely), but the fact that these actions need to be taken in the first place? Well, that really sucks. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s home theater and AR/VR expert, and your go-to source of information and recommendations for game consoles and accessories, smart displays, smart glasses, smart speakers, soundbars, TVs, and VR headsets. I’m an ISF-certified TV calibrator and THX-certified home theater technician, I've served as a CES Innovation Awards judge, and while Bandai hasn’t officially certified me, I’m also proficient at building Gundam plastic models up to MG-class. I also enjoy genre fiction writing, and my urban fantasy novel, Alex Norton, Paranormal Technical Support, is currently available on Amazon.

item.title: Open and Neutral? Nvidia Says Don't Worry About Its Hugging Face Acquisition
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.16
Nvidia’s $13 billion deal to acquire Hugging Face might spark concerns about the future of the popular AI model platform, but both companies insist that Hugging Face will remain “open and neutral” for AI developers and enthusiasts. “We want to continue to work with all AI developers globally,” Nvidia’s VP for enterprise computing, Justin Boitano, said in a press briefing after the acquisition was confirmed this morning. “To make sure that they’ve got an open and neutral platform that interoperates with every cloud provider, every hardware company in the world.” “We think this operation, this announcement, will allow the world and AI to be more distributed all over the world, and to avoid too much concentration of power,” added Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue. The concern is that Hugging Face hosts numerous open-source and open-weight AI models, effectively operating as the "App Store of the AI world" for over 200,000 companies, notes PCMag’s Brian Westover. Nvidia, on the other hand, is the top seller of enterprise GPUs to power AI models and is preparing consumer-focused chips with its RTX Spark line to drive AI use on laptops. Will the Hugging Face deal push the platform to favor Nvidia technology? Boitano says no. The priority is to keep the platform open and neutral so that it can grow, which requires maintaining trust with the software developer community. In turn, Nvidia will benefit as AI developers and businesses buy its chips to run AI models. Boitano also addressed whether the deal might face antitrust scrutiny from government regulators, saying Nvidia’s role is focused on helping Hugging Face “scale and expand access to AI globally," adding, “We think regulators are going to see this as overwhelmingly positive because it's going to infuse AI into every country, into every industry." Hugging Face’s Delangue also noted that “the vast, vast majority of what we do is open-source, open models, open datasets, that are by definition, neutral. Everyone can take them. Everyone can optimize them, everyone can fork our open-source if they are not happy about it.” He added that a major goal is to grow the platform’s user base to 100 million AI software developers over the next few years, up from the current 18 million. “We think that this announcement is really going to be fantastic and massively impactful for all the players in the ecosystem, not just Nvidia, but all the players,” Delangue said. Still, analysts at research firm Forrester noted that the deal gives Nvidia significant influence over the AI ecosystem, including a potential competitive edge over other GPU designers. "Nvidia gains visibility into customers' preferences and the AI models they use. They can see which models are trending, what datasets customers are downloading, and the architectures that are gaining traction weeks before they hit mainstream tech news,” says analyst Naveen Chhabra. "Nvidia also gets data-driven foresight into what next-generation chip architectures they need to build based on developer habits.” About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: DLSS 5 Spikes Power Consumption
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.13
DLSS 5 doesn't just tank frame rates and weather faces; it might also spike power consumption on GPUs. Tom's Hardware tested various games with high-end graphics cards running DLSS 5 and found that, in some cases, power consumption jumped by hundreds of watts when the card had headroom. Where it didn't, performance fell further, suggesting the already fire-happy 12v-2x6 connector may be limiting performance with DLSS 5 enabled. DLSS 5, which brings AI-powered photorealism to PC games, launched today on NBA 2K27. Whether it actually makes games look better is still up for debate. It's more efficient than when we first saw it, but the RTX 5090 still loses nearly half its FPS. When running Hogwarts Legacy at 4K with ray tracing and DLSS set to Performance mode, Tom's Hardware found that the RTX 5090 FE jumped from 417 watts without it to 547 watts with it. For the RTX 5090 Lightning Z, with a much higher power limit, it leaped from 480W without DLSS 5 to 720W with it. In comparison, the Founders Edition 5090 performance dipped by 49% with DLSS 5 enabled, while the Lightning dropped by just 42%, and its 1% lows were much less impacted. You can argue the Lightning Z is the more powerful card, but it was only 3fps higher than the FE card without DLSS 5, so DLSS 5 has the biggest impact here. The same story was true in Cyberpunk 2077, where the Lightning Z version went from 580W to 723W, losing 39% of its overall FPS in the process. The 5090 FE went from 482W to 551W but lost 42% performance, dropping below 60fps even with DLSS on Performance. Control had the highest power consumption and, therefore, the greatest limitation on the FE card. The Lightning Z version went from 691W to 802W, while the standard 5090 pulled 563W and only 575W with DLSS 5 enabled. While both cards saw their frame rates drop by 42% with DLSS 5 enabled, the Lightning Z still held above 60fps average, while the 5090 fell to just 51fps. So, DLSS 5 appears to benefit most from the latest tensor cores and greater power limits. Like the original DLSS release, it is likely to be a multi-generational technology that will be far more useful in the years and generations to come. More powerful cards with faster tensor units, with greater power limits, may be needed to take full advantage of it. But Nvidia will have to address that connector if it tries to push even more power through these things. Maybe something extra stealthy like the BTF method? About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: Move Over, DJI: Hohem's Eyepic 4K Vlogging Camera Has a Massive Twist
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.03
Vlogging cameras are the hot ticket right now, and the space just got a brand new player. Hohem, a brand best known to date for its iSteady smartphone gimbals, is bringing its first-ever camera to IFA in Berlin. The Eyepic is a tiny 4K video camera that can be handheld, worn, or magnetically mounted to a three-axis gimbal—making it a true triple threat for content creation. A Pocket Gimbal That Snaps Apart for Underwater Action The Eyepic draws inspiration from the DJI Osmo Pocket series, which has proven to be the go-to choice for vloggers who want to record handheld video and has inspired competitors such as the Insta360 Luna Ultra. Like others in the class, the Eyepic has a long, skinny body that fits comfortably in your hand, a touch screen, and a small joystick to control its powered gimbal. The gimbal promises to keep footage smooth and steady, even for walk-and-talk shots, and the Eyepic camera records clips at up to 4K60 quality. That's not as ambitious as some competitors—the DJI Osmo Pocket 4P and Insta360 Luna Ultra both support higher frame rates for slow motion and include dual lenses for wide and telephoto views, while the Eyepic is a single-lens device. But the Eyepic does one thing that DJI and Insta360 can't—its camera works separately from the gimbal. It pops on and off with a quick magnetic attachment, so you can go between handheld vlogging and mounting the camera to an object in a snap. That makes the Eyepic the first gimbal camera that's also a waterproof action camera, one that works down to 32.8 feet underwater. It also makes it easy to switch between widescreen and vertical video—the camera mounts to the gimbal in either direction. Pro Audio Upgrade: The AI-Powered Hohem Mic 2 Kit Vloggers know that a video is only as good as its soundtrack. Built-in mics tend to sound hollow and pick up a lot of background noise, so the company is releasing a wireless mic kit for the Eyepic: the Hohem Mic 2. The kit ships with a receiver and two body mics, and supports up to four mics in total. It supports 48kHz/24-bit audio, has AI-powered noise cancellation, and promises an incredible 984-foot transmission range. Availability: Targeting CES 2027—And an Opening in the US Market Like many of the products making their debut at IFA, the Eyepic isn't quite ready to ship to customers, so we don't know how much it will cost or which regions it will be sold in. Hohem says it plans to release a general version in the first quarter of 2027, and we'll be sure to have more information closer to that date. The early 2027 timing is conspicuously timed with CES, which takes place in Las Vegas and is a traditional launchpad for the coolest consumer tech, so we're hopeful that the Eyepic makes it US debut then. On paper, it looks like a great choice for US-based vloggers and content creators who can't get the latest DJI Osmo Pocket models because of the FCC's ban on new DJI products. Stay tuned to PCMag for more information as it develops. About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: Microsoft Defender is falsely flagging Google links as malicious
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.71
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Microsoft Defender for Office 365 is incorrectly flagging legitimate Google search URLs as malicious, causing false security alerts for users. - The issue stems from the Safe Links feature, which is mistakenly blocking valid Google URLs instead of protecting against genuine threats. - Microsoft has identified the cause and is working on a fix, though no timeline for an official patch has been confirmed yet. Even though Microsoft Defender is more than enough security on its own, its reputation has taken a bit of a hit this year. Over the last few months, vulnerabilities like RedSun and RoguePlanet were discovered (and later patched), while just last month Defender was showing false warnings that it was disabled even when it wasn’t. The latest Defender issue to crop up is that it’s now incorrectly classifying Google links as malicious, reports Neowin. Specifically affecting Microsoft Defender for Office 365, and confirmed by Microsoft, this bug shows an “Opening this website might not be safe” warning when trying to open legitimate Google links. Microsoft says it has identified the cause of the issue, clarifying that it isn’t an actual security threat with Google links: Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links may block the opening of Google search links (URLs), identifying them as malicious. In addition, admins may receive related alerts and incidents in the Microsoft Defender portal and Microsoft Sentinel as a result of these detections. We’ve determined that an inaccurate security classification is causing legitimate Google search URLs to be incorrectly identified as malicious, resulting in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links blocking access to affected links. We’re working to correct the misclassification to remediate impact. Microsoft says it’s working on a fix, but hasn’t given a specific timeline regarding when the fix will be released.

item.title: How ad-free streaming became so much less affordable
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.52
Ad-free streaming used to be one of the biggest benefits of cutting the cable TV cord. Now it’s become a luxury. Inspired by some new research into the growing price gap between ad-supported and ad-free streaming, I decided to calculate how much the cost to avoid commercials has increased over time. Depending on which services you have, you could be paying an extra $42.50 just to skip ads, up 60 percent from a few years ago. Not all hope is lost for affordable ad-free TV, but you might have to get a bit creative to get it.
