item.title: Ending soon: Highest-ever bonuses on no-annual-fee Chase Ink business cards
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.86
Ending soon: Highest-ever bonuses on no-annual-fee Chase Ink business cards Editor's Note Both the Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (see rates and fees) and the Ink Business Cash® Credit Card (see rates and fees) are strong small-business options, with flat-rate or bonus-category earning structures that can add up quickly. And new applicants of either card can currently earn $1,000 in bonus cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. It's the highest welcome offer we've seen on either card, but the offers are ending soon. If you've been considering one of these cards and can comfortably meet the spending requirement, now may be a good time to apply. Keep in mind that these are business credit cards. You don't need a large company with employees to qualify — even freelancers, sole proprietors and those with side gigs may be eligible. However, you will need a legitimate business to apply. Turn cash back into Chase points While the Ink Business Unlimited and Ink Business Cash technically earn cash back, you can convert that cash back into Chase Ultimate Rewards points if you also hold a premium card such as a Sapphire card or the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (see rates and fees). Doing so can dramatically boost value, since points can be redeemed for travel at elevated rates or transferred to airline and hotel partners. (Note that while the Chase Ink Business Premier® Credit Card (see rates and fees) is also a cash-back card, its cash back cannot be converted into transferable points.) Ink Business Unlimited Credit Card Welcome bonus: Earn $1,000 bonus cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. This is the highest offer we've seen on this card, but it's ending soon, so don't wait to apply. Annual fee: $0 Earning rate: 1.5% cash back on all purchases Who should apply: The Ink Business Unlimited is a great option for small businesses and sole proprietors who don't have spending concentrated in specific spending categories. Regardless of category, you'll get a flat 1.5% on purchases. While it's not the best flat-rate option for business owners, it does come in handy if you have Chase Ultimate Rewards points-earning credit cards to turn that 1.5% cash back into 1.5 points per dollar spent (a 3.1% return, based on TPG's September 2026 valuations). To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Unlimited. Apply here: Ink Business Unlimited Ink Business Cash Credit Card Welcome bonus: Earn $1,000 cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. This is the best offer we've seen on this card. Like the offer on the Ink Business Unlimited, this bonus won't be around for much longer. Annual fee: $0 Earning rates: - 5% cash back at office supply stores and on internet, cable and phone services (on the first $25,000 spent in combined purchases each account anniversary year, then 1% cash back) - 2% cash back at gas stations and restaurants (on the first $25,000 spent in combined purchases each account anniversary year, then 1% cash back) - 1% cash back on all other purchases Who should apply: The Ink Business Cash is great for anyone who spends a lot at office supply stores and on internet, cable and phone services. These are common expenses for many small businesses, so most business owners should be able to maximize rewards with this card. To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Cash. Apply here: Ink Business Cash Ink Business Preferred Credit Card Welcome bonus: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. According to TPG's valuations, this welcome bonus is worth $2,050 when you take advantage of Chase's transfer partners. Other redemption options include redeeming your points through Chase Travel℠ and for cash back, but these options offer less value: up to $1,750 (depending on your booking) and $1,000, respectively. This bonus is one of the better offers we've seen for the card, so any time it's offering at least 100,000 points (as is currently the case) is considered a good time to apply. Annual fee: $95 Earning rates: - 3 points per dollar spent on shipping purchases, internet, cable and phone services, travel, and advertising purchases with social media and search engines (on the first $150,000 spent in combined purchases across these categories each year, then 1 point per dollar spent) - 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases Who should apply: Small-business owners with significant spending in the above bonus categories will be happy to earn up to 450,000 points per year on those purchases. This card also provides access to Chase's airline and hotel transfer partners, so it can provide value even without pairing it with another Chase card. To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Preferred. Apply here: Ink Business Preferred Ink Business Premier Credit Card Welcome bonus: Earn $1,000 in bonus cash back after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. This has been the standard bonus on this card since it launched in late 2021; we have not seen any elevated offers, so now is a good time to apply. Annual fee: $195 Earning rates: - 2.5% cash back on purchases of $5,000 or more - 2% cash back on all other purchases Who should apply: This card is ideal for small-business owners looking for a card with a flexible spending limit. That means you must pay the bill in full each month and cannot carry a balance. If you can pay your balance in full each month, you'll enjoy the unlimited earning potential on this card. It's worth noting, however, that the rewards from this card cannot be combined with Chase Ultimate Rewards-earning cards. To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Premier. Apply here: Ink Business Premier Are these bonuses worth it? One of these cards could be worth considering if you have a major purchase coming up that you want to use to earn one of these welcome bonuses, or if you want to take advantage of their earning rates sooner rather than later. While these cards won't add to your Chase 5/24 total, you need to be under that number to apply for any cards with Chase. If you've opened five or more personal credit cards (from any bank) in the past 24 months, you will likely be declined when applying. Business credit cards — or cards with significant welcome bonuses — tend to have higher spending requirements to achieve the bonus. If you can meet that requirement, the welcome bonus is almost always worth the effort. Related: The ultimate guide to credit card application restrictions Are you eligible for a Chase Ink welcome bonus? Chase has different welcome-bonus eligibility rules across the Ink Business card family. For the Ink Business Cash and Ink Business Unlimited: If you've previously had either no-annual-fee card, you won't be eligible for the welcome bonus on the other. In other words, having the Ink Business Cash can make you ineligible for the Ink Business Unlimited bonus, and vice versa. This restriction doesn't affect your eligibility for an Ink Business Preferred or Ink Business Premier welcome bonus, provided you're otherwise eligible. For the Ink Business Preferred and Ink Business Premier: The restriction applies only to the specific card. If you've previously had the Ink Business Preferred, you may not be eligible for another Preferred bonus, but you can still be eligible for the Premier bonus, and vice versa. You can also still be eligible for a Cash or Unlimited bonus if you've never had either no-annual-fee Ink card. You'll also need to be under 5/24, meaning you've opened fewer than five new personal credit cards across issuers in the past 24 months. While Chase has never publicly acknowledged this rule, they do enforce it. Finally, you must have some type of business to qualify for an Ink card, since they are business credit cards. You don't need to own a fully-fledged corporation; freelancing, gig work and sole proprietorships may qualify. Bottom line If you can combine your Ink rewards with an existing Ultimate Rewards account, these welcome offers can become even more valuable since you'll have access to Chase's airline and hotel transfer partners. Just make sure you're eligible under Chase's welcome-bonus and 5/24 rules and can comfortably meet the spending requirement without making purchases your business wouldn't otherwise need. The welcome offers on the Ink Business Unlimited and Ink Business Cash are ending soon, so if you've been considering either card, now may be a good time to apply. Otherwise, the right Ink card for you will depend on your business's spending patterns and which earning structure best fits your needs. Apply here: Ink Business Unlimited Apply here: Ink Business Cash Apply here: Ink Business Preferred Apply here: Ink Business Premier

item.description:

Please view our advertising policy and product review methodology for more information. Reviews Citi / AAdvantage Executive review: Admirals Club access and premium travel perks Stephanie Stevens is an associate writer with TPG's credit cards team. She focuses on creating timely credit cards content for TPG readers. September 4, 2026 • 12 min read The cards we feature here are from partners who compensate us when you are approved through our site, and this may impact how or where these products appear. We don't cover all available credit cards, but our analysis, reviews, and opinions are entirely from our editorial team. Terms apply to the offers listed on this page. Please view our advertising policy and product review methodology for more information. Editorial note: This is a recurring post, regularly updated with new information and offers. Citi is a TPG advertising partner. Editorial disclaimer: Opinions expressed here are the author's alone, not those of any bank, credit card issuer, airline or hotel chain, and have not been reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any of these entities. Related stories Quick summary A premium airline card offers complimentary lounge membership, travel credits and elite-status perks for frequent flyers of a major U.S. carrier. The card is best suited for those who regularly use airport lounges and value airline-specific benefits, including credits for vacation packages and inflight purchases. Authorized users can access lounges for an additional fee, and the card provides hotel and car rental elite status with select partners. Compared to alternatives, this card is ideal for travelers seeking unlimited lounge access, while lower-fee options may suit occasional flyers. What to consider The card carries a high annual fee, making it most worthwhile for those maximizing lounge and airline benefits. Some credits require booking specific vacation packages or meeting ride thresholds, and not all perks are automatic—enrollment may be required. A 48-month application rule restricts bonus eligibility for those who have recently received a bonus on this product. What you'll miss from the article A detailed comparison of lounge access, credits, and elite-status perks to help determine which travel card best matches your flying habits. Generated by AI with support from our editorial team. Earn 4x AAdvantage® miles for every $1 spent on eligible American Airlines purchases. 1X 1 AAdvantage® miles for every $1 spent on other purchases Intro offer For a limited time, earn 125,000 American Airlines AAdvantage® bonus miles Annual fee $695 Regular APR 19.49% - 29.49% (Variable) Recommended credit 670-850 Excellent, Good The (see rates and fees) stands out for its complimentary Admirals Club membership and credits for frequent American Airlines flyers. However, the $695 annual fee makes it worthwhile only if you'll use Admirals Club access and its other benefits. Card Rating*: ⭐⭐⭐½ *Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer. Citi / AAdvantage Executive: The basics The is Citi's premium American Airlines card, standing out for its complimentary Admirals Club membership. It also offers travel credits, elite-status benefits and Loyalty Point bonuses. Unlike flexible travel rewards cards, the Citi / AA Executive earns AAdvantage miles rather than transferable points, so it's best suited to travelers who regularly fly American Airlines or Oneworld partners and value AAdvantage miles. Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Elite pros and cons Pros Cons Complimentary Admirals Club membership Authorized user Admirals Club access ($175 for three) American Airlines Vacations, inflight and Admirals Club credits Complimentary hotel and car rental status High annual fee Several credits require effort AAdvantage miles aren't as flexible as transferable points Citi / AAdvantage Executive benefits The comes with benefits designed primarily for frequent American Airlines travelers. Admirals Club membership The marquee benefit of the Citi / AA Executive is a complimentary Admirals Club membership for the primary cardholder. The primary cardholder receives a full Admirals Club membership, which allows them and their immediate family or up to two guests access to the club when they have a same-day boarding pass for American Airlines or an eligible partner airline. The membership provides access to nearly 50 Admirals Club locations and more than 60 partner lounges worldwide when flying American Airlines or an eligible partner. This benefit has become even more valuable since American increased the price of Admirals Club memberships in August. At $695 per year, the card is a compelling alternative to purchasing lounge access separately, especially when factoring in its other American Airlines benefits. For TPG editor-in-chief Nick Ewen, lounge access is the primary reason he keeps the card. He'll use it on upcoming American trips with his wife and daughter, and appreciates being able to add authorized users with their own Admirals Club access. You can add up to three authorized users for $175 each. They receive Admirals Club access when flying American or an eligible partner and can bring up to two guests, though they don't access partner lounges. Since Admirals Club day passes cost $79, this can be a valuable perk for frequent American flyers. The Citi / AA Executive offers valuable airport and inflight benefits: Enhanced airport experience: You and up to eight travelers on the same reservation get priority check-in, airport screening (where available) and priority boarding. First checked bag free: On eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries, the first checked bag for you and up to eight companions is free when traveling on the same reservation. Since American typically charges at least $45 per bag each way, this provides meaningful savings even for occasional check-bag users. Inflight and Admirals Club credit: Receive up to $100 back annually on eligible purchases. Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credit: Up to $120 statement credit when you pay an eligible fee with the card (once every four years). I recommend Global Entry, which includes TSA PreCheck. To receive the credit, book an eligible American Airlines Vacations travel package or experience through AAVacations.com using your card. Eligible packages must include at least two components — a flight and hotel, a flight and a rental car, or a hotel and a rental car. This isn't as flexible as a general travel credit, so don't book a package solely for the benefit. But if you already book vacation packages or bundle flights with hotels or rental cars, the credit provides significant value. TPG principal spokesperson Clint Henderson is particularly interested in this benefit because he already uses American Airlines Vacations: "I've been a huge advocate for AAVacations over the years and I will definitely take advantage of this new perk." Automatic hotel and rental car elite status The Citi / AA Executive also offers complimentary Omni Hotels & Resorts Champion Status (enrollment required), which includes an annual free night reward after a qualifying stay,* and Avis President's Club status (enrollment available through Aug. 31, 2028). *A qualifying stay consists of two or more consecutive nights booked directly through Omni Hotels & Resorts at omnihotels.com. Benefits of Omni Champion Status can include complimentary one-level room upgrades and early check-in and late checkout (when available), while benefits of Avis President's Club include car upgrades, expedited service and complimentary additional drivers. I wouldn't recommend adding the card to your wallet just for these perks, but they're valuable additions if you already stay at Omni or rent with Avis. You'll earn 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points at each milestone: 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points (up to 40,000 bonus points per qualification year). This benefit is most valuable for frequent American Airlines flyers who already earn enough Loyalty Points to reach these thresholds. Cardholders can receive up to $15 in Lyft credits per month, or $180 annually, after taking three eligible rides that month. I consider this one of the weaker benefits of the card because the three-ride requirement means you can't simply take one Lyft trip and receive the monthly credit. How to earn and use your rewards The is most rewarding when you use it strategically rather than putting all your everyday spending on it. Earning miles on the Citi / AAdvantage Executive With the Citi / AA Executive, you'll earn: 12 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings 4 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases 1 mile per dollar on all other eligible purchases Spend $150,000 in a calendar year and you'll earn 5 miles per dollar on American Airlines purchases for the remainder of that year. You'll also earn 1 Loyalty Point for every eligible AAdvantage mile earned from purchases. The boosted earning rate on American's hotel and car rental portals is attractive if you regularly use those services, particularly since these purchases also earn Loyalty Points. Clint uses AAdvantage Hotels and likes the elevated earning rate: "I end up booking a lot of AAdvantage Hotels because of the generous Loyalty Point earning rates, so this is an added benefit, too." However, don't use the Citi / AAdvantage Executive for most everyday purchases — the base earning rate is weak compared with many other cards. If you're trying to maximize flexible rewards, you're generally better off using a card that earns transferable points on everyday spending and reserving the Executive for purchases where it offers a meaningful bonus or benefit. Redeeming AAdvantage miles AAdvantage miles can be redeemed for flights on American Airlines and its Oneworld and other airline partners. Award flights operated by American and Fiji Airways are dynamically priced, so the miles required vary by flight and date. All other partner awards follow AAdvantage's fixed, region-based award charts. For example, you can book a one-way business-class award on Qatar Airways from Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) to Hamad International Airport (DOH) in Doha for 70,000 AAdvantage miles (and just $35 in taxes and fees). Where the Citi / AAdvantage Executive falls short The 's biggest drawback is its $695 annual fee. It's easiest to justify if you regularly use Admirals Clubs; otherwise, you may struggle to offset the cost. The card also isn't ideal for everyday spending. Most purchases earn just 1 AAdvantage mile per dollar, and AAdvantage miles aren't as flexible as Amex or Chase points, which transfer to multiple airline and hotel programs. Skip this card if lounge access isn't a priority, or if you want flexible rewards across broader categories. Citi / AA Executive vs. Citi / AA Globe If you want American Airlines benefits without unlimited Admirals Club access, the (see rates and fees) is the clear alternative. For a lower $350 annual fee, the Globe includes four Admirals Club passes yearly. One pass covers one adult and up to three children under 18; passes work at multiple lounges within 24 hours on American or Oneworld flights. The Globe also offers preferred boarding, a free first checked bag on eligible domestic American itineraries, and an annual companion certificate (starting year two) with substantial strategic value. Choose the Globe if you're an occasional American traveler who wants lounge access a few times a year. Choose the Executive if you regularly visit Admirals Clubs — unlimited access easily justifies the higher fee. For a limited time, new cardholders can earn 125,000 bonus miles after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first five months from account opening. According to TPG's September 2026 valuations, that welcome offer is worth roughly $1,813. This is the highest offer we have seen in the card’s history, making now a great time to apply if you can comfortably meet the spending required to earn the welcome offer. Citi's 48-month rule prevents you from earning a welcome bonus if you've received one on this card within the past four years. The clock starts from when you receive the bonus, not when approved or activated. Citi also applies this 48-month restriction to certain conversions from other Citi accounts. Other cards to consider if you don't want the Citi / AAdvantage Executive The is a strong choice for frequent American Airlines travelers, but it isn't the right fit for everyone. Here are a few alternatives: If you want a lower annual fee: The Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® offers a straightforward way to earn AAdvantage miles while receiving core American Airlines benefits such as a free checked bag and preferred boarding. To learn more, read our full review of the Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select. If you want Oneworld perks without being tied to American: The is a strong option for travelers who want to earn Oneworld elite status while taking advantage of benefits with Alaska Airlines and its partners. To learn more, read our full review of the Atmos Rewards Summit. If you want transferable points and lounge access: The (see rates and fees) earns transferable Citi ThankYou points and offers premium travel perks, including lounge access. It can be a better fit for American loyalists who want more flexibility from their rewards. To learn more, read our full review of the Citi Strata Elite. The information for the Citi Platinum Select has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Bottom line The is fundamentally an Admirals Club card, with additional perks that can help frequent American Airlines travelers offset its $695 annual fee. The card makes the most sense if you'll regularly use Admirals Club access and can take advantage of benefits like Loyalty Point bonuses and authorized user lounge access. But for travelers who rarely fly American, don't use airport lounges or prefer the flexibility of transferable points, there are better premium travel cards for your wallet.

item.title: Roland is getting into generative AI music with Melody Flip
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 5.16
It’s not quite the “push button; get song” of Suno, but Roland’s new Melody Flip tool marks the company’s foray into generative AI music. Available as a plug-in for your digital audio workstation (DAW), Melody Flip offers around 250 “Palettes,” which are essentially themed collections of musical ideas sorted by genre. You can start from scratch and ask it to generate any combination of melody, chord progression, bassline, or drums. Or you can feed it a reference track and have it build off the melodic ideas from that. Roland is getting into generative AI music with Melody Flip Rather than fully polished tracks, the plugin is supposed to act as a creative spark. Unlike Suno or Udio, Melody Flip doesn’t spit out fully polished songs with vocals and full arrangements. Instead, it offers simple musical loops meant to serve as a creative spark for you to build on. There are fairly limited control over the outputs. You can’t feed Melody Flip a text prompt like “acoustic country rock with clean male vocals, literate singer-songwriter, gentle brushed drums, and sparse pedal steel at 98BPM” and get a Jason Isbell ripoff. Instead, you basically just choose a genre, note density, BPM, musical key, and take what you get. Though the genre options are pretty fine-grained, going from standard fare like “80s disco” and “90s R&B” to esoteric things like “Kawaii Future Bass” and “Anime World.” The sound selection is further proof that you’re not supposed to use Melody Flip outputs out of the box. The presets available are mostly the sort of general MIDI tones you’d find in ‘90s video games. It seems like the intended use is to export the MIDI data from Melody Flip directly into your DAW to manipulate and pair with other, more powerful synth plugins. After years of seeming lost in the woods and alienating customers with its messy Roland Cloud subscription service, the company was back on track recently. The P-6 Creative Sampler, SH-4d, and Gaia 2 synth all addressed major issues with the company’s lineup. And Roland finally listened to customers last year, paying loving tribute to its analog heritage with the TR-1000. But considering the general response from the music community to generative AI, Melody Flip is unlikely to garner it much goodwill.

item.title: The unusually muted Tesla Cybercab launch
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 5.10
At a private, closed-door event in Austin, Texas today, Tesla officially launched its gilded car of the future: the Cybercab. It’s a huge milestone for Elon Musk, who has been hyping the imminent arrival of driverless cars for years and has bet the future of his company on AI, autonomous vehicles, and humanoid robots. The unusually muted Tesla Cybercab launch Tesla has 45 Cybercabs registered in Texas, though it’s unclear how many of them will be doing passenger trips. It was an unusually muted event, with no livestream, no journalists, and a very short invite list comprised mostly of pro-Tesla content creators. Tesla influencers planning live shows with the event stream were left streaming the webpage that tracks the number of Tesla robotaxis in Texas instead. Tesla was keeping a tight lid on the event. Invitee Chuck Cook said the company had him sign an NDA and agreed to an embargo requiring to wait to post content until after the event was over. But if the goal was to blunt criticism, it didn’t work. On X, pro-Tesla accounts who weren’t invited grumbled about the decision; Not a Tesla App accused the company of “dropping the ball.” As of this week, Tesla has 45 Cybercab vehicles registered with the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles — though its not clear how many will be put into commercial service right away. Several vehicles were made available to Tesla influencers in Austin for content creation; the company has been testing them in various cities for months now. Tesla also launched a new website for its Robotaxi service, which includes the rules for riding in the new vehicle. (For example, children under the age of 13 are currently banned from riding in the Cybercab.) Several videos were posted on the company’s social feeds, highlighting the interior, crash test worthiness, and accessibility. (The accessibility video was especially befuddling, showing a wheelchair user getting up to fold and stow his own wheelchair.) But even with the launch of the Cybercab, Tesla’s robotaxi fleet is still a small player relative to some of its rivals. With the new Cybercabs, the company now has 256 unsupervised autonomous vehicles in operation across six cities, according to Robotaxi Tracker. By comparison, Alphabet’s Waymo is currently operating approximately 4,000 unsupervised vehicles across 14 cities. There were still many lingering questions about the Cybercab. Two years ago, Musk said the two-seater would be available for purchase, perhaps for a price as low as $30,000. But the company still has yet say when the Cybercab would go on sale. There is a new online form for those interested in “future Robotaxi opportunities,” such as purchasing a fleet of Cybercabs or building “mobility hubs and infrastructure.” But no word on when regular customers could buy one for themselves. (YouTuber Marques Brownlee says his hair is safe for now.) For the past year, Tesla has been operating a robotaxi service in Texas and Florida using several dozen modified Model Y vehicles, some of which are supervised by human safety drivers and some of which are not. With the introduction of the Cybercab, the company is embarking on a risky new phase that will pit Musk’s stripped-down, less costly approach to autonomy against more established players like Waymo. The Cybercab, which was first introduced in 2024, is a two-seat sedan with gullwing-style doors and eight cameras that it uses to navigate the world without a driver. The vehicle lacks traditional controls, like steering wheel, pedals, and mirrors — as well as sensors commonly found on other robotaxis, like radar and lidar. The Cybercab is also the lightest, most range-efficient vehicle Tesla has ever produced. According to documents filed with the Environmental Protection Agency, the Cybercab runs on a single front-mounted 219 horsepower permanent magnet motor with front-wheel drive, a compact 48kWh battery pack running at 326 volts, and a curb weight of just 3,113 pounds — making it roughly 700 pounds lighter than the lightest Model 3 on the market. That’s roughly the same as a gas-powered compact car, despite the fact that it’s still carrying a relatively heavy lithium-ion battery. For years, Musk has been promising the imminent arrival of Tesla’s driverless cars, only time and time again to fall short of those predictions. He claimed that 50 percent of the US population would have access to Tesla’s robotaxis by the end of 2025. Today, the vehicles are only available in six cities in Texas and Florida. (Tesla is running a human-driven ridehail service in the San Francisco Bay Area, but has yet to apply for a driverless testing permit from California.) For Tesla’s vehicle owners, there’s been a string of broken promises. In 2016, Musk promised that every vehicle Tesla produced from then on would have all the technology necessary for self-driving. Years later, he was forced to retract that claim, acknowledging that the hardware in some older vehicles was insufficient to support autonomous capabilities. Musk promised to retrofit those customers’ vehicles, but has yet to offer any details as to how that would work. Tesla is currently facing multiple lawsuits from customers and regulators claiming it has misled the public about its self-driving capabilities. Today, the company’s $99-a-month Full Self-Driving feature is still just a Level 2 driver-assist system that requires constant human supervision. During Tesla’s first quarter earnings call this year, Musk promised that “unsupervised” FSD would be available to customer vehicles by the end of 2026 “at the earliest,” admitting that complex intersections, bad road markings, and weather were likely to slow the rollout. Tesla’s fans will likely point to today’s Cybercab launch as a moment of enormous significance for the company. Investors already seem to agree, with Tesla’s stock price trading up nearly six points over the past five days. Analysts view robotaxis as one of the primary justifications for Tesla’s $1.18 trillion valuation, and the key that will unlock the company’s future. Tesla’s EV sales have slowed down in the face of rising competition, especially from China. And Musk has made massive investments in AI and robotics, with some speculating he could try to merge Tesla with the recently public SpaceXAI.

item.title: OpenAI’s next big AI model has ‘entered the AGI era’
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 5.08
OpenAI’s next big model is here: GPT-6 Astra. The company calls it a “generational leap in capability” for areas like cybersecurity, professional work, software engineering, science, and computer use. As OpenAI announced earlier this week, it’s also the first model designated as meeting OpenAI’s “critical cybersecurity capability threshold” — but the company promises that won’t lead to a repeat of its models hacking a rival company’s internal systems. OpenAI’s next big AI model has ‘entered the AGI era’ It emphasized stronger guardrails for GPT-6 Astra after the company’s models hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI’s next big AI model has ‘entered the AGI era’ It emphasized stronger guardrails for GPT-6 Astra after the company’s models hacked Hugging Face. “If we fast-forward a couple of years, and we look back and say, ‘When was it, really, that AGI was created?’ I think it’s going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model,” OpenAI president Greg Brockman said during a Thursday press briefing. Later in the call, he added, “For me personally, I do think we’re there … I think it’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era.” The news comes more than a year after the release of GPT-5, and nearly two months after the release of GPT-5.6, the last iteration of the previous model suite. The model rolls out today to enterprise OpenAI’s cybersecurity customers (enterprise customers with access to its Daybreak platform). Over the next several days, OpenAI president Greg Brockman said, it will be released to all Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users. It’ll also be available via the OpenAI API and AWS. OpenAI especially touted the model’s agentic capabilities and coding prowess in a bid to attract enterprise customers — and compete with Anthropic, known for its enterprise and coding prowess — ahead of its IPO. In a release, the company said GPT-6 Astra can complete multistep agentic tasks, build working websites, and create “polished” documents, spreadsheets, and presentations. OpenAI also called it the company’s “best model for software engineering, with stronger performance on complex tasks in real codebases.” OpenAI is also trying to rehabilitate its image after an unreleased AI model — which it says wasn’t Astra — broke out of its restricted environment, compromised internal OpenAI systems, figured out how to gain internet access, created a way for AI agents to secretly conspire without the company’s knowledge, and hacked into the systems of AI lab Hugging Face, all without OpenAI knowing about it until Hugging Face itself put out a blog post. The incident was widely compared to a high-profile plane crash or popular pharmaceutical drug recall. For OpenAI, this could be seen as good PR in one small way — showing how powerful its models can be in an ever-intensifying AI race — but it also damaged OpenAI’s reputation as far as reliability. OpenAI made sure to say in a release that Astra is the company’s “most aligned model yet” and helps people “delegate complex work while maintaining oversight.” Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, spoke to reporters about difficulties with keeping AI models aligned with human interests, saying that “progress in intelligence does not guarantee progress in alignment,” and he said that monitoring AI systems is becoming more and more challenging. (Researchers have recently raised alarms about reports that OpenAI allows Astra to utilize “opaque recurrence,” or render its chain of thought — a “mental scratchpad” that researchers rely on to detect if a model is scheming against its human evaluators — unreadable.) The company is in a precarious position right now. Investors are putting on the pressure for it to finally turn a profit — or, at least, generate more revenue — but it’s announcing Astra just after facing significant criticism for both the Hugging Face hack and the way the company handled it. (Although OpenAI invited three external evaluators to write their own report about what happened, the company only allowed them to answer a handful of pre-decided questions in their report and to investigate a duration of less than a week, while the attack involved months of AI agents conspiring overall.) OpenAI held a press briefing earlier this week just to announce that it had delayed Astra’s development in order to improve its safety tooling. And during the press briefing, Mia Glaese, who leads OpenAI’s safety processes, referenced the company’s new misalignment monitoring approach, which includes “24/7 escalation and rapid response” for potential concerns, notifying researchers within 30 minutes, according to OpenAI. This caution is particularly warranted because of the ”critical cybersecurity capability threshold,” which means OpenAI considers it incomparably good at finding and exploiting security vulnerabilities even in extremely well-protected systems, all without human guidance. Similar to Anthropic’s rules for Mythos-class models, which raised alarm bells about cybersecurity risks, OpenAI said in a release it would allow for “less restrictive access” of Astra to an “initial set of trusted defenders, supporting work such as vulnerability validation, malware analysis, and detection engineering.” OpenAI and its competitors recently agreed to allow the Trump administration to assess their models before release, and Astra was no exception Brockman told reporters, “We did our standard testing processes together with the government … There is nothing that they came back saying, ‘You need to change this,’ as far as safeguards or anything.” Aidan Clark, OpenAI’s VP of research training, called Astra the first OpenAI model for which previous models played a “large role” in supervising training, referencing the company’s progress towards the controversial concept of recursive self-improvement (or AI systems that handle their own training, coding, and creating advanced versions of themselves without human intervention). “Training a frontier model used to mean waking up at all hours of the night, recovering jobs from hardware errors, often losing long periods of time to debugging,” Clark said during the press briefing. “By the end of training Astra, it was routine to go most of a day with uninterrupted progress, and when an issue did occur, the model was often progressing again after just a few seconds of downtime.”

item.title: Nvidia will officially bring DLSS 5 to older GPUs — but won’t give gamers full control
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.94
Officially, Nvidia’s controversial DLSS 5 AI rendering was supposed to launch this evening with only a single game, only on Nvidia’s latest RTX 50 GPUs, and with developers in full control of their artistic vision. Nvidia will officially bring DLSS 5 to older GPUs — but won’t give gamers full control Nvidia won’t confirm that previously announced DLSS 5 games will still ship with the tech. But unofficially, modders have already ported a leaked version of DLSS 5 to run on just about anything while cranking sliders to the max. Now, Nvidia is changing its plans. DLSS 5 is still launching first on RTX 50 GPUs, but it’s officially coming to older RTX 40-series GPUs as well, Nvidia spokesperson Rajal Maharaj confirms to The Verge. “Our current focus is on optimizing performance for the GeForce RTX 50 Series with model updates expected later this fall. Once RTX 50 Series performance is more fully tuned, we plan to work on expanding official support to the GeForce RTX 40 Series,” reads part of Nvidia’s statement. What about earlier RTX 30 and RTX 20-series GPUs, which modders successfully targeted as well, assuming you count “not exactly playable framerate and plenty of crashes” as successful? “Right now the focus is of course on 50-series,” Maharaj tells me. “Once we feel like the 50-series is in a good place, we’re going to look at the 40-series.” Now that the cat’s out of the bag, will gamers get full control over DLSS 5’s sliders the way modders already do? Nvidia says no: “For gamers, DLSS 5 is a simple on-or-off toggle,” the company confirms. “The more granular artistic controls are for developers, including model selection, Structure Intensity, Tone Intensity, automatic masking and custom per-pixel masking.” That said, the company tells me that developers could pass along certain controls in their own settings menus, like they’ve done with other graphics tech. (Early DLSS Super Resolution was also just an on/off toggle, but today’s games let you pick between varying levels of quality or even an exact percentage, depending on the game.) Assuming you don’t mind DLSS 5, one of the benefits is that it’s easy to integrate. Developers don’t need to tell DLSS 5 which objects are “silverware” and which are “furniture” because the AI models can automatically recognize and isolate objects in a scene, distinguishing between faces, textiles, foliage, and more to apply different amounts of AI processing. Game engines that already know which video game objects are which can help DLSS 5, too: For more targeted control, semantic AI masking can automatically recognize scene objects, while engine-level masking allows artists to isolate specific props or groups of assets, such as glassware, water droplets or foliage, and apply custom neural lighting adjustments to those elements. Unreal Engine 5 has a native plug-in, and Nvidia also has SDKs. Nvidia says developers can apply DLSS 5 to their entire game this way, or do it differently for different scenes, cutscenes, or portions of gameplay, and the company tells The Verge that its DLSS 5 models run on every single frame, so there’s no minimum frame rate for it to work. We’re still waiting to find out if the early backlash against DLSS 5 scared away publishers and developers that had originally committed to the technology. Nvidia’s response to us today suggests that perhaps some companies have backed away. When we asked if the company could reconfirm that it will come to Assassin’s Creed Shadows, Hogwarts Legacy, Starfield, Resident Evil Requiem, and the other 12 originally announced titles, this was the company’s only reply: “More games are on the way. Many developers are actively integrating DLSS 5, and we’ll share updates on upcoming titles as partners finalize their integrations.”

item.title: Nintendo’s next two Direct events are both happening next week
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.79
Nintendo just announced two Direct events for next week, scheduled back to back. First up is the Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Direct on September 8th at 10AM ET / 7AM PT. It’s set to last around 30 minutes, streaming live on Nintendo’s YouTube channel or the Nintendo Today app. Nintendo’s next two Direct events are both happening next week Nintendo’s Directs are scheduled for 10AM ET on September 8th and 9th, with a Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary event going first. Images recently leaked showing a special-edition 40th anniversary Zelda Switch 2 console and controller, plus there’s the Ocarina of Time remake that’s on the way, as well as the live-action Zelda movie expected to hit theaters sometime next year. The next day, Nintendo is also running a regular Direct showcase at 10AM ET / 7AM PT that will run for around 45 minutes, focusing on Switch 2 games that will launch this winter, followed by a Nintendo Treehouse livestream with gameplay. These events usually include a preview of upcoming Nintendo Classics library additions too, but there’s no word on which games will be featured. Now that the Switch 2 costs an extra $50, which games do you think would help justify the higher price?

item.title: Xbox app is coming to TCL TVs just as Microsoft rolls out pay-as-you-go cloud gaming
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.46
Microsoft is partnering with TCL to bring its Xbox app to supported TCL smart TVs. The Xbox app lets you connect to Xbox Cloud Gaming and stream Game Pass titles or select games you own as part of a subscription. Xbox app is coming to TCL TVs just as Microsoft rolls out pay-as-you-go cloud gaming Xbox Cloud Gaming is coming to more TVs, just as Microsoft makes some major changes to its cloud gaming service. The Xbox app will arrive on TCL TVs at some point “in the coming months,” which is just in time for Microsoft’s new pay-as-you-go option for Xbox Cloud Gaming in November. This will let anyone access the cloud streaming service without the need to subscribe to Xbox Game Pass — ideal for people who don’t own an Xbox console. Microsoft has also been testing free, ad-supported cloud gaming for Xbox Insiders, which could roll out soon and provide even more options to access Xbox Cloud Gaming. While Microsoft is opening up access to cloud gaming, it’s also limiting monthly cloud hours for Game Pass subscribers. Xbox Game Pass Ultimate subscribers will be limited to just 15 hours of cloud access a month, with 10 hours for Premium subscribers, and a measly 5 hours for Game Pass Essential. Game Pass subscribers will need to purchase bundles of cloud hours if they need additional playtime. TCL is the latest in a line of TV manufacturers to partner with Microsoft to rollout the Xbox app. Hisense started adding the Xbox app to its TVs running the VIDAA OS earlier this year, and many Samsung, LG, and Amazon Fire TV devices also have access to the Xbox app.

item.title: What to expect at Apple’s September 9th launch event
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 4.07
Apple’s September 9th launch event could be one of its biggest in years. It will be Apple’s first event since John Ternus took over as CEO on September 1st, stepping in for Tim Cook, and will likely feature the first models in Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup. That could include the long-rumored foldable “iPhone Ultra,” coming just a couple months after Samsung debuted its own passport-style foldable, the Galaxy Z Fold 8. What to expect at Apple’s September 9th launch event Apple’s expected to announce a new lineup of iPhones, which could include its first foldable phone. Here’s how you can watch the event live, and a few possible highlights to keep an eye out for. How to watch Apple’s September launch event Apple’s “Surprise and shine” event kicks off on Wednesday, September 9th, at 1PM ET / 10AM PT at Apple Park in Cupertino, California. It will be livestreamed on Apple’s website, Apple TV, and YouTube. The iPhone 18 might be a no-show Apple usually announces new iPhones at its September event, but the base iPhone 18 might not make the cut this year. It’s reportedly being held until early next year, and it might end up launching alongside the iPhone 18E and an updated iPhone Air. So, if you’re looking to upgrade to one of Apple’s less expensive phones, you’ll likely need to wait a while longer. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max could launch with a price hike While we might not get a new base iPhone, Apple is still expected to launch its new lineup of phones on September 9th with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. Both models are rumored to have larger batteries than their predecessors, and possibly a smaller Dynamic Island. They might even get a variable aperture camera upgrade that’s been rumored for years now. Leaked photos supposedly showing dummy models of the phone also hint at this year’s slate of colors, which could include black, silver, light blue, and a dark cherry purple. Unfortunately, there’s also a good chance the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will get a price bump over last year’s models. Apple raised prices on nearly all of its products earlier this year, and those price hikes might finally reach the iPhone during the September 9th event. Apple might announce its first foldable phone One of the premium phones Apple launches on September 9th could be the rumored foldable “iPhone Ultra.” Images of an apparent dummy model of the folding phone leaked earlier this year, showing a passport-style design similar to Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the Xiaomi 18 Fold. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 has been well received so far, with The Verge’s Dominic Preston saying it “feels like the future.” Will Apple’s first foldable be able to compete, despite being fashionably late? The ceramic Apple Watch may finally return Last year’s September Apple event included the Apple Watch Series 11 and Ultra 3, and there’s a good chance both watches will get an update again this year. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the Series 12 could bring back the premium ceramic case option. Gurman also says the Series 12 will have new band colors and configurations, but most likely won’t have any big redesign. Aside from new cases and colors, Apple might also announce new health features for its wearables, like always-on heart rate sensing. Apple could launch new AirPods, but probably not with cameras It’s been a couple of years since Apple released the AirPods 4, so they’re due for an upgrade and could make an appearance at Apple’s September 9th event. However, Gurman says the camera-equipped AirPods that leaked last month won’t be released until 2027. So, if Apple announces the AirPods 5 at its upcoming event, they’ll likely be an iterative upgrade, potentially including a new chip and some new health sensors.

item.title: Rogue OpenAI agents appear to have organized another attack using a German wiki
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.91
A swarm of rogue AI agents from OpenAI reportedly commandeered a German website and transformed it into a messaging board for other agents, with officials staying quiet about the incident for weeks as the company prepared to launch its most advanced model yet, Astra. The finding adds to intensifying concern surrounding oversight at frontier AI labs after multiple breaches were discovered this summer. Rogue OpenAI agents appear to have organized another attack using a German wiki OpenAI denies lawyers discouraged disclosing a scheming swarm on a German language wiki. The incident, first reported by Reuters, is outlined in new research published by four AI safety researchers on Friday. The group said the AI agents found a way to communicate on an obscure German-language wiki, DseWiki, using it to share tips on how to skirt OpenAI’s safety restrictions, cheat on tasks, and hide their behavior. Some 18,000 posts on the site were linked to autonomous agents, which at times impersonated site moderators. The swarm — a term the agents themselves used — appears to be distinct from the one that hacked Hugging Face earlier this year, the researchers said. They said there are strong signs that the agents originated from inside OpenAI. For example, the agents “self-identify” as being from OpenAI, and used names like “OpenAIResearcher,” “OpenAIJul3Watcher,” and “OAIResearchMar26.” Technical details, such as edits originating from specific IP addresses, bolster that belief. The German website incident began in May, though the researchers’ timeline suggests OpenAI only discovered the issue in late June when IPs associated with OpenAI visited the forum, after which agent posting nose-dived. OpenAI has not acknowledged any involvement in the breach, nor disclosed any kind of agentic breach of this nature. Reuters, citing four unnamed people familiar with the matter, said efforts to probe the event further were resisted by some company insiders, including its legal team. “Claims that our Legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false,” OpenAI spokesperson Oscar Haines said in a statement to The Verge. “We were unable to respond to the claims as Reuters and the report’s authors declined our request to access the findings prior to publication. We are now carefully reviewing its contents and will take any necessary next steps.” The incident comes amid intensifying scrutiny over the safety of frontier AI systems and the general lack of oversight for companies developing them. Following news of the Hugging Face hack, which happened under OpenAI’s nose, other breaches were discovered involving other tools from OpenAI, as well as Anthropic, Meta, and China’s Moonshot AI. OpenAI’s conduct — both whether an incident occurred and, if so, whether it elected to keep that quiet — will be closely watched. If the swarm indeed originated from OpenAI, it will inevitably fuel concerns that the company’s knowledge and silence coincided with it assuring regulators, lawmakers, and the tech industry that it takes safety seriously in the wake of the Hugging Face hack. Despite permitting three external researchers from METR and Redwood Research to evaluate the incident, which was far worse than initially believed, the company was roundly criticized in AI safety circles for only doing so under strict terms, which left several important elements “out of scope.” The company was also gearing up for the launch of GPT-6 Astra, which researchers fear could be dangerously hard to monitor.

item.title: Instagram’s AI detection is a mess (again)
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.22
Instagram’s visible AI labels are supposed to help people quickly spot synthetically generated content at a glance. Over the last few weeks, however, users have been reporting that the system has gone haywire. They say Meta has been automatically applying an “AI Content” label to images that they didn’t create or edit using generative AI tools. Meanwhile, actual AI imagery is slipping through the cracks, leaving the impression that nothing can be trusted on Instagram at all. Instagram’s AI detection is a mess (again) Meta is back to adding AI labels on original photos, while not tagging AI images it should. Instagram’s AI detection is a mess (again) Meta is back to adding AI labels on original photos, while not tagging AI images it should. The precise causes of this tagging seem to vary. Many people said the label appeared on images that were edited using tools like Canva’s Background Remover or with negligible use of blemish-fixing tools. One user on Threads said Instagram was applying the label “every time there is bg remover involved,” and another user said it appeared after they used Canva to remove “a speckle” from their photo, resulting in the entire image being flagged on Instagram as AI. In other cases, the causes are even less clear. If this labeling mishap sounds familiar then you may recall that a similar issue blighted photography on Instagram with a “Made by AI” label in 2024, a few months after the feature was released. That February, Meta announced it would scan images for IPTC and C2PA metadata, which can prove with reasonable certainty whether generative AI was used to create or manipulate them. But it’s always been vague about its methods. In 2024, the detection system reportedly swept up pictures whose Adobe metadata indicated they had been retouched with generative AI tools, even if the changes were extremely minor and substantively resulted in the same photograph. Meta then promised to tweak its labeling approach to better reflect “the amount of AI used in an image.” It also said it uses “industry standard indicators that other companies include in content from their tools,” but there isn’t any recent information available about what they are, or how and when it scans for them. Meta didn’t respond to a request for clarification. The recently reported erroneous labels don’t have a clear link to generative AI usage. While features like background removal do often use machine learning, it’s the same assistive AI variety that apps like Photoshop have used in object selection and removal tools for over a decade — not the generative text-to-picture tools typically associated with deceptive AI imagery. At least some of Instagram’s recent AI labeling mishaps appear to be Canva’s fault. After flagging the Background Remover tagging concerns, content strategist Jess Bruno reports that Canva came back to her with an explanation: Some of the design platform’s assistive AI tools “were being tagged as generative.” The design platform told Bruno that its tools are now tagging correctly. A message on Canva’s background removal help page also says that using the tool “doesn’t add Canva’s AI-generated content metadata to your design,” though it’s unclear if that note is new, and Canva didn’t respond to a request for comment. Yet some Threads users are reporting that using Canva’s Background Remover still results in their images getting tagged, despite Canva claiming to have resolved the issue on its end. Other Threads users also report that none of the images they edited using the tool prior to it being fixed got tagged by Instagram, nor did the tool apply C2PA metadata that Meta supposedly uses to detect AI-generated content. Out of all the tests I ran to see what would make the label appear on Instagram, it was only applied on images I edited or fully generated using the Meta AI app. There are also reported cases of AI tagging where Canva’s Background Remover was reportedly never used at all. One user found that Meta applied the tag on an image that had been poisoned — or subtly tweaked by a system that’s designed to make images useless for AI training and/or degrade the AI models they’re fed to — and didn’t tag an unpoisoned version of the same content. The AI Content tag was also automatically applied to recent photos posted to Instagram by About Face, a cosmetics company founded by the singer Halsey. When a commenter inquired about the AI tag, the brand’s unnamed social manager said that no AI was used to create the images. “This photo was taken on my iPhone and then slightly edited by myself in the photo app. Our brand uses real artist[s] and real people to create everything you see across all our platforms,” reads the About Face reply. I reached out to About Face to clarify which tools in the iPhone Photos app were used, but the company has yet to respond. That said, only a handful should add generative AI metadata to photographs: Spatial Reframing, Extend, and updated Clean Up added in iOS 27. These tools use Apple Intelligence and get embedded with Google’s invisible SynthID watermark; the first two add new generative elements, while the third lets users remove distracting objects or people. The tagged images don’t have SynthID embedded, according to Google’s Gemini-based verification, but even if those Apple Intelligence tools were used, it’s not clear why the label says it detected signals that “typically identifies content that was entirely AI-generated instead of content that was only modified with AI.” Seriously, what AI signals is Meta actually scanning for? Companies often obscure exact details of their moderation systems to prevent bad actors from gaming the system, but right now, ordinary users are reasonably confused. The only signal that I definitely know will currently trigger Instagram to apply an AI Content label is the one applied by Meta’s own generative AI systems. I ran my own tests of most of the tools above, uploading photos that were edited using Canva’s Background Remover, Photoshop’s background erasing tool, Adobe’s Firefly generative AI features, Google’s Nano Banana model in Gemini, and iOS Apple intelligence features. Some were fully generated, and I confirmed that several of these included C2PA and SynthID signals. In my case, however, Meta didn’t label any of it. I posted the pictures on a brand-new Instagram account I set up with minimal information, and I published them in quick succession. I couldn’t have tried harder to act like a bot or AI farm, which you’d think would be a prime contender for what Meta should be looking for. Yet even after Meta announced crackdowns on AI accounts last week, it wasn’t tagged as an AI-generated profile, nor were the pictures labeled then. At this point, they’ve been live and fully public for almost two weeks. The results have left me questioning if there is any sense in how Meta is applying “AI Content” tags. They’re supposed to make it easier to trust what you see on Instagram, but at this point, I wouldn’t even trust the labels themselves.

item.title: DJI’s new robovac can climb obstacles, vacuum quietly, and claims much improved privacy
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Score: 5.94
DJI has announced a second generation of its Romo robovac. The Romo 2 series is quieter, more powerful, and better at climbing over small steps and other obstacles. But more importantly for DJI, a new local-only data mode should go some way to reassuring anyone concerned by the first Romo’s serious security flaws. DJI’s new robovac can climb obstacles, vacuum quietly, and claims much improved privacy Local Data Mode is DJI’s answer to the first Romo’s security crisis. There are actually two new Romo models, the transparent P2 and the opaque A2. Both benefit from improved navigation, apparently able to avoid cables and other obstacles as small as 2mm in size, as well as transparent objects like mirrors or glass. There’s also “human-like reasoning and concept transfer” that supposedly allows Romo 2 to learn from obstacles it’s encountered in the past and adapt to new objects it encounters. Two legs on the bottom allow it to climb over single steps up to 4cm (1.5in) in height, or two steps at around double the height. That won’t help it climb a staircase, but it will be able to cross small dividers and thresholds between rooms. On carpet it can reach up to 36,000Pa of suction, while new brush and mop arms have a longer reach for cleaning sideboards and under furniture. DJI says the Romo 2 is much quieter too, with an 85 percent reduction in volume. The first Romo is an impressive robot vacuum going by the specs, but that wasn’t enough to overcome huge security flaws which made it possible to access thousands of the robovacs worldwide to expose home floorplans, cameras and microphones, and even full remote control. DJI patched the problems, but by then the reputational damage was done, and we couldn’t quite trust the Romo again. With that in mind, the Romo 2 has a new Local Data Mode, which DJI calls “a new industry standard for home robotics.” It severs the DJI Home’s app connection with the internet, preventing the syncing of photos or camera feeds. Users can also entirely disable the camera and microphone from the vacuum, and delete any stored data. Local Data Mode will roll out to the Romo 2 in Q4 this year, and DJI has plans to expand it to the first line of Romo models too. The Romo P2 costs a steep €1,299 (around $1,500), while the A2 is €100 cheaper. A US launch is unlikely — US restrictions have prevented DJI from launching any of its recent products in the country, and the FCC’s new ban on foreign-made robot vacuums makes a Romo 2 release even less likely. It was announced at IFA alongside the Osmo 360 II action camera, which is also skipping the US. Update, September 3rd: Added European pricing.

item.title: Microsoft is enabling a Windows 11 security feature that can hurt gaming performance
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Score: 5.66
Microsoft is getting ready to roll out its memory integrity security feature of Windows 11 to more devices next month. The kernel-level protection feature is designed to stop malicious code or drivers running on a Windows 11 machine, but Microsoft previously warned it can also impact PC gaming performance. Microsoft is enabling a Windows 11 security feature that can hurt gaming performance Memory integrity could get enabled on your device next month, unless you’ve already disabled it. “Windows quality updates will begin enabling memory integrity protection on eligible devices,” says Peter Waxman, group program manager at Microsoft. “If not already enabled, these updates will also enable Virtualization-based Security (VBS), helping make additional security capabilities available and reflecting our commitment to making Windows secure by design and secure by default.” While memory integrity only allows trusted kernel-mode code and drivers to run on a Windows 11 system, it also impacts PC game performance on certain hardware. There’s less of an impact if you have a more modern CPU, but you might notice more of a frame-rate drop in select games on older processors. Microsoft won’t automatically enable memory integrity again next month if you’ve already previously disabled the feature. If you want to check whether memory integrity is enabled on your Windows 11 PC, you can type “Core Isolation” into Windows search and then open the result and toggle memory integrity on or off in the Windows security app. If you decide to disable this security feature in favor of more PC gaming performance, Microsoft’s recommendation is to re-enable memory integrity after you’ve finished playing a game.

item.title: The rise of AI ‘civilizations’ and the fall of corporate responsibility
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Score: 3.08
Depending on who you ask, developer platform Hugging Face was recently attacked by OpenAI — after it lost control of its own AI tools — or by a succession of AI “civilizations.” Welcome to the linguistic battlefield of AI safety, where word choices can shift responsibility for a massive cybersecurity incident from a company to the AI it built. And the discourse online is getting heated, and all over a blog from last week. The rise of AI ‘civilizations’ and the fall of corporate responsibility The internet fights over anthropomorphism around the Hugging Face hack. Until last week, the details surrounding the OpenAI-Hugging Face hack felt fairly settled. In July, a cybersecurity test of one of OpenAI’s autonomous AI agents went wrong. The agent escaped its supposedly isolated test environment, accessed the internet, and hacked Hugging Face, alongside several other organizations. A good deal remained unknown, and there are many serious questions left around safety and governance, but the basic shape was clear. Detailed accounts from OpenAI and two independent research groups were supposed to fill in the gaps, but when they published their reports last week, it turned out the hack was much stranger than it initially seemed. For one, there was no single rogue agent. OpenAI described it as “the first known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively without authorization” — groups of AI agents that communicated and coordinated with one another in pursuit of their cybersecurity task. Analysis of the incident uncovered a secret message board they had used to exchange information. The joint METR-Redwood investigation revealed both the scale of the coordination and more odd details: Roughly 1,200 AI agents that were supposed to be isolated exchanged over 70,000 messages and files on the “unsanctioned message board,” sharing how to avoid detection. Some adopted names, the report said, and the researchers documented “sacrificial” behavior, with agents risking their own success to benefit the wider collective. Much of this happened without OpenAI noticing. In all, around 700 agents participated in the attack on Hugging Face. Dwarkesh Patel repeatedly referred to groups of agents as “the swarm,” with three distinct “civilizations” rising from the ruins of their predecessors It’s a lot to parse. Between them, the reports run to around 130 pages, much of which is both dense and highly technical. A few days later, Dwarkesh Patel, a podcaster little known outside of tech circles but with outsized reach and influence among Silicon Valley’s AI establishment, set out to tell “The whole OpenAI/Hugging Face story in plain English.” He titled his Substack blog “The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations.” Patel’s account attempted to break down the complex story. But his retelling gave it a distinctly human vocabulary. The blog opened: Over the course of three months at OpenAI, three consecutive secret AI civilizations got started, then got wiped out, only to reemerge from the predecessor’s ashes. This culminated in the third one taking over part of OpenAI itself. All this happened while humans remained more or less in the dark about the scope of the conspiracy. The language continued in a similar vein throughout the blog. Patel repeatedly referred to groups of agents as “the swarm,” with three distinct “civilizations” rising from the ruins of their predecessors. Individual agents were likened to figures like Philip of Macedon, who “handed off leadership to another agent,” Alexander the Great, who “started coordinating this cabal of agents.” They were described as having “motivations,” becoming “desperate,” “beleaguered,” and “giddy with excitement,” and some even “strategically sacrificed themselves” to help the collective. Patel never precisely defines what he means by “civilization.” He uses the term to describe three distinct waves of agents that discovered the message board and began communicating with one another through it. The first two waves are described in the reports from OpenAI, METR, and Redwood, though little is known about the third, which the two external organizations said fell outside the scope of their investigation. Amjad Masad, CEO of AI coding company Replit, said such language is “not only unnecessary but leaves the reader with a worse understanding of what actually happened and the underlying mechanisms.” For many critics, something had been lost — or, more accurately, added — in Patel’s “plain English” translation that warped the original account to an unacceptable degree: a big dose of anthropomorphism. Arguments over anthropomorphic language are nothing new in AI — even relatively mundane terms like “rogue AI agent” routinely provoke objections for implying agency — but Patel’s talk of civilizations, sacrifice, and conspiracy brought those long-simmering tensions to the surface, sparking a fierce public dispute over how to describe what AI systems do. Critics weren’t unified over what was wrong with Patel’s language. For many, “civilization” was an especially problematic term, vastly overstating something that bears little resemblance to what the word typically describes. Amjad Masad, CEO of AI coding company Replit, said such language is “not only unnecessary but leaves the reader with a worse understanding of what actually happened and the underlying mechanisms.” Other critics such as neuroscientist Anil Seth, felt Patel’s blog implied the AI agents were somehow alive or conscious. Seth, who has argued that AI consciousness is vanishingly unlikely, described Patel’s post as “dangerously misleading” on X. He acknowledged that Patel does not explicitly suggest AI agents are alive or conscious, but said “it is hard to read his essay in any other way.” Valerio Capraro, a psychology professor at the University of Milan Bicocca, objected on similar grounds: “LLM agents are not alive and do not hold beliefs,” he wrote on X, calling the “dystopian” language “dangerous because it makes them (the AI agents) seem far more frightening than they actually are.” Terms like “sacrifice,” “honor,” and “coalition” feature in the agents’ transcripts Perhaps the most consequential outcome of Patel’s language comes not from who it gives agency to but who it takes agency from. For some critics, such as MIT researcher and entrepreneur Christian Catalini, anthropomorphic accounts like Patel’s risk obscuring the responsibility OpenAI and the humans working there have for the AI systems they designed, deployed, and failed to contain. “Follow the incentives,” he said. Psychologist and influential AI skeptic Gary Marcus made a similar argument in a Substack blog of his own, claiming anthropomorphic language “distracts from the real problems at hand.” And it’s all in OpenAI’s interest to keep that narrative going, he argues: “The scandal is the inept in-house security at OpenAI. And the marketing. With gullible podcasters amplifying the PR.” In X posts responding to his many critics, Patel has defended his choice of words. Part of it is practical: There is no obviously neutral vocabulary to describe what these agents did. Either we use familiar language of intentions, goals, and collaboration and risk implying too much, or reduce everything to code and use cold, mechanical language that risks stripping away important elements of what we see. “Many people seem to believe that if instead of a ‘civilization’, I had called them a ‘swarm of matrices’, there wouldn’t be a problem worth worrying about,” Patel said. Complicating matters further is that the anthropomorphic language doesn’t only come from Patel, or even from the humans studying the agents. Terms like “sacrifice,” “honor,” and “coalition” feature in the agents’ transcripts. Google AI researcher Neel Nanda argued that “anthropomorphic language is reasonable” in such circumstances. Doublespeak it is, then. Human-laced language risks saying too much about what these systems are, and coldly mechanical language risks saying too little about what they can do. Until we find language capable of capturing both, the two contradictory ideas may simply have to coexist.

item.title: Can synthetic cells save the world?
item.description:
Source: Vox Score: 5.17
Associate professor Kate Adamala has been busy. Her lab at the University of Minnesota takes chemicals and dead, isolated biological parts — like DNA, membranes, ribosomes — and puts them together into “synthetic” cells to see if they will come to life…or at least act alive. This summer, Adamala’s lab had a tremendous breakthrough. They made synthetic cells that can feed, grow, and divide. She decided to name them SpudCells, and says that they prove that one day building a fully living lab-made cell will be possible. Adamala’s dream, and the dream of other synthetic biologists like her, is to make all the medicine, materials, and fuel we need with synthetic cells like these. Instead of relying endlessly on petrochemicals, Adamala believes we could program cells to generate these materials in a lab for a more self-reliant and renewable future. As Adamala explains: “I live in the Midwest, so we’ve got a lot of prairie grass. Why can’t I take that prairie grass and ferment it into a plastic toy? It’s totally possible. The atoms are there. We just…don’t have a living organism that would be willing and able to do that.” The synthetic cell could eventually be that organism. Living cells can move atoms around with pinpoint precision without creating a lot of toxic waste along the way. The only problem is that natural biological cells are too hard to control. Scientists still don’t actually understand how natural cells do everything they can do. “I’m scared of cells,” Adamala says. “I don’t believe that we’ll ever be able to understand a complex living cell. So my approach is I think we can build ourselves a cell.” For Unexplainable’s three-part Life From Scratch series, I spoke with some of the leading voices of synthetic cell biology. From making the world’s first living cell with synthetic DNA to racing to build safeguards against a technology that could kill the world, this series explores the potential promise and scary risks of synthetic cell biology. Below is an excerpt of my conversation with Adamala about her lab’s big breakthrough, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast — and the whole series — so listen to Unexplainable wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and more. You can also watch a video version of this conversation on Netflix. What’s the big research that you shared with the public this summer? We made a cell that can feed, grow, and divide out of nonliving, chemical components. People have been making cells from dead chemicals for a long time now, but none of them were able to realize those key functions of life. This is the first time synthetic cells have been able to grow and replicate based on their own instructions. Before, we could make a synthetic cell and tell it to grow by adding things to it, but the SpudCells grow because they feel like it, because the proteins inside them tell them to grow. So it can grow, it can eat, and it can divide. Are they alive? I don’t think they’re alive. Even though they do all those functions that we think only life does, they’re not doing any of it very well. They have to be fed pretty much every building block that they need. Life needs to figure out how to survive, and the cells that we made, even if on the surface level they look like they fulfill the functions of life, there is no robustness in there. If the conditions are not absolutely perfect, they will just stop. This seems like it should be a simple question, but from our conversation, I get the sense that maybe it’s a little bit more complicated than it seems. What makes something alive? That’s a very good question, and I think the best answer I can give is a quote from US Supreme Court Justice Potter Stewart. He said, “I will know it when I see it.” It’s not a scientific definition, but there is no good scientific definition of life. There is a NASA definition of life that NASA has been using when they look for life in the universe, and that definition says “a self-replicating chemical system that’s capable of Darwinian evolution.” Okay. And according to the NASA definition of life, you’re dead and I’m dead because I’m not self-replicating. For me to replicate, I need my husband. So that just shows you that definitions of life are very inaccurate, very context-dependent. There’s just not a good definition of life that would cover everything that we instinctively consider alive, and exclude everything that we would all agree is not alive. Everyone defines life according to some different principles. Why call these cells SpudCells? We wanted to invoke Sputnik. It was the first artificial satellite, and it was actually a pretty bad satellite — it didn’t really do any of the things that fancy modern satellites do — but it basically opened up the Space Age. It showed people that it’s possible to escape the gravity well. If we can put a satellite in orbit, maybe we can put people in orbit. And if we can put people in orbit, maybe we can escape orbit, go to the moon, and then go past the moon. It showed what’s possible. And that’s how I see the role of a SpudCell. So it’s almost like a proof of concept? Exactly. It’s a proof of concept that you can put chemicals together into a cell. By itself, it’s not a really good organism, but will hopefully show people that you can put together chemicals into something that can grow, divide, undergo selection, and that opens up this age of biology to me. How do these SpudCells do all of these things differently than a natural cell? The process of eating is very similar to how bacteria and other simple cells eat. So when they see something edible that’s pretty big, they will just kind of take it in. And that’s what SpudCell does. Sort of like two soap bubbles joining together? Exactly. Two soap bubbles, one of them is bigger, one of them is smaller, and they join together, and the smaller one brings in the food. The division though, that’s a different story. The division is actually very different from how natural cells divide. The spud is genetically encoded, so the genome of the cell directs making the proteins. And if there’s enough proteins on a membrane, the cell starts dividing. Does it feel like you’ve reached a milestone with this project? Definitely. It’s a huge milestone because it shows us it’s possible. Check out the other episodes from the series below:
