item.title: This iPhone Feature Makes It Much Harder for Thieves to Ruin Your Life
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 5.45
It’s a stomach-dropping scenario: Your phone gets stolen, and all your information is gone along with it. If that hasn’t happened to you already, it may never, thanks to a useful feature in Apple’s iPhones. The feature, called Stolen Device Protection, makes it a lot more difficult for thieves to gain access to your most private information. Here’s what you need to know. How to use Stolen Device Protection Your iPhone likely already has Stolen Device Protection enabled, but you should check to be certain. First, make sure your iPhone is running the latest version of iOS. If you’re not running at least iOS 17.3 you won’t see the option to enable this feature. Then open the Settings app, tap Face ID & Passcode, and toggle on Stolen Device Protection. (If you have an older iPhone with Touch ID, your settings will look different.) With Stolen Device Protection, your iPhone will require additional authentication for the user to access some information, and it will also prevent certain changes if it detects that it isn’t at a trusted location such as your house or your workplace. For example, if you try to change your Apple account password or your phone's passcode when your iPhone isn't at a trusted location, Stolen Device Protection requires you to wait an hour and then authenticate your identity a second time with Face ID or Touch ID. Even if a thief knows the passcode to unlock your iPhone, that delay gives you time to use Apple’s Find My tool to remotely lock or wipe the stolen device. Without the delay, a thief could deactivate the anti-theft and security features using only your iPhone’s passcode. You can also require a one-hour security delay on changes to your Apple account, even if you’re at a familiar location. To activate it, go to the Stolen Device Protection page in Settings, and check Always in the section labeled Require Security Delay. This can guard against malicious activity in familiar locations and prevent accidental changes, for example from handing your phone to a child to play with. Stolen Device Protection also limits what information a thief can access on your iPhone by requiring biometric authentication (Face ID or Touch ID, depending on which iPhone you have) to do things like view saved passwords or make changes to an Apple savings account. This prevents thieves from using your unlocked iPhone to steal your money or open an Apple credit card in your name. This feature may in part be a response to reports of thieves snatching devices after observing iPhone owners logging in with their PIN. According to a report in The Wall Street Journal, iPhone thieves were able to steal money, open credit card accounts, and more once they access the devices. And thieves can completely lock victims out of their Apple accounts, making it very difficult for the victims to disable or track their stolen iPhones with Apple’s Find My feature. Victims are sometimes unable to access their photos and files saved on iCloud as well. Stolen Device Protection makes it harder for thieves to use a stolen iPhone to ruin your life. It might pose an inconvenience for you in some moments, but it’s still worth switching on. It won’t always work at home, though When it launched with iOS 17.3, Stolen Device Protection only applied these enhanced security features when the iPhone was turned on and away from a “familiar location,” which Apple defines as “your home, work, and certain other locations where you regularly use your iPhone.” You have to enable a Significant Locations setting under Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services > System Services > Significant Locations for your iPhone to recognize familiar locations. Your options to view or change familiar locations is limited, but you can easily delete all of them by tapping Clear History at the bottom of the screen. But iOS now gives you the option to always require a security delay, even when you’re at home. It may be more convenient to not encounter these security features while you’re at home. If you go that route, just be aware that if someone in your home knows your passcode, these security measures won’t apply. Other tips to protect your iPhone You can take a few other steps to make your iPhone more secure: Make your passcode longer. If you have only a four-digit pin to unlock your device, change it to a six-digit one or even an alphanumeric passcode. Protect sensitive photos that contain personal information. Delete photos in your camera roll that show important documents, which can help thieves find more personal information about you. If you need quick access to them for some reason, you can instead move them to the Photos app’s hidden album by long-pressing a photo and then selecting Hide. From the Photos section of Settings, you can change whether the hidden album is visible at all, and you can require the use of Face ID to open the hidden album. You can also store photos of documents in a secure online cloud storage service or a password manager. Wherever you put the images, make sure that some kind of authentication—a passcode, Face ID, or the like—is required to view them. Protect individual apps with a PIN or Face ID. Most apps on iPhones don’t often (or ever) require you to log back in; as a result, a thief with an unlocked iPhone can easily access all of your apps. Some apps, especially those related to credit cards and banking, allow you to set an individual PIN or use your face or fingerprint to unlock them. Be sure to switch these settings on. Require Face ID or Touch ID to view saved passwords. Stolen Device Protection requires biometric authentication to use or view your saved passwords or to have the iPhone autofill those logins when you navigate to a site. But you can require that even without Stolen Device Protection: Go to Settings, tap Face ID & Passcode, and toggle on the Password AutoFill option. You can also use a standalone password manager such as our top pick, 1Password, which has many features that built-in password managers can’t match. Enable Find My on your iPhone. If your iPhone is stolen, you can use the Find My app to track it down and disable it remotely. Take some time to try this tool out before you need it in an emergency. This article was edited by Caitlin McGarry. Further reading - by Dave Gershgorn Losing a phone or laptop can throw your life into chaos, but taking a few easy steps before anything happens can turn a catastrophe into a minor inconvenience.

item.title: So, You Want to Start Composting
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 5.14
Listen and follow The Wirecutter Show Apple Podcasts | Spotify | Amazon Music | YouTube | iHeartRadio Before you dump your vegetable peels and coffee grounds into the trash, consider the many reasons to compost. Keeping food waste out of landfills reduces greenhouse-gas emissions, and nutrient-rich compost helps to sequester carbon and rejuvenates soil. You’ll also likely need to empty your regular trash less frequently. For many people, the biggest barrier to composting is simply getting started. In this episode, Wirecutter sustainability editor Katie Okamoto shares practical tips for collecting kitchen food scraps, navigating composting options without municipal pickup, and understanding what actually belongs in your bin — including why you might want to skip those biodegradable liner bags. Plus, Wirecutter staff members break down their own real-world setups. They share how to manage commercial pickup services and why “compostable” plastics don’t work in backyard bins, and they outline strategies for keeping odors at bay. This episode covers - Composting options for every space: If you don’t have municipal green-bin pickup, you can use private commercial services, drop off scraps at community gardens or farmers markets, or even try the “cardboard box method” to compost slowly inside your home. - Backyard composting 101: A successful pile requires a balance of “greens” (fresh food waste) and “browns” (dry leaves, paper, or cardboard). - Strategies for collecting food scraps: You don’t need a special bin. Wide-mouthed mixing bowls or restaurant Cambro bins work well. - The freezer scrap method: Keeping a squishable storage bag in your freezer to collect vegetable peels and eggshells eliminates odors, saves counter space, and makes it easy to tote scraps to a drop-off site. Products we recommend A stainless steel option with a replaceable charcoal filter, this bin is sleek, sturdy, easy to clean, and less expensive than similar styles. Note that you need to buy the right-size filters online. If you prefer the flexibility and portability of a bag, this nylon tote is lightweight, washable, and squishable, so it can fit in the freezer. DEAL, original price $46, sale price $28 from Nordstrom Rack (pack of three), opens in a new tab With store pickup (fancy animals) A workhorse in professional kitchens, this low-maintenance container has a tight-fitting lid and a square base that allows it to fit efficiently into corners of a freezer, fridge, or countertop. Additional reading Episode transcript CHRISTINE: I’m Christine Cyr Clisset, and you’re listening to The Wirecutter Show. Hey there. If you cook a lot, if you’re trying to reduce the food waste in your regular garbage, or if you’re concerned with being kinder to the environment, you may compost, and if you don’t, maybe you aspire to. This episode, I’m talking with Wirecutter’s sustainability editor, Katie Okamoto, about how to get started composting. We’re talking about the best containers to use for gathering food scraps, what you can safely put in your compost, and strategies for making it easier and tidier. We’ll hear some voice memos from our staff who have compost piles in their backyards or elsewhere on their property. We’ll also link to a guide we have for outdoor composting in the show notes. CHRISTINE: Katie, welcome back to the show. KATIE: I’m so happy to be here. CHRISTINE: We are talking about gathering food scraps for composting. There’s so many different ways to compost, but today we’re going to talk about what to do in your kitchen, because I think this can be a little bit tricky for some people. First of all, though, I want to ask, what is the argument to compost? Why should someone compost if they’re not currently composting? Why should they consider doing it? What are the environmental impacts of composting, essentially? KATIE: Composting is basically a method to create a nutrient-rich material out of organic waste, so food scraps, right? And food waste is a major contributor to greenhouse-gas emissions, actually. What you’re doing with composting is, you’re taking that food waste that would normally be bound for, say, a landfill and turning it into this material that sequesters carbon and can be used to grow other produce. So it kind of gets put back into the soil and into the nutrient cycle. In a landfill, what happens is that it will decompose, it’ll release methane, which is a really potent greenhouse gas. And more food is coming into landfills in the United States than any other material in the solid-waste stream, which is significant. On an individual level, the average American household can be tossing a couple pounds of food a week. I will add the caveat that if we’re kind of looking at the big context of our individual carbon emissions, if that’s something that you’re concerned about, food waste is not the biggest contributor in your diet; it’s actually cutting back on meat and dairy. But composting and reducing food waste in general is a really powerful thing that we can all do as individuals, and a lot of municipalities are now requiring. In Los Angeles, where I live, and in New York as well, they’re now requiring a lot of households to put “green waste,” as it’s called, into the municipal composting system to reduce the emissions from food waste. CHRISTINE: I think that’s so interesting to think about the bigger impact, because various people compost for different reasons. I have family members who compost just because they don’t want all that in their regular garbage. It means they have to take their garbage out less. But just thinking about your overall impact on the planet, it’s obviously important. I want to talk a little bit about the options, if you don’t have the option to just take out your scraps to a garbage can in front of your home. But before you and I get into the options, we actually have a voice memo from our colleague who uses a local service that comes and picks up her compost. Let’s listen. ANNEMARIE: Hello. I’m Annemarie Conte, deputy editor at Wirecutter, and we use a commercial composting service. We used to backyard-compost, but now we really like the service, because we can include things like meat or animal bones, things that you really don’t want to put in a backyard compost, because it takes a long time to break down, or because you don’t want to attract pests like, I don’t know, bears. We really love it. They come weekly, they pick up all of our food scraps, and then every few months we get a bag of compost in return. And it’s just been really great. So there might be one in your area. I would encourage you to check it out. The costs vary depending on what service you have, but we find it to be something that we can absolutely budget for. CHRISTINE: So Annemarie just spoke about a private company that does this pickup service that she signed on for. For other people who don’t have municipal pickup or don’t have access to a private service like this, what are some options that they could look into for composting? KATIE: Yeah. It’s easiest, potentially, to drop off. You could certainly look for a community garden, if you happen to have those in your area. Sometimes those are available, and you can bring compost even to the farmers market, if that’s available to you. So even if you don’t have municipal composting through your city or town, sometimes there are options to not have to do the composting yourself. But a lot of people do find composting at home rewarding. There are a lot of resources about various methods of composting, but they very broadly can break down into inside or outside. That’s number one. So if you have space in your yard, or you have a yard to begin with, which I don’t, there are backyard-composting options that might look like creating a pile where you bury food scraps and keep them covered with a layer of soil. I might be using a bin that’s above ground. There are also these above-ground tumblers that kind of make the mixing a little bit easier. There are advantages and disadvantages to all of these methods, but there’s also ways that you can actually compost inside at a smaller scale. And that might seem a little strange, but Hiroko Tabuchi, who covers climate for The New York Times, has written about having a box method in her apartment in New York City. So this is a method where you put food scraps into a cardboard box, mix it with “browns” or sort of drier organic material, and that is actually a way of making compost slowly in your own home. It actually doesn’t have a smell, if you mix it frequently enough. Some people also get into worm bins, but that’s a little bit higher-maintenance and a bigger commitment for home use. So yeah, I think there’s actually a plethora of options that you can consider depending on your lifestyle, your amount of space that’s available to you, and the amount of fresh fruit and produce that you’re going through on a daily or weekly basis. CHRISTINE: That’s good to know, that there are lots and lots of options, if you are really committed to composting, and you don’t have that drop-off method in the front of your home. So I am so curious about this one: Is there a general rule about what you can and can’t put into a compost bin? Does it just depend on where you live and the compost method you’re using? KATIE: Yeah. I mean, certainly on a municipal level, if you’re doing pickup in a green bin, or you are dropping off to, say, a community garden or a farmers market, they will have rules that you can check, and they often will prohibit certain items. It really depends on what their composting method is. If you’re composting at home, it does a little bit depend on your circumstances. I’ve spoken with sources. Cass Marketos is one person who’s, like, a composting expert here in LA. She maintains that if it’s organic — meaning, made of previously living material — that it’s compostable, technically, but there are certain things that you may want to avoid, either because they’re more likely to attract pests or because it can just take a lot longer and require more monitoring of the heat in your compost pile. So avoiding things like meat, dairy, bread, things that are sugary. But generally a good rule of thumb is that you want to have a mixture of what they call “greens,” so think lettuce, apples, basically produce that’s fresh, and “browns,” so things like dry leaves, yard waste, even torn-up pieces of paper. And this mixture will allow for the kind of ideal moisture levels and nutrient levels for the microorganisms that create compost to thrive and do their magic. And I will say one thing that helps is “prepping your inputs.” What that means is chopping up and preparing your food scraps so that they’re smaller. That can really help to prevent just huge hunks of food from sitting in a compost pile for months or even longer than that; it’ll prolong the composting process, but it may also attract animals. So if you chop it up, it’s kind of like chewing, right? When you chew your food, it helps you digest. When you chop up the greens, the fruits, whatever it is that you’re putting into the compost pile in your yard, you’re helping the process of breaking it down. CHRISTINE: We have another tip from one of our colleagues, who composts in her backyard, about something else to keep out of your compost. Let’s listen. ROSE: Hi, this is Rose Lorre. I’m a senior staff writer, and I’ve been very thrilled to write a bunch of stories for Wirecutter about composting over the years. Please remember that any consumable good that’s labeled or certified as compostable — a dog-poop bag, cutlery made out of plant-based plastic, what have you — is not compostable in a home-composting setup. No matter what kind of DIY setup you have, it’s almost definitely not going to generate enough heat for long enough to fully break down those materials. A large-scale commercial or industrial composting facility can sustain temperatures as high as 160 or 165 degrees Fahrenheit, for days or weeks on end, but a small backyard compost pile probably won’t ever get that hot, and if it does, it won’t stay that way long enough. I am likewise not thrilled to tell you that something like a compostable fork that’s made out of bioplastics likely won’t be accepted in your local recycling, although you should check with your municipality to make sure of that. So opt for reusable cutlery and similar products as much as you can, and even if it’s existentially painful for you to do so, please dispose of used compostable dog-poop bags in the regular trash. CHRISTINE: Katie, you wrote a guide to the best compost bins for collecting food scraps in the kitchen. You and I worked on this piece a long time ago, and you’ve been updating it. And because of this piece that you worked on, I actually stopped using the compost bin I was using in my kitchen, which was, like, a plastic bin with a lid, and I transitioned to using a big metal mixing bowl because it was easier to empty, and I feel like you gave me permission to do this. What is your advice for picking a compost bin that you’re using in your kitchen? KATIE: So these kinds of buckets or vessels are ways of collecting food waste as you’re cooking and then sort of stashing it or stowing it until you decant that vessel into either your backyard composting system or a green bin or taking it wherever you take it. I’m so happy to hear that you changed to a bowl, because I think the takeaway from testing compost buckets for a home storage is really that you don’t need something that’s marketed for composting specifically. Anything works. There are really so few barriers to collecting the food that you’re prepping. For me, a wide-mouthed vessel like a mixing bowl is just more intuitive; I feel like I can scrape my cutting board more easily into that vessel. But some people really like having something that has a lid. Of course, if you have a mixing bowl, you can always place a plate on it or put some cloth over it to keep it contained. But lids, some of them have a carbon filter that helps manage odors. I live in LA, I don’t have central air conditioning, it gets really hot in the summer, and I’ve found that really the best way to reduce smells or prevent fruit flies is, there’s two things. First is try not to put a lot of produce in there. Try not to waste food. So reducing food waste will reduce the amount of compost-bound produce you need to deal with. But also just emptying that vessel frequently enough. It depends on where you are, but I find that I have to empty it every day instead of just kind of keeping it and letting it acquire that kind of liquidiness. Another method is putting it in the freezer, if you have the space. CHRISTINE: Ooh, I like that one. And we actually have a tip from one of our staffers about this exact method. Let’s listen. ANTARA: This is Antara, I’m a writer on the kitchen team. And my tip, especially if you live in a small space or don’t compost in your own home, is to freeze your food scraps. So I collect veggie peels, eggshells, other compostable food scraps in a gallon food-storage bag throughout the week in the freezer, and that way, when it’s full, it usually takes me about a week or two. I can drop it off on my neighborhood compost site, and then this way I don’t have to worry about any smells or take up any counter or floor space with a compost bin. CHRISTINE: Okay, I think this is a great option. Katie, what would you recommend using in the freezer? Antara is using a bag. Is this the best way to do it? What are your best tips here? KATIE: Yeah, of course, it depends on your freezer, and it depends on what you keep in your freezer on a regular basis. So the freezer is actually a really great tool in the kitchen to reduce food waste in general, because you can freeze extras, and then that reduces the amount of stuff you’re having to toss or compost. But I do really like a bag, because bags are squishable, so they can kind of fit into the door, they can fit into weird nooks and crannies. I mentioned that I use a mixing bowl like you, Christine, but I sometimes will kind of do a double method, where I’ll collect the scraps while I’m cooking, and then I’ll toss them into a bag in the freezer for emptying later on, so it’s not just sitting there. I know other staffers use compost bins that they find that just fit really neatly inside. I’ve also used, like, a Cambro before, which … they’re used in restaurant kitchens a lot. They’re like a plastic kind of Tupperware-type bin. And because they have really nice, tight right angles, they don’t take up a lot of space, they’re more efficient. But anything is good. I do really recommend a bag. Don’t overthink it. You can also then tote that bag to wherever you’re going. You don’t have to hold something that’s super cold. CHRISTINE: Is there anything else to think about if you’re … any kind of bin that you’re going to use, whether it has a lid or not? What should you be thinking about here? KATIE: Yeah, I think a lot of it does come down to knowing thyself, as they say. So if you use a lot of produce, you want something probably that’s a little bit bigger. I think about the opening of the vessel, so I want something that’s not so narrow and tiny that scooping scraps into it feels tedious and finicky. I also look for vessels that have a smoother interior, don’t have a lot of kind of weird edges or molded plastic pieces that can be harder to clean out, because I do recommend that you forgo a compost liner. So things like that, kind of like the practicalities of how are you going to clean this thing. I do prefer compost bins that are reusable, obviously, meaning that you already have them in your home, but if you’re going to go out and buy one, stainless steel is going to last a lot longer in the long run than plastic. So that’s just something to consider. CHRISTINE: We’re going to take a quick break, and when we’re back, Katie, we’re going to talk about some tips for keeping compost neat and odor-free. We’ll be right back. CHRISTINE: Welcome back. Katie, I want to return to something that we talked about in the first half of this episode, whether or not it’s okay to use a plastic bag in your compost bin. I know from editing you that you don’t love this option, but I do know that my neighbors, and even I’ve kind of gone back to using a biodegradable bag, because it just makes it easier to take out into the compost bin. What are the pros and cons? What should people be thinking about if they’re using a liner in their compost? KATIE: Yeah, I mean, primarily from a practical standpoint, you should make sure that the compost system that you are feeding into will accept these compostable liners. They also are not necessary. I understand the sort of desire to make it easier to tote things, and I also think mentally it feels cleaner. I have found in my own personal experience that they get sort of, like, waterlogged quite quickly, and they end up being drippy anyway. So rather than doing that, you might reuse just a straight-up plastic bag or even a paper bag and just use that and empty it and reuse it multiple times rather than going out and buying compostable liners. If you are going to get one, you should look for the BPI logo on the product. So that stands for Biodegradable Products Institute. This certification, it’s from a nonprofit organization that issues a compostability certification that’s considered the gold standard in the United States. They prohibit the addition of PFAS, and they just have certain requirements that it’s going to completely and safely compost in municipal and commercial facilities. And just know, I would point you to Rose’s reporting here too, on Wirecutter’s site; she’s done a lot of research into this. There are often petrochemicals that are used to mix into the plant-based plastics for these bags to help them be pliable, to give them a little bit of give. So there’s just a few caveats in using these bags. CHRISTINE: We talked a little bit before the break about ways to reduce odor. Freezing is one way. Emptying it often, I think you mentioned. But is there anything else that will help you reduce odor? KATIE: You can also try using a bin that has a built-in carbon filter. Some of the bins that we recommend on our site have that, but they’re fairly common, and those filters can be washed and reused a couple more times than they claim. Those still need to be brought out and dumped, though, to manage odor, ultimately. That filter won’t preserve you in the depths of August for weeks and weeks. You still do need to empty the compost bucket. And I would say that if there’s anybody listening who feels hesitant about composting, and it’s because of the odor factor, it actually can help reduce smells in your kitchen, because you’re taking the stuff that decomposes out of your kitchen rather than letting it sit in a hot trash can with your other waste. You may actually find that it reduces smells in the long run. CHRISTINE: Ooh, I like that. Okay, I think we have to talk about cleaning compost bins, because these can get gross. So we have some advice from one of our colleagues, Ciara Murray Johnson. Let’s listen. CIARA: Hi, I’m Ciara. I’m a writer on the kitchen team at Wirecutter, and I wrote our guide to cleaning trash cans and compost bins. One of the best ways to avoid a stinky compost bin is regular maintenance. Take your compost out regularly, spray the bin down with a 1:1 mix of white vinegar and water, and always let the bin dry before using it again. If you can, it also helps to avoid adding warm food scraps to the bin. CHRISTINE: Okay. Katie, anything you would add to Ciara’s advice here? KATIE: Yeah. I mean, if the bin is dishwasher-safe, you can also throw it in the dishwasher. Old-school washing by hand using dish soap and water also works. You just want to try to get it to dry completely before you start to reuse it. If it’s a bigger bin — sometimes people use big buckets if they really have a lot of produce — same thing kind of goes for that, as well. But yeah, unfortunately, sometimes it is just a matter of cleaning regularly. CHRISTINE: Oh, that’s always the answer, right? KATIE: I know. CHRISTINE: Okay. One last category of products I want to talk about. What about countertop composters? These are also called indoor food recyclers. What’s the deal with these? KATIE: These were advertised a couple years ago as “countertop composters,” and they’ve actually seemed to have pivoted more to “food recyclers,” like you mentioned, Christine, and the reason for that is because what they produce is not technically compost. It’s dehydrated, broken-down food scraps. That’s not a bad thing per se, but it is not compost. It’s just food-scrap material that is drier. So these are countertop electronic devices that will take food scraps, and they’ll dehydrate them, they’ll make this material. One advantage to this for some people is that it makes the volume of the food waste smaller, and these dehydrated food scraps can either be added to a compost pile, they reduce the volume of your trash, you can kind of save them until you add them to home composting and other methods. But they are not themselves compost, and so they’re not doing the same kind of carbon sequestration off the bat. You’re not going to be able to add them to get the benefits of compost for plants and your garden. We tested these a few years ago, and we came out feeling like they were not worth the squeeze. They’re expensive. They’ll eventually go kaput, and then it’s e-waste. And when I say “expensive,” they’re often, like, hundreds of dollars, but for some people, maybe it’s worth it. CHRISTINE: All right. We’ve got one more tip from our colleague about a favorite way of dealing with food waste. Let’s take a quick listen. SAMANTHA: Hi, this is Samantha Schoech, I’m a gifts writer at Wirecutter. And for the first 10 years of my twins’ life, we kept chickens in our backyard in San Francisco and had this whole compost circle-of-life thing going, whereby we used our big plastic composter and then used all that beautiful compost that came out to fertilize our veggie beds, and then grew veggies and fed them to our children, who then did not eat them, and we would use their scraps to feed the chickens, and then the chickens would make us eggs. And the whole beautiful circle of life would start all over again. The whole thing just made me feel a lot better about all the food my kids wasted. KATIE: I love that. CHRISTINE: Well, Katie, thank you so much for joining today. KATIE: Thank you so much for having me. I hope everyone starts composting. CHRISTINE: Yes. The Wirecutter Show is executive produced by Rosie Guerin and produced by Abigail Keel. Engineering support from Maddy Masiello and Nick Pitman. Today’s episode was mixed by Catherine Anderson. Original music by Dan Powell, Marian Lozano, Rowan Niemisto, Catherine Anderson, and Diane Wong. Cliff Levy is Wirecutter’s deputy publisher and general manager. Ben Frumin is Wirecutter’s editor-in-chief. I’m Christine Cyr Clisset. Thanks for listening. Credits The Wirecutter Show is executive produced by Rosie Guerin and produced by Abigail Keel. Engineering support from Maddy Masiello and Nick Pitman. Episodes are mixed by Catherine Anderson, Efim Shapiro, Rowan Niemisto, Sophia Lanman, and Sonia Herrero. Original music by Dan Powell, Marion Lozano, Elisheba Ittoop, Catherine Anderson, Rowan Niemisto and Diane Wong. Wirecutter’s deputy publisher and general manager is Cliff Levy. Ben Frumin is Wirecutter’s editor-in-chief. Hosted by Rosie Guerin, Caira Blackwell, and Christine Cyr Clisset. Meet your guides Christine Cyr Clisset Christine Cyr Clisset is the special projects director for Wirecutter, and co-host of The Wirecutter Show podcast. She previously edited cookbooks and craft books for Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia, and she started reviewing kitchen gear back in 2013. She sews many of her own clothes, which has made her obsessive about high-quality fabrics—whether in a dress or bedsheets. Wirecutter’s podcast features interviews with journalists from our newsroom about their reporting and testing. I help choose what the podcast will cover and edit the episodes that appear on the show. I also read the emails that listeners send to the show to make sure we investigate their biggest questions and concerns. I focus on the intersections of shopping, sustainability, and environmental health. I also lead and advise on standards for reporting on environmental impacts and green marketing claims of products in Wirecutter’s coverage. I write the Ask Wirecutter advice column, review trending products, and dig into product-focused investigations. Whenever possible, I like to offer free fixes, low-cost solutions, and bigger investments so that readers can decide which option works best for them. I write about what is worth buying, what is overhyped junk, and everything in between. Rose Maura Lorre Unlike many of my colleagues, my job isn’t about being an expert in one product category. Instead, I write about how to get the most value, longevity, and enjoyment out of the stuff you already own (or are thinking about buying) across all of our product categories. One day I might interview a dermatologist about the pros and cons of lanolin, and the next I might smoke a turkey with the founder of New York Times Cooking. Antara Sinha is an associate staff writer reporting on cooking and kitchen gear at Wirecutter. She was previously at Bon Appétit, Food & Wine, and Cooking Light, and she has over seven years of experience writing about food, drink, and culture. She considers herself an ice cream connoisseur and believes the Chipwich to be a perfect food. Ciara Murray Jordan Ciara Murray Jordan is a writer on the kitchen team at Wirecutter. She previously worked as an artisanal cheesemaker on a small farm in Vermont. Samantha Schoech I discover, vet, and write about gifts of all kinds from my office in San Francisco. I am particularly drawn to all things shiny or bookish, but I try not to impose my taste more than is strictly necessary.
